The same postpositions can also take the reflexive-possessive suffix. In this case the latter indicates that the object designated by the word governed by the postposition belongs to the person acting :
<uig rom="toluγai deger-e-ben talbiba">ᠲᠣᠯᠤᠭᠠᠢ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ ᠡ ᠎ᠪᠡᠨ ᠲᠠᠯᠪᠢᠪᠠ</uig> He put (it) on his (own) head.

The postpositions governing various oblique cases will be given in the respective sections where the cases are discussed. Only such postpositions as govern the simple stem will be mentioned here. Postpositions governing the simple stem are the following:
<uig rom="deger-e">ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ᠎ᠡ</uig> on:
<uig rom="aγula deger-e">ᠠᠭᠤᠯᠠ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ ᠡ</uig> on the mountain
<uig rom="nama deger-e">ᠨᠠᠮᠠ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ᠎ᠡ</uig> on me
<uig rom="tegün deger-e">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ᠎ᠡ</uig> on him
<uig rom="door-a">ᠳᠣᠣᠷ᠎ᠠ</uig> under:
<uig rom="γajar door-a">ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ ᠳᠣᠣᠷ᠎ᠠ</uig> under the earth
<uig rom="dotor-a">ᠳᠣᠲᠣᠷ᠎ᠠ</uig> in:
<uig rom="ger dotor-a">ᠭᠡᠷ ᠳᠣᠲᠣᠷ᠎ᠠ</uig> in the house
<uig rom="γarui">ᠭᠠᠷᠤᠢ</uig> exceeding, more than:
<uig rom="arba γarui">ᠠᠷᠪᠠ ᠭᠠᠷᠤᠢ</uig> more than ten

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - General remarks

paragraphs.paragraph: There are two categories of groups of juxtaposed nouns:
a) juxtaposed nouns constituting a compound word serving as a single part of sentence
b) juxtaposed nouns mutually independent and serving as two or more equal parts of sentence.

The difference between these two categories can be easily discovered by eliminating one of the two nouns from such groups : while the elimination of a noun from a group of the former category results in another word, the elimination of a member from a group of the latter category merely transforms a sentence with two equal members into a sentence with one member: e. g., instead of two direct objects there will be but one. This can be illustrated by the following examples:

<uig rom="γajar usun">ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ ᠤᠰᠤᠨ</uig> "territory" consists of two words : <uig rom="γajar">ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ</uig> "earth" and <uig rom="usun">ᠤᠰᠤᠨ</uig> "water" ; the sentence <uig rom="γajar usun-i anu buliyaju abuba">ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ ᠤᠰᠤᠨ ᠢ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠪᠤᠯᠢᠶᠠᠵᠤ ᠠᠪᠤᠪᠠ</uig> means "He took their territory." If we eliminate the word <uig rom="γajar">ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ</uig> "earth" the sentence <uig rom="usun-i anu buliyaju abuba">ᠤᠰᠤᠨ ᠢ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠪᠤᠯᠢᠶᠠᠵᠤ ᠠᠪᠤᠪᠠ</uig> means "He took their water." On the other hand,

<uig rom="ger mal-i inu buliyaju abuba">ᠭᠡᠷ ᠮᠠᠯ ᠢ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠪᠤᠯᠢᠶᠠᠵᠤ ᠠᠪᠤᠪᠠ</uig> means "He took his house and cattle." If we eliminate the word <uig rom="ger">ᠭᠡᠷ</uig> "house" the sentence <uig rom="mal-i inu buliyaju abuba">ᠮᠠᠯ ᠢ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠪᠤᠯᠢᠶᠠᠵᠤ ᠠᠪᠤᠪᠠ</uig> means "He took his cattle." The examples given above show that a compound word like <uig rom="γajar usun">ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ ᠤᠰᠤᠨ</uig> "territory" becomes something quite different, if one of the elements is eliminated, while, on the other hand, the sentence only loses one of its two objects if <uig rom="ger">ᠭᠡᠷ</uig> is eliminated from the compound <uig rom="ger mal">ᠭᠡᠷ ᠮᠠᠯ</uig>.

Both categories possess the common trait that only the last noun of a group takes the requisite case ending. Thus, if there are two or more nouns standing in a dative-locative relation to the governing word, only the last of them takes the dative-locative suffix. The same is true of all oblique cases. Thus, in Mongolian, a case suffix can refer to a whole group of words. This resembles, to some degree, such algebraic expressions as n(a+b) instead of an+bn. For example, <uig rom="tegün-ü ger mal keüked ekener-i abuba">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠤ ᠭᠡᠷ ᠮᠠᠯ ᠺᠡᠦᠺᠡᠳ ᠡᠺᠡᠨᠡᠷ ᠢ ᠠᠪᠤᠪᠠ</uig> "He took his house, cattle, children, and wife." Here the accusacive suffix refers to a whole group : tegün-ü + (ger mal keüked ekener)-i + abuba, i. e., to all words put in parentheses.

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Compound nouns

paragraphs.paragraph: In compound numbers the higher numbers are followed by the lower ones as in English: <uig rom="qorin tabun">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ</uig> "twenty-five." The number of hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, hundred thousands, and millions is expressed by numerals placed before the numerals <uig rom="jaγun">ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ</uig> "hundred," <uig rom="mingγan">ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> "thousand," <uig rom="tümen">ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> "ten thousand," <uig rom="bum">ᠪᠤᠮ</uig> "hundred thousand," and so on.
All numerala ending in the consonant n keep it, when followed by other numerals.
<uig rom="arban nigen">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ</uig> eleven
<uig rom="qorin tabun">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ</uig> twenty-five ,
In the modern language the numerals <uig rom="nigen">ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ</uig> "one" and <uig rom="mingγan">ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> "thousand" often drop their final n when followed by other numerals.
<uig rom="nige mingγan">ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> one thousand
<uig rom="mingγa tabun jayun">ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠵᠠᠶᠤᠨ</uig> thousand five hundred
The numeral <uig rom="nigen">ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ</uig> "one" can be omitted in such expressions as:
100 <uig rom="jaγun">ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ</uig> instead of <uig rom="nige jayun">ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠵᠠᠶᠤᠨ</uig>
1,000 <uig rom="mingγan">ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> instead of <uig rom="nige mingγan">ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
100,000 <uig rom="bum">ᠪᠤᠮ</uig> instead of <uig rom="nige bum">ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠪᠤᠮ</uig>

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Compound nouns

paragraphs.paragraph: The numerals 11-19 are composed of <uig rom="arban">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ</uig> "ten" and the respective units.
11 <uig rom="arban nigen">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ</uig>
12 <uig rom="arban qoyar">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ</uig>
13 <uig rom="arban γurban">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ</uig>
14 <uig rom="arban dörben">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ</uig>
15 <uig rom="arban tabun">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ</uig>
16 <uig rom="arban jirγuγan">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠵᠢᠷᠭᠤᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
17 <uig rom="arban doloγan">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠳᠣᠯᠣᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
18 <uig rom="arban naiman">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠨᠠᠢᠮᠠᠨ</uig>
19 <uig rom="arban yisün">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠶᠢᠰᠦᠨ</uig>

The numerals 21-29, 31-39, 41-49, and so on consist of the numerals <uig rom="qorin">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ</uig> "twenty," <uig rom="γucin">ᠭᠤᠴᠢᠨ</uig> "thirty," <uig rom="döcin">ᠳᠥᠴᠢᠨ</uig> "forty," and so on and the respective units.
21 <uig rom="qorin nigen">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ</uig>
22 <uig rom="qorin qoyar">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ</uig>
23 <uig rom="qorin γurban">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ</uig>
24 <uig rom="qorin dörben">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ</uig>
25 <uig rom="qorin tabun">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ</uig>
26 <uig rom="qorin jirγuγan">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠵᠢᠷᠭᠤᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
27 <uig rom="qorin doloγan">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠳᠣᠯᠣᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
28 <uig rom="qorin naiman">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠨᠠᠢᠮᠠᠨ</uig>
29 <uig rom="qorin yisün">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠶᠢᠰᠦᠨ</uig>
31 <uig rom="γucin nigen">ᠭᠤᠴᠢᠨ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ</uig>
45 <uig rom="döcin tabun">ᠳᠥᠴᠢᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ</uig>
51 <uig rom="tabin nigen">ᠲᠠᠪᠢᠨ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ</uig>
62 <uig rom="jiran qoyar">ᠵᠢᠷᠠᠨ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ</uig>
73 <uig rom="dalan γurban">ᠳᠠᠯᠠᠨ ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ</uig>
84 <uig rom="nayan dörben">ᠨᠠᠶᠠᠨ ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ</uig>
85 <uig rom="nayan tabun">ᠨᠠᠶᠠᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ</uig>
86 <uig rom="nayan jirγuγan">ᠨᠠᠶᠠᠨ ᠵᠢᠷᠭᠤᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
87 <uig rom="nayan doloγan">ᠨᠠᠶᠠᠨ ᠳᠣᠯᠣᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
88 <uig rom="nayan naiman">ᠨᠠᠶᠠᠨ ᠨᠠᠢᠮᠠᠨ</uig>
89 <uig rom="nayan yisün">ᠨᠠᠶᠠᠨ ᠶᠢᠰᠦᠨ</uig>
91 <uig rom="yiren nigen">ᠶᠢᠷᠡᠨ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ</uig>
99 <uig rom="yiren yisün">ᠶᠢᠷᠡᠨ ᠶᠢᠰᠦᠨ</uig>

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Compound nouns

paragraphs.paragraph: The numerals 200, 300, 400, 500, 2,000, 3,000, 4,000, 5,000, and so on are composed of the respective units and the words <uig rom="jaγun">ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ</uig> "hundred" and <uig rom="mingγan">ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> "thousand."

100 ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ or ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ

200 ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ

300 ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ

400 ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ

500 ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ

600 ᠵᠢᠷᠭᠤᠭᠠᠨ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ

700 ᠳᠣᠯᠣᠭᠠᠨ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ

800 ᠨᠠᠢᠮᠠᠨ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ

900 ᠶᠢᠰᠦᠨ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ

1000 ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ or ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ

2000 ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ

3000 ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ

4000 ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ

5000 ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ

6000 ᠵᠢᠷᠭᠤᠭᠠᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ

7000 ᠳᠣᠯᠣᠭᠠᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ

8000 ᠨᠠᠢᠮᠠᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ

9000 ᠶᠢᠰᠦᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Compound nouns

paragraphs.paragraph: The word expressing the concept of "ten thousand" is <uig rom="tümen">ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ.</uig> . Combined with the numerals <uig rom="nigen">ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ,</uig> , <uig rom="qoyar">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ,</uig> , <uig rom="γurban">ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ,</uig> , and so on, this expresses the concepts of "ten thousand," "twenty thousand," "thirty thousand," and so on. But the same concepts can be also expressed by the numerals <uig rom="arban">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ,</uig> , <uig rom="qorin">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ,</uig> , <uig rom="γucin">ᠭᠤᠴᠢᠨ,</uig> , and so on, and <uig rom="mingγan">ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> "thousand." Thus there are two systems: either two ten-thousand (tümen) or twenty thousand (mingγan).
10,000 <uig rom="tümen">ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="nige tümen">ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="arban mingγan">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
20,000 <uig rom="qoyar tümen">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="qorin mingγan">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
30,000 <uig rom="γurban tümen">ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="γucin mingγan">ᠭᠤᠴᠢᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
40,000 <uig rom="dörben tümen">ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="döcin mingγan">ᠳᠥᠴᠢᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
50,000 <uig rom="tabun tümen">ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="tabin mingγan">ᠲᠠᠪᠢᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
60,000 <uig rom="jirγuγan tümen">ᠵᠢᠷᠭᠤᠭᠠᠨ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="jiran mingγan">ᠵᠢᠷᠠᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ.</uig> .
70,000 <uig rom="doloγan tümen">ᠳᠣᠯᠣᠭᠠᠨ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="dalan mingγan">ᠳᠠᠯᠠᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
80,000 <uig rom="naiman tümen">ᠨᠠᠢᠮᠠᠨ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="nayan mingγan">ᠨᠠᠶᠠᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
90,000 <uig rom="yisün tümen">ᠶᠢᠰᠦᠨ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="yiren mingγan">ᠶᠢᠷᠡᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig>

Numbers such as 12,000, 15,000, and so on are expressed by the word <uig rom="tümen">ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> "ten thousand" and the respective thousand or by the numerals twelve, fifteen, and so on, and <uig rom="mingγan">ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> "thousand."
11,000 <uig rom="tümen nige mingγan">ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> nige or <uig rom="arban nige mingγan">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ</uig>
12,000 <uig rom="nige tümen qoyar mingγan">ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="arban qoyar mingγan">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ</uig>
13,000 <uig rom="nige tümen γurban mingγan">ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="arban γurban mingγan">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
14,000 <uig rom="nige tümen dörben mingγan">ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="arban dörben mingγan">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
15,000 <uig rom="nige tümen tabun mingγan">ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="arban tabun mingγan">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ</uig>
In the same manner, numbers such as 24,000, 36,000, and so on, can be expressed either by <uig rom="tümen">ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="mingγan">ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> with the respective numerals
25,000 <uig rom="qoyar tümen tabun mingγan">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="qoyar qorin tabun mingγan">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig>
32,000 <uig rom="γurban tümen qoyar mingγan">ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="γucin qoyar mingγan">ᠭᠤᠴᠢᠨ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig>

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Compound nouns

paragraphs.paragraph: The hundred thousands can be expressed in two different manners: with the numerals 200, 300, etc. and <uig rom="mingγan">ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> "thousand" or with the numerals two, three, and so on, and the Tibetan word <uig rom="bum">ᠪᠤᠮ</uig> hbum "hundred-thousand."
200,000 <uig rom="qoyar jaγun mingγan">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="qoyar bum">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠪᠤᠮ</uig>
300,000 <uig rom="γurban jaγun mingγan">ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="γurban bum">ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠪᠤᠮ</uig>
500,000 <uig rom="tabun jaγun mingγan">ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="tabun bum">ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠪᠤᠮ</uig>

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Compound nouns

paragraphs.paragraph: Only the last word of such groups takes the necessary grammatical ending:
<uig rom="arban doloduγar">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠳᠣᠯᠣᠳᠤᠭᠠᠷ</uig> the seventeenth
<uig rom="arban yisüdüger">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠶᠢᠰᠦᠳᠦᠭᠡᠷ</uig> the nineteenth
<uig rom="qorin tabuduγar">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠳᠤᠭᠠᠷ</uig> the twenty-fifth
<uig rom="mingγan tabun jaγun tabin γurbaduγar">ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠢᠨ ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠳᠤᠭᠠᠷ</uig> the one thousand five hundred and fifty-third
<uig rom="arban tabun-aca">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ</uig> from fifteen
<uig rom="qorin tabun-u">ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠤ</uig> of twenty-five

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Compound nouns

paragraphs.paragraph: Compound nouns are pairs of words. The meaning of any given pair is not a mechanical total of the meaning of each element taken separately. Thus <uig rom="oron toγ-a">ᠣᠷᠣᠨ ᠲᠣᠭ᠎ᠠ</uig> ("place-number") is "office staff" or "personnel," not "number of places." Such pairs are sometimes called binoms.

There are binoms consisting of two synonymous nouns but, on the other hand, there are also binoms of which the component parts have opposite meanings. Binoms are very numerous and dictionaries contain many of them. Only a few examples will be given here.
<uig rom="emegel qajaγar">ᠡᠮᠡᠭᠡᠯ ᠬᠠᠵᠠᠭᠠᠷ</uig> (saddle-bridle) harness
<uig rom="öngge düri">ᠥᠩᠭᠡ ᠳᠦᠷᠢ</uig> (color-shape) appearance
<uig rom="jer jebseg">ᠵᠡᠷ ᠵᠡᠪᠰᠡᠭ</uig> (top of a lance-weapon) arms
<uig rom="bujar bulai">ᠪᠤᠵᠠᠷ ᠪᠤᠯᠠᠢ</uig> (dirt-vice) immorality
<uig rom="aci tusa">ᠠᠴᠢ ᠲᠤᠰᠠ</uig> (merit-usefulness) benefit
<uig rom="erke cilüge">ᠡᠷᠺᠡ ᠴᠢᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> (right-freedom) liberty
<uig rom="γajar usun">ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ ᠤᠰᠤᠨ</uig> (earth-water) territory
<uig rom="küiten qalaγun">ᠺᠦᠢᠲᠡᠨ ᠬᠠᠯᠠᠭᠤᠨ</uig> (cold-hot) temperature
<uig rom="orolγ-a jarulγ-a">ᠣᠷᠣᠯᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠵᠠᠷᠤᠯᠭ᠎ᠠ</uig> (income-expenditure) budget
<uig rom="urtu boγoni">ᠤᠷᠲᠤ ᠪᠣᠭᠣᠨᠢ</uig> (long-short) length
<uig rom="γal usun">ᠭᠠᠯ ᠤᠰᠤᠨ</uig> in: <uig rom="γal usun-u ayul">ᠭᠠᠯ ᠤᠰᠤᠨ ᠤ ᠠᠶᠤᠯ</uig> (fire-water) fatal emergency
<uig rom="caγ uliral">ᠴᠠᠭ ᠤᠯᠢᠷᠠᠯ</uig> (time-vicissitude) climate
<uig rom="erdem soyul">ᠡᠷᠳᠡᠮ ᠰᠣᠶᠤᠯ</uig> (science-civilization) culture
<uig rom="kög daγun">ᠺᠥᠭ ᠳᠠᠭᠤᠨ</uig> (tune-song) music

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Compound nouns

paragraphs.paragraph: Only the second component of a binom takes the requisite case Suffix.
<uig rom="caγ uliral-un">ᠴᠠᠭ ᠤᠯᠢᠷᠠᠯ ᠤᠨ</uig> of the climate (genitive)
<uig rom="aci tusa-bar">ᠠᠴᠢ ᠲᠤᠰᠠ ᠎ᠪᠠᠷ</uig> through the benefit (instrumental)
<uig rom="küiten qalaγun-i">ᠺᠦᠢᠲᠡᠨ ᠬᠠᠯᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠢ</uig> the temperature (accusative)

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences
entry.title2: Syntax - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences

paragraphs.paragraph: Juxtaposed equal parts of a sentence can be connected by means of conjunctions, but the latter are not indispensable and such groups of words may be used without them.
The simplest case of juxtaposition is a group of two nouns not connected by anything.
<uig rom="idegen umdaγan-u amtan-i kelen medekü">ᠢᠳᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠤᠮᠳᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠠᠮᠲᠠᠨ ᠢ ᠺᠡᠯᠡᠨ ᠮᠡᠳᠡᠺᠦ</uig> The tongue knows the taste of food (and) drink.
<uig rom="ecige eke-degen aci qariγulqu">ᠡᠴᠢᠭᠡ ᠡᠺᠡ ᠳ᠋ᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠠᠴᠢ ᠬᠠᠷᠢᠭᠤᠯᠬᠤ</uig> to return the benefits to one's own father (and) mother
<uig rom="tedeger inu tala aγulas-iyar negüdellemüi">ᠲᠡᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠲᠠᠯᠠ ᠠᠭᠤᠯᠠᠰ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠨᠡᠭᠦᠳᠡᠯᠯᠡᠮᠦᠢ</uig> They transhume along the plains (and) mountains.

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences
entry.title2: Syntax - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences

paragraphs.paragraph: The most usual conjunction is a numeral indicating the total of the objects concerned and occupying the place after the last word of such a group. The numeral can take any grammatical ending.
<uig rom="bi ci qoyar-i">ᠪᠢ ᠴᠢ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠢ</uig> me and you (accusative; lit., "me thee two")
<uig rom="baqsi sabi qoyar-tur">ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠰᠠᠪᠢ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠲᠤᠷ</uig> to the teacher and the pupil (lit., "to the teacher, the pupil, two")
<uig rom="qaγan qatun tayiji γurban-dur">ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠬᠠᠲᠤᠨ ᠲᠠᠶᠢᠵᠢ ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ</uig> to the khaghan, the queen, and the prince (lit., "to the khaghan, the queen, the prince, three")
<uig rom="tere ebügen emegen qoyar yeke bayan aqsan ajuγu">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠡᠪᠦᠭᠡᠨ ᠡᠮᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠶᠡᠺᠡ ᠪᠠᠶᠠᠨ ᠠᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠠᠵᠤᠭᠤ</uig> That old man and the old woman were very rich.
<uig rom="köbegün tayaq süke qoyar-iyan abuγad eke-degen kürcü iremüi">ᠺᠥᠪᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠲᠠᠶᠠᠬ ᠰᠦᠺᠡ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠠᠪᠤᠭᠠᠳ ᠡᠺᠡ ᠳ᠋ᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠺᠦᠷᠴᠦ ᠢᠷᠡᠮᠦᠢ</uig> The boy has taken his stick and axe and comes to his mother.
ᠪᠤᠷᠤᠭᠤ ᠵᠥᠪ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠢ ᠢᠯᠭᠠᠬᠤ to distinguish between good and bad.

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences
entry.title2: Syntax - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences

paragraphs.paragraph: There are several conjunctions. One of them is <uig rom="ba">ᠪᠠ</uig> "and." In the classical and modern language this occupies the place before the last word of a group (as the English "and").
Only the last word (noun) of a group takes the requisite case suffix, but plural suffixes are taken by all words, if it is necessary to point out that each of them expresses a multitude.

<uig rom="omoq kiged ülü süsülküi ba tusalan ülü keregleküi kiged γadaγadu-da alγasqui ba sedkil-iyen quricaqui kiged uyidqui-bar sonosqui anu kkir-tü bolai">ᠣᠮᠣᠬ ᠺᠢᠭᠡᠳ ᠦᠯᠦ ᠰᠦᠰᠦᠯᠺᠦᠢ ᠪᠠ ᠲᠤᠰᠠᠯᠠᠨ ᠦᠯᠦ ᠺᠡᠷᠡᠭᠯᠡᠺᠦᠢ ᠺᠢᠭᠡᠳ ᠭᠠᠳᠠᠭᠠᠳᠤ ᠳ᠋ᠠ ᠠᠯᠭᠠᠰᠬᠤᠢ ᠪᠠ ᠰᠡᠳᠺᠢᠯ ᠢᠶᠡᠨ ᠬᠤᠷᠢᠴᠠᠬᠤᠢ ᠺᠢᠭᠡᠳ ᠤᠶᠢᠳᠬᠤᠢ ᠎ᠪᠠᠷ ᠰᠣᠨᠣᠰᠬᠤᠢ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠺᠺᠢᠷ ᠎ᠲᠦ ᠪᠣᠯᠠᠢ</uig> Pride and lack of faith, not taking care to be useful, passion for external things, passion in thoughts, and hearing with boredom are unclean.
<uig rom="qaγan ba albatan">ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠪᠠ ᠠᠯᠪᠠᠲᠠᠨ</uig> the khaghan and the subjects
<uig rom="ene ba tere γajar-a">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠪᠠ ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ ᠠ</uig> in this and in that country
<uig rom="ene ba qoyitu nasun-dur">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠪᠠ ᠬᠣᠶᠢᠲᠤ ᠨᠠᠰᠤᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ</uig> in this and in the future life
<uig rom="tngri-ner asuri-nar ba olan amitan-nuγud-tur">ᠲᠩᠷᠢ ᠎ᠨᠡᠷ ᠠᠰᠤᠷᠢ ᠎ᠨᠠᠷ ᠪᠠ ᠣᠯᠠᠨ ᠠᠮᠢᠲᠠᠨ ᠎ᠨᠤᠭᠤᠳ ᠲᠤᠷ</uig> to the gods, the Asura-deities, and to all the living beings

<uig rom="ene nom-un gün ba gün busu-yin kedüi bükü kiri-yi üjesü">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠨᠣᠮ ᠤᠨ ᠭᠦᠨ ᠪᠠ ᠭᠦᠨ ᠪᠤᠰᠤ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠺᠡᠳᠦᠢ ᠪᠦᠺᠦ ᠺᠢᠷᠢ ᠶᠢ ᠦᠵᠡᠰᠦ</uig> I shall see what the degree of the profoundness and ("or" is better here) the shallowness of this doctrine is.

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences
entry.title2: Syntax - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences

paragraphs.paragraph: In the pre-classical language the conjunction <uig rom="ba">ᠪᠠ</uig> may be repeated after each word of a group. Here, too, only the last word takes the requisite case suffix.

<uig rom="surtaban ba sakardagam ba anagam ba arqad ba bratikabud ba dörben jüg-ün ayaγ-qa tegimlig-ün quvaraq-ud-tur">ᠰᠤᠷᠲᠠᠪᠠᠨ ᠪᠠ ᠰᠠᠺᠠᠷᠳᠠᠺᠠᠮ ᠪᠠ ᠠᠨᠠᠺᠠᠮ ᠪᠠ ᠠᠷᠬᠠᠳ ᠪᠠ ᠪᠷᠠᠲᠢᠺᠠᠪᠤᠳ ᠪᠠ ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ ᠵᠦᠭ ᠤᠨ ᠠᠶᠠᠭ ᠎ᠬᠠ ᠲᠡᠭᠢᠮᠯᠢᠭ ᠤᠨ ᠬᠤᠸᠠᠷᠠᠬ ᠤᠳ ᠲᠤᠷ</uig> to the śrota-āpanna and Sakṛdāgāmī, Anāgāmī, and Arkhat, and Pratyeka-Buddhas, and the monkhood of the four quarters

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences
entry.title2: Syntax - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences

paragraphs.paragraph: Instead of <uig rom="ba">ᠪᠠ</uig> another conjunction, <uig rom="kiged">ᠺᠢᠭᠡᠳ</uig> , is used often. The latter is the converbum perfecti of the verb <uig rom="ki-">ᠺᠢ ᠎</uig> "to do" and its literal translation is "having done" or "he did and ..."

In the classical and modern language <uig rom="kiged">ᠺᠢᠭᠡᠳ</uig> is placed before the last word of a group, but in the pre-classical language and even in the early stage of the classical period <uig rom="kiged">ᠺᠢᠭᠡᠳ</uig> was placed after the last word of a group and took the requisite case suffix.
<uig rom="qaγan kiged qatun">ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠺᠢᠭᠡᠳ ᠬᠠᠲᠤᠨ</uig> the khaghan and the queen
<uig rom="eldeb erdenis ünürten küjis kiged-i ergümüi">ᠡᠯᠳᠡᠪ ᠡᠷᠳᠡᠨᠢᠰ ᠦᠨᠦᠷᠲᠡᠨ ᠺᠦᠵᠢᠰ ᠺᠢᠭᠡᠳ ᠢ ᠡᠷᠭᠦᠮᠦᠢ</uig> I offer various jewels and incense.

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences
entry.title2: Syntax - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences

paragraphs.paragraph: The conjunction <uig rom="bolun">ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠨ</uig> and <uig rom="büged">ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠳ</uig> are converbs of the verbs <uig rom="bol-">ᠪᠣᠯ ᠎</uig> "to become" and <uig rom="bü-">ᠪᠦ ᠎</uig> "to be". They are used as conjunctions connecting nouns in the same manner as the aboce-mentioned conjunctions with the difference that they cannot be put at the end of a group.
<uig rom="baγsi büged šabi">ᠪᠠᠭᠰᠢ ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠳ ᠱᠠᠪᠢ</uig> the teacher and the pupil
<uig rom="eldeb erdenis bolun küjis-i ergümüi">ᠡᠯᠳᠡᠪ ᠡᠷᠳᠡᠨᠢᠰ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠨ ᠺᠦᠵᠢᠰ ᠢ ᠡᠷᠭᠦᠮᠦᠢ</uig> I offer various jewels and incense

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences
entry.title2: Syntax - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences

paragraphs.paragraph: As stated above, only the last word of a group takes the case suffix. Yet, if there are more than three equal parts of speech, each pair of words may take a common case suffix; compound words always take them.
<uig rom="ekener keüked-iyen aduγu mal-iyan abcu">ᠡᠺᠡᠨᠡᠷ ᠺᠡᠦᠺᠡᠳ ᠢᠶᠡᠨ ᠠᠳᠤᠭᠤ ᠮᠠᠯ ᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠠᠪᠴᠤ</uig> taking his wife and children, his horses and cattle
<uig rom="tegün-ü küiten qalaγun-i könggen kündü-yi ülü medemüi">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠤ ᠺᠦᠢᠲᠡᠨ ᠬᠠᠯᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠢ ᠺᠥᠩᠭᠡᠨ ᠺᠦᠨᠳᠦ ᠶᠢ ᠦᠯᠦ ᠮᠡᠳᠡᠮᠦᠢ</uig> One does not know its temperature or weight.

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences
entry.title2: Syntax - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences

paragraphs.paragraph: If each of the equal parts of sentence has an attribute qualifying only it, each word of a group obtains the requisite case suffix.

<uig rom="bi kögsin eke-lüge-ben baγ-a degüü-lüge-ben qamtu saγuju amui">ᠪᠢ ᠺᠥᠭᠰᠢᠨ ᠡᠺᠡ ᠯᠦᠭᠡ ᠎ᠪᠡᠨ ᠪᠠᠭ ᠠ ᠳᠡᠭᠦᠦ ᠯᠦᠭᠡ ᠎ᠪᠡᠨ ᠬᠠᠮᠲᠤ ᠰᠠᠭᠤᠵᠤ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> I am living together with my old mother and my little brother.

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences
entry.title2: Syntax - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences

paragraphs.paragraph: In the modern language, verbal noun forms cannot be connected with conjunctions nor are there any groups of verbal forms as there are in English, e. g., "He saw and recognized him." In one sentence there can be only one finite verb and all the remaining verbs must be converbs. Only verbal nouns can constitute groups of equal parts of sentence. They can be used together without conjunctions or they can be connected by the conjunction <uig rom="büged">ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠳ</uig> or (rarely) <uig rom="kiged">ᠺᠢᠭᠡᠳ</uig> .
<uig rom="tegün-i medegsen büged darui kemjiy-e-nügüd-i abuqsan amui">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠮᠡᠳᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠳ ᠳᠠᠷᠤᠢ ᠺᠡᠮᠵᠢᠶ ᠡ ᠎ᠨᠦᠭᠦᠳ ᠢ ᠠᠪᠤᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He learned it and immediately took measures.

entry.title: Syntax - Juxtaposed nominal groups - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences
entry.title2: Syntax - Juxtaposed equal parts of sentences

paragraphs.paragraph: In the pre-classical language there occurred groups of indicative forms connected by the conjunction <uig rom="kiged">ᠺᠢᠭᠡᠳ</uig> .

<uig rom="seceg-üd-iyer takimui kiged ... terigüten cimeg-üd-iyer takimui">ᠰᠡᠴᠡᠭ ᠤᠳ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠲᠠᠺᠢᠮᠤᠢ ᠺᠢᠭᠡᠳ ... ᠲᠡᠷᠢᠭᠦᠲᠡᠨ ᠴᠢᠮᠡᠭ ᠤᠳ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠲᠠᠺᠢᠮᠤᠢ</uig> I sacrifice with flowers and I sacrifice with ... and other jewels (lit., "adornments").

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Members of a sentence

paragraphs.paragraph: The main members of a sentence are the subject, predicate, object, and attribute. A sentence may consist of only a subject and predicate without an object or attribute. The subject, too, may be omitted, if it is understood.
The subject is always the nominative case of a declinable part of speech : a noun, a pronoun, a numeral, or a verbal noun.

The subject usually occupies the place before the predicate, but in the pre-classical language and, under the influence of the colloquial language, in modern popular books it sometimes occupies the place after the predicate.
a) Noun as subject:
<uig rom="baqsi irebe">ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡ</uig> The teacher came.
<uig rom="mungqaq ese medemüi">ᠮᠤᠩᠬᠠᠬ ᠡᠰᠡ ᠮᠡᠳᠡᠮᠦᠢ</uig> The fool does not know.
ᠬᠠᠨ ᠺᠥᠪᠡᠭᠦᠨ qan köbegün yeke bolba The prince (lit., "the khan's son") became big (i. e., an adult).

<uig rom="jirγuγan üsüg orcilang-aca getülgekü ongγoca sal mön">ᠵᠢᠷᠭᠤᠭᠠᠨ ᠦᠰᠦᠭ ᠣᠷᠴᠢᠯᠠᠩ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠭᠡᠲᠦᠯᠭᠡᠺᠦ ᠣᠩᠭᠣᠴᠠ ᠰᠠᠯ ᠮᠥᠨ</uig> The six letters (i. e., the syllables om ma ni pad me hum) are the ship rescuing from the rebirths.
<uig rom="ebügen nocoba juru-yi">ᠡᠪᠦᠭᠡᠨ ᠨᠣᠴᠣᠪᠠ ᠵᠤᠷᠤ ᠶᠢ</uig> The old man struggled with Juru.
<uig rom="irebe geser">ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡ ᠭᠡᠰᠡᠷ</uig> Geser came.
b) Pronoun as subject:
<uig rom="bi ese üjebe">ᠪᠢ ᠡᠰᠡ ᠦᠵᠡᠪᠡ</uig> I have not seen.

<uig rom="bi nigen caq-tu nökör-lüge-ben arγamji-bar usun-aca morin-i γarγabai">ᠪᠢ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠴᠠᠬ ᠎ᠲᠤ ᠨᠥᠺᠥᠷ ᠯᠦᠭᠡ ᠎ᠪᠡᠨ ᠠᠷᠭᠠᠮᠵᠢ ᠎ᠪᠠᠷ ᠤᠰᠤᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠢ ᠭᠠᠷᠭᠠᠪᠠᠢ</uig> Once, together with my friend, I pulled a horse from the water with a rope.
<uig rom="bi nige sibaγu alabai">ᠪᠢ ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠰᠢᠪᠠᠭᠤ ᠠᠯᠠᠪᠠᠢ</uig> I killed a bird.
<uig rom="ken iregsen bui">ᠺᠡᠨ ᠢᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> Who has come?
<uig rom="ene yaγun bui">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠶᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> What is this?
<uig rom="ci qamiγ-a odumui">ᠴᠢ ᠬᠠᠮᠢᠭ ᠠ ᠣᠳᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> Where will you go?
c) Numeral as subject:

<uig rom="qoyar anu daqutai qoyar anu daqu ügei">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠳᠠᠬᠤᠲᠠᠢ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠳᠠᠬᠤ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> Two of them have put on fur coats, two of them have no fur coats. (Lit., "Their two with fur coats, their two without fur coats.")
<uig rom="tede γurban ali bui kemebesü">ᠲᠡᠳᠡ ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠠᠯᠢ ᠪᠤᠢ ᠺᠡᠮᠡᠪᠡᠰᠦ</uig> if one asks what those three are, ...
d) Verbal noun as subject:
<uig rom="suruqci ungsimui">ᠰᠤᠷᠤᠬᠴᠢ ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠮᠤᠢ</uig> The pupil (lit., "the learning") reads.
<uig rom="suruqsan dalai, suruγ-a ügei balai">ᠰᠤᠷᠤᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠳᠠᠯᠠᠢ᠃ ᠰᠤᠷᠤᠭ ᠠ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ ᠪᠠᠯᠠᠢ</uig> One who has learnt is an ocean (of wisdom) ; one who has not learnt is blind.

<uig rom="yabuqsan inu yasu möljikü, kebtegsen inu kegeli-ben aldaqu">ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠶᠠᠰᠤ ᠮᠥᠯᠵᠢᠺᠦ᠃ ᠺᠡᠪᠲᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠺᠡᠭᠡᠯᠢ ᠎ᠪᠡᠨ ᠠᠯᠳᠠᠬᠤ</uig> One who has gone will gnaw at a bone; one who has lain down will lose his belly (i. e., will starve). This is a proverb meaning that one who works will have food and one who is idle will die of starvation.
e) Verbal-nominal construction (see sections §642-§643) as subject
<uig rom="manu baqsi-yin bicigsen inu cöm ünen">ᠮᠠᠨᠤ ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠪᠢᠴᠢᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠴᠥᠮ ᠦᠨᠡᠨ</uig> bui Everything our teacher has written is true.

<uig rom="ene caq samaγu boluqsan inu er-e em-e qoyar-aca bolba">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠴᠠᠬ ᠰᠠᠮᠠᠭᠤ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠡᠷ ᠡ ᠡᠮ ᠡ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠ</uig> The fact that the present times are troubled comes from the man and (his) wife.

<uig rom="jegün nidü-ben qaraqsan minu ene jayaγan tere jayaγan qoyar-i tegsi qaraqsan minu buyu">ᠵᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠨᠢᠳᠦ ᠎ᠪᠡᠨ ᠬᠠᠷᠠᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠡᠨᠡ ᠵᠠᠶᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠵᠠᠶᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠢ ᠲᠡᠭᠰᠢ ᠬᠠᠷᠠᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠪᠤᠶᠤ</uig> That I looked (into the distance) with my left eye means that I considered this life and that (i. e., the future) life equal.
it has been stated that the subject is usually placed before the predicate.

In the pre-classical language, personal and demonstrative pronouns are often placed after the finite verb. Sometimes a personal pronoun is placed, as usual, before the predicate, but is repeated after the latter.
<uig rom="tere metü jalbarin ügülemüi bi">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠮᠡᠲᠦ ᠵᠠᠯᠪᠠᠷᠢᠨ ᠦᠭᠦᠯᠡᠮᠦᠢ ᠪᠢ</uig> I am praying in that manner.
<uig rom="qamuγ teden-ü ilede anu nasuda saγuju amu bi">ᠬᠠᠮᠤᠭ ᠲᠡᠳᠡᠨ ᠤ ᠢᠯᠡᠳᠡ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠨᠠᠰᠤᠳᠠ ᠰᠠᠭᠤᠵᠤ ᠠᠮᠤ ᠪᠢ</uig> I shall live always, evident to all of them.
<uig rom="γar köl terigüten-iyen tebciküi-e ayumu bi">ᠭᠠᠷ ᠺᠥᠯ ᠲᠡᠷᠢᠭᠦᠲᠡᠨ ᠢᠶᠡᠨ ᠲᠡᠪᠴᠢᠺᠦᠢ ᠡ ᠠᠶᠤᠮᠤ ᠪᠢ</uig> I fear I shall lose my hands, feet, and so on.

<uig rom="ükül-ün ejen-ü aman-dur oduqsan-iyan ejiyede ese kü medebe ci">ᠦᠺᠦᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠡᠵᠡᠨ ᠤ ᠠᠮᠠᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠣᠳᠤᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠡᠵᠢᠶᠡᠳᠡ ᠡᠰᠡ ᠺᠦ ᠮᠡᠳᠡᠪᠡ ᠴᠢ</uig> You never knew that you had gone into the mouth of the Master of the Death.
<uig rom="yekin ene metü nuta amui ci">ᠶᠡᠺᠢᠨ ᠡᠨᠡ ᠮᠡᠲᠦ ᠨᠤᠲᠠ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ ᠴᠢ</uig> Why are you so calm?
<uig rom="inegeldüküi-yi yekin taγalamu ci">ᠢᠨᠡᠭᠡᠯᠳᠦᠺᠦᠢ ᠶᠢ ᠶᠡᠺᠢᠨ ᠲᠠᠭᠠᠯᠠᠮᠤ ᠴᠢ</uig> Why do you like laughter?
<uig rom="öd ügei orcin tögerin yabumu tede">ᠥᠳ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ ᠣᠷᠴᠢᠨ ᠲᠥᠭᠡᠷᠢᠨ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠮᠤ ᠲᠡᠳᠡ</uig> They go around aimlessly.
<uig rom="cimayi bi ene edür minu dergede saγu gejü ese kelebeüü bi">ᠴᠢᠮᠠᠶᠢ ᠪᠢ ᠡᠨᠡ ᠡᠳᠦᠷ ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠳᠡᠷᠭᠡᠳᠡ ᠰᠠᠭᠤ ᠭᠡᠵᠦ ᠡᠰᠡ ᠺᠡᠯᠡᠪᠡᠦᠦ ᠪᠢ</uig> Did I not tell you to sit by me today?

This repetition of the pronoun after a verb has produced personal endings on verbal forms in certain colloquial languages, e. g., in Buriat, Kalmuck, and others, e. g., Buriat bi abanab I take, si abanas you take, etc.

As said above, the subject is a nominative. Not infrequently the subject is emphasized by special words: <uig rom="inu">ᠢᠨᠤ</uig> or <uig rom="anu">ᠠᠨᠤ</uig> , <uig rom="bolbasu">ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤ</uig> , <uig rom="bügesü">ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠰᠦ</uig>, <uig rom="ber">ᠪᠡᠷ</uig>. The latter are the so-called subject designators. They will be discussed in the sections dealing with the nominative (§495-§499).
See also §280
The predicate is a verb, a noun, a pronoun, or a numeral. The predicate is placed after the subject, although, as remarked above (§ 440), the subject is sometimes placed after the predicate.

The predicate is the most important member of the sentence and is omitted only in some inscriptions or signboards, e. g., <uig rom="utasun medegen-ü qoriy-a">ᠤᠲᠠᠰᠤᠨ ᠮᠡᠳᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠤ ᠬᠣᠷᠢᠶ ᠠ</uig> "telegraph." But old book titles are always complete sentences with a predicate, e. g., <uig rom="altan gerel kemekü yeke kölgen sudur orosibai">ᠠᠯᠲᠠᠨ ᠭᠡᠷᠡᠯ ᠺᠡᠮᠡᠺᠦ ᠶᠡᠺᠡ ᠺᠥᠯᠭᠡᠨ ᠰᠤᠳᠤᠷ ᠣᠷᠣᠰᠢᠪᠠᠢ</uig> "The Mahāyāna Sutra called the Golden Ray (i. e., Suvarṇaprabhāsa) has begun."
A verbal predicate is either an imperative, optative, or indicative form. Such a predicate does not need a copula.
All other sorts of predicate have a copula. The latter is a finite verb of an auxiliary verb.

A predicate in the form of a converb always has a copula, as, without the latter, the sentence could not be complete. If the predicate is a noun, pronoun, numeral, or verbal noun, the copula can be omitted. A predicate expressed with one of the latter parts of speech is a nominal predicate.
Verbal Predicate
Imperative or optative as predicate
<uig rom="ta cai uγuqtun">ᠲᠠ ᠴᠠᠢ ᠤᠭᠤᠬᠲᠤᠨ</uig> You, drink tea!
<uig rom="bi tegün-i üjesügei">ᠪᠢ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠦᠵᠡᠰᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> Let me see it!
Indicative forms as predicates:
<uig rom="sabi ungsimui">ᠰᠠᠪᠢ ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠮᠤᠢ</uig> The pupil reads.
<uig rom="baqsi irebei">ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡᠢ</uig> The teacher has come.
Converbal Predicate
Converbum imperfecti as predicate:
<uig rom="bi ende saγuju amui">ᠪᠢ ᠡᠨᠳᠡ ᠰᠠᠭᠤᠵᠤ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> I am living here.
<uig rom="sabi ungsiju amui">ᠰᠠᠪᠢ ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠵᠤ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> The pupil is reading.
Converbum modale as predicate :
<uig rom="sibaγun nisün irebe">ᠰᠢᠪᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠨᠢᠰᠦᠨ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡ</uig> The bird flew in. (Lit., "came flying.")
<uig rom="ebügen güin γaruba">ᠡᠪᠦᠭᠡᠨ ᠭᠦᠢᠨ ᠭᠠᠷᠤᠪᠠ</uig> The old man ran out. (Lit., "Went out running.")
Nominal Predicate
Noun as predicate :
<uig rom="tanu köbegün baqsi bolba">ᠲᠠᠨᠤ ᠺᠥᠪᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠ</uig> Your son became a teacher.
<uig rom="tegün-ü üge qudal amui">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠤ ᠦᠭᠡ ᠬᠤᠳᠠᠯ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> amui His speech is a lie.
<uig rom="ene morin sayin bui">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> This horse is good.
Pronoun as predicate:
<uig rom="tere γurba ali bui">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠ ᠠᠯᠢ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> What are those three?
<uig rom="ene kümün ken bui">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠺᠡᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> Who is this person?
Numeral as predicate :
<uig rom="kümün-ü erdem γurban bui">ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠤ ᠡᠷᠳᠡᠮ ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> Man's virtues are three.
Verbal noun as predicate :
<uig rom="tere kümün ükügsen ajuγu">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠦᠺᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠠᠵᠤᠭᠤ</uig> That man had been dead.
<uig rom="ci qamiγ-a odqu bui">ᠴᠢ ᠬᠠᠮᠢᠭ ᠠ ᠣᠳᠬᠤ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> Where will you go?
As said above, the copula can be omitted:
<uig rom="suruqsan dalai, suruγ-a ügei balai">ᠰᠤᠷᠤᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠳᠠᠯᠠᠢ᠃ ᠰᠤᠷᠤᠭ ᠠ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ ᠪᠠᠯᠠᠢ</uig> One who has learnt is an ocean (of wisdom), one who has not learnt is blind.
<uig rom="ene yaγun">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠶᠠᠭᠤᠨ</uig> What is this?
<uig rom="qoyar anu daqutai, qoyar anu daqu ügei">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠳᠠᠬᠤᠲᠠᠢ᠃ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠳᠠᠬᠤ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> Two of them are with fur coats, two of them are without fur coats.
<uig rom="nasun inu tabun">ᠨᠠᠰᠤᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ</uig> His age is five.
<uig rom="tere kümün ükügsen">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠦᠺᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ</uig> That man is dead.
There is no agreement in number of person between the predicate and subject. As all indicative forms refer to all persons of both singular and plural, there cannot be any such agreement.

In the pre-classical language there seemed to be agreement in gender between the predicate and subject (sometimes also object) as there were several verbal forms used only in reference to female beings. These were the past tense in <uig rom=" -ba/-bi">᠎ᠪᠠ/᠎ᠪᠢ</uig> referring to male and female beings, respectively, the past tense in <uig rom="-juγu/-jiγai">ᠵᠤᠭᠤ/ᠵᠢᠭᠠᠢ</uig> (<uig rom="-jiγi"> ᠎ᠵᠢᠭᠢ</uig>) referring to male and female respectively, but in the classical and modern language there is no such agreement.
The imperative and certain optative forms refer to definite persons, although in popular books even these forms are not always used in reference to the same persons.
The nominal predicate does not agree with the subject in number today, but in the pre-classical language there was agreement in number between the verbal noun and the subject.
bi (ci, baqsi, bida, ta, baqsi-nar) iremüi I (thou, the teacher, we you, the teachers) will come.
<uig rom="bi iresügei">ᠪᠢ ᠢᠷᠡᠰᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> Let me come!
<uig rom="ci buu ire">ᠴᠢ ᠪᠤᠤ ᠢᠷᠡ</uig> Do not come !
<uig rom="sabi iretügei">ᠰᠠᠪᠢ ᠢᠷᠡᠲᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> Let the pupil come !
<uig rom="bida marγasi irey-e">ᠪᠢᠳᠠ ᠮᠠᠷᠭᠠᠰᠢ ᠢᠷᠡᠶ ᠡ</uig> We shall come to-morrow.
<uig rom="ta iregtün">ᠲᠠ ᠢᠷᠡᠭᠲᠦᠨ</uig> You, come please !
bi (ci, baqsi, bida, ta, baqsi-nar) iregesei If only I (thou, the teacher, we, you, the teachers) came!
<uig rom="manu baqsi sayin">ᠮᠠᠨᠤ ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ</uig> Our teacher is good.
<uig rom="manu baqsi-nar sayin">ᠮᠠᠨᠤ ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠎ᠨᠠᠷ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ</uig> Our teachers are good.
The following sentences taken from a pre-classical work (Bodhicaryāvatāra) are examples of agreement in number between the predicate and subject :

<uig rom="qamuγ tngri-ner asuri-nar ker ber minu dayisun bolbasu ber tede ber ayus tamu-yin γal-un dotor-a uduridcu oroγulun ülü cidaqun">ᠬᠠᠮᠤᠭ ᠲᠩᠷᠢ ᠎ᠨᠡᠷ ᠠᠰᠤᠷᠢ ᠎ᠨᠠᠷ ᠺᠡᠷ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠳᠠᠶᠢᠰᠤᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠲᠡᠳᠡ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠠᠶᠤᠰ ᠲᠠᠮᠤ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠭᠠᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠳᠣᠲᠣᠷ ᠠ ᠤᠳᠤᠷᠢᠳᠴᠤ ᠣᠷᠣᠭᠤᠯᠤᠨ ᠦᠯᠦ ᠴᠢᠳᠠᠬᠤᠨ</uig> Even if all deities and Asura became my enemies, they could not lead me into the fire of the horrible hell.
<uig rom="meses-iyer jocilalduqun ber ... seceg-üd uγurulcaqun boltuqai">ᠮᠡᠰᠡᠰ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠵᠣᠴᠢᠯᠠᠯᠳᠤᠬᠤᠨ ᠪᠡᠷ ... ᠰᠡᠴᠡᠭ ᠤᠳ ᠤᠭᠤᠷᠤᠯᠴᠠᠬᠤᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠲᠤᠬᠠᠢ</uig> Let those stabbing with knives begin strewing flowers!

<uig rom="minu buyan-u kücün-dür tngri-ner-ün bey-e olju bürün tngri-ner-ün ökid-lüge nigen-e ... naγur-tur aqun boltuγai">ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠪᠤᠶᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠺᠦᠴᠦᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠲᠩᠷᠢ ᠎ᠨᠡᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠪᠡᠶ ᠡ ᠣᠯᠵᠤ ᠪᠦᠷᠦᠨ ᠲᠩᠷᠢ ᠎ᠨᠡᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠥᠺᠢᠳ ᠯᠦᠭᠡ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠡ ... ᠨᠠᠭᠤᠷ ᠲᠤᠷ ᠠᠬᠤᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠲᠤᠭᠠᠢ</uig> Let them be together with the daughters of the deities in the lake, because they have obtained divine bodies by virtue of my punya.
Sometimes the predicate is a plural of a verbal noun while the subject is formally a singular:

<uig rom="kölösün ögküi talbiqsan-u siltaγa-bar ene ba qoyici ber töröl-ün tusa inu ebderekün">ᠺᠥᠯᠥᠰᠦᠨ ᠥᠭᠺᠦᠢ ᠲᠠᠯᠪᠢᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠰᠢᠯᠲᠠᠭᠠ ᠎ᠪᠠᠷ ᠡᠨᠡ ᠪᠠ ᠬᠣᠶᠢᠴᠢ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠲᠥᠷᠥᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠲᠤᠰᠠ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠡᠪᠳᠡᠷᠡᠺᠦᠨ</uig> Because of suspension of payment of wages, the profit of this rebirth and the future one will break down.
The nominal predicate is a nominative or an oblique case.
<uig rom="minu aq-a blam-a bui">ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠠᠬ ᠠ ᠪᠯᠠᠮ ᠠ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> My elder brother is a lama.
<uig rom="ene nom minu bui">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠨᠣᠮ ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> This book is mine.

<uig rom="mori unuqui dur-a-bar, ekener abqui jayaγa-bar">ᠮᠣᠷᠢ ᠤᠨᠤᠬᠤᠢ ᠳᠤᠷ ᠠ ᠎ᠪᠠᠷ, ᠡᠺᠡᠨᠡᠷ ᠠᠪᠬᠤᠢ ᠵᠠᠶᠠᠭᠠ ᠎ᠪᠠᠷ</uig> Riding horsebaek is something depending upon one's desire; marrying is something depending upon destiny. (A proverb ; lit. "Riding horsebackthrough desire, marrying-through destiny.")
The object is a word governed by either a verb or a noun. There are two main types of object: an object governed directly by a verb or a noun, and an object governed by a postposition.

Any declinable part of speech can serve as an object which is always an oblique case. Of the cases the only one which is not directly governed by a verb is the genitive, but it can depend upon a verb, if there is a postposition.

The object usually immediately precedes the governing word, but, if the latter is a verb, the object sometimes follows the verb, especially in poetical works of the pre-classical period, but also in popular books of recent periods.
Object governed by a noun
<uig rom="mal-iyar bayan">ᠮᠠᠯ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠪᠠᠶᠠᠨ</uig> rich in cattle
Object governed by a verb :
<uig rom="bi tegün-i ese medemüi">ᠪᠢ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠡᠰᠡ ᠮᠡᠳᠡᠮᠦᠢ</uig> I do not know it.
Object with a postposition:
<uig rom="amitan-u tula buyan üiledkü">ᠠᠮᠢᠲᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠲᠤᠯᠠ ᠪᠤᠶᠠᠨ ᠦᠢᠯᠡᠳᠺᠦ</uig> to practise virtue for the sake of living beings

Just as in other languages, there is a direct and an indirect object. The direct object takes an accusative suffix or no suffix whatever. Only transitive verbs govern a direct object. In many cases the equivalent of an English transitive verb is an intransitive one in Mongolian and vice versa.
Verbs which are transitive in both Mongolian and English
<uig rom="ala-">ᠠᠯᠠ ᠎</uig> to kill
<uig rom="ol-">ᠣᠯ ᠎</uig> to find
<uig rom="ab-">ᠠᠪ ᠎</uig> to take
<uig rom="yabuγul-">ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠭᠤᠯ ᠎</uig> to send
<uig rom="ög-">ᠥᠭ ᠎</uig> to give
<uig rom="usadqa-">ᠤᠰᠠᠳᠬᠠ ᠎</uig> to liquidate
Verbs which are intransitive in both Mongolian and English:
<uig rom="ükü-">ᠦᠺᠦ ᠎</uig> to die
<uig rom="saγu-">ᠰᠠᠭᠤ ᠎</uig> to sit down
<uig rom="umta-">ᠤᠮᠲᠠ ᠎</uig> to sleep
<uig rom="ire-">ᠢᠷᠡ ᠎</uig> to come
<uig rom="kebte-">ᠺᠡᠪᠲᠡ ᠎</uig> to lie down
<uig rom="nis-">ᠨᠢᠰ ᠎</uig> to fly
Verbs which are intransitive in Mongolian but transitive in English
<uig rom="asaγu-">ᠠᠰᠠᠭᠤ ᠎</uig> to ask
<uig rom="ayu-">ᠠᠶᠤ ᠎</uig> to fear
As remarked above, the object precedes the predicate. As for the subject, it precedes the object. The usual word order in a sentence is Subject - Object-Predicate.
<uig rom="sabi nom ungsimui">ᠰᠠᠪᠢ ᠨᠣᠮ ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠮᠤᠢ</uig> The pupil reads a book.
<uig rom="bi tegün-i ese medemüi">ᠪᠢ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠡᠰᠡ ᠮᠡᠳᠡᠮᠦᠢ</uig> I do not know it.
In popular books and in the pre-classical language, especially in poetry, the object may follow the predicate.
<uig rom="erten-ü burqad ker dügüregsen bolqu öglige baramid">ᠡᠷᠲᠡᠨ ᠤ ᠪᠤᠷᠬᠠᠳ ᠺᠡᠷ ᠳᠦᠭᠦᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠬᠤ ᠥᠭᠯᠢᠭᠡ ᠪᠠᠷᠠᠮᠢᠳ</uig> How could the Buddhas of the former (time) complete the Pāramitā of alms?
<uig rom="uran ber busu bi nayiraγulun jokiyaqui-a">ᠤᠷᠠᠨ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠪᠤᠰᠤ ᠪᠢ ᠨᠠᠶᠢᠷᠠᠭᠤᠯᠤᠨ ᠵᠣᠺᠢᠶᠠᠬᠤᠢ ᠠ</uig> I am not skilful in writing poetry.
<uig rom="minu kücü-ber abtaqui tegün-i">ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠺᠦᠴᠦ ᠎ᠪᠡᠷ ᠠᠪᠲᠠᠬᠤᠢ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ</uig> It is necessary to take him by my strength.

<uig rom="jobalang-ud qotala bolbai öber-iyen jirγaqui küseküi-ece">ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠤᠳ ᠬᠣᠲᠠᠯᠠ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠢ ᠥᠪᠡᠷ ᠢᠶᠡᠨ ᠵᠢᠷᠭᠠᠬᠤᠢ ᠺᠦᠰᠡᠺᠦᠢ ᠡᠴᠡ</uig> The sufferings became enormous as a consequence of the desire to be happy himself.

<uig rom="ciγulγabasu tere bodicid sedkil-i qoyar jüil kemen uqaqdaqui">ᠴᠢᠭᠤᠯᠭᠠᠪᠠᠰᠤ ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠪᠣᠳᠢᠴᠢᠳ ᠰᠡᠳᠺᠢᠯ ᠢ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠵᠦᠢᠯ ᠺᠡᠮᠡᠨ ᠤᠬᠠᠬᠳᠠᠬᠤᠢ</uig> If one summarizes that holy idea (the accusative follows here <uig rom="ciγulγabasu">ᠴᠢᠭᠤᠯᠭᠠᠪᠠᠰᠤ</uig> ), it must be understood that it consists of two categories.
When there are several objects depending upon the same word, the object which bears the logical stress is placed immediately before the governing word.
<uig rom="bi cimadur qoyar bicig ilegebe">ᠪᠢ ᠴᠢᠮᠠᠳᠤᠷ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠪᠢᠴᠢᠭ ᠢᠯᠡᠭᠡᠪᠡ</uig> I sent you two letters.
<uig rom="bi qoyar bicig cimadur ilegebe">ᠪᠢ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠪᠢᠴᠢᠭ ᠴᠢᠮᠠᠳᠤᠷ ᠢᠯᠡᠭᠡᠪᠡ</uig> I sent two letters to you.

Only the last of a group of equal objects takes the requisite case Suffix. When equal objects are followed by a numeral serving as a conjunction (or by the conjunction <uig rom="kiged">ᠺᠢᠭᠡᠳ</uig> in the pre-classical language, See § 399, §432) the grammatical ending is taken by the latter.
<uig rom="qaγan inu qatun tüsimed kiy-a-nar-iyan daγudabai">ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠬᠠᠲᠤᠨ ᠲᠦᠰᠢᠮᠡᠳ ᠺᠢᠶ ᠠ ᠎ᠨᠠᠷ ᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠳᠠᠭᠤᠳᠠᠪᠠᠢ</uig> The khaghan called his wife, officers, and adjutants.

<uig rom="negüdelcin arad-ud anu ger mal ekener keüked-iyen daγaγulun negüdellemüi">ᠨᠡᠭᠦᠳᠡᠯᠴᠢᠨ ᠠᠷᠠᠳ ᠤᠳ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠭᠡᠷ ᠮᠠᠯ ᠡᠺᠡᠨᠡᠷ ᠺᠡᠦᠺᠡᠳ ᠢᠶᠡᠨ ᠳᠠᠭᠠᠭᠤᠯᠤᠨ ᠨᠡᠭᠦᠳᠡᠯᠯᠡᠮᠦᠢ</uig> The nomads transhume carrying with them (lit., "letting follow") their tents, cattle, wives, and children.
<uig rom="köbegün tayaγ süke qoyar-iyan abuγad eke-degen kürcü iremüi">ᠺᠥᠪᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠲᠠᠶᠠᠭ ᠰᠦᠺᠡ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠠᠪᠤᠭᠠᠳ ᠡᠺᠡ ᠳ᠋ᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠺᠦᠷᠴᠦ ᠢᠷᠡᠮᠦᠢ</uig> The boy has taken his stick and axe and comes to his mother.
<uig rom="bi ceceg küjis sayin ünürten kiged-i takin ergümüi">ᠪᠢ ᠴᠡᠴᠡᠭ ᠺᠦᠵᠢᠰ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠦᠨᠦᠷᠲᠡᠨ ᠺᠢᠭᠡᠳ ᠢ ᠲᠠᠺᠢᠨ ᠡᠷᠭᠦᠮᠦᠢ</uig> I offer flowers, sticks of incense, and perfume.

An active verb with a direct object can be converted into a passive one. In such a case, the direct object (an accusative or a suffixless form) becomes the grammatical subject and the subject becomes an object. The logical agent is expressed by a dative-locative (dativus actoris).
<uig rom="qonin cinu-a-dur bariqdaba">ᠬᠣᠨᠢᠨ ᠴᠢᠨᠤ ᠠ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠪᠠᠷᠢᠬᠳᠠᠪᠠ</uig> The sheep was caught by the wolf.
<uig rom="ken-dür cu ülü dabaqdaqu aγula">ᠺᠡᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠴᠤ ᠦᠯᠦ ᠳᠠᠪᠠᠬᠳᠠᠬᠤ ᠠᠭᠤᠯᠠ</uig> a mountain impossible to scale by anybody
<uig rom="ada-dur bariqdaqsan kümün">ᠠᠳᠠ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠪᠠᠷᠢᠬᠳᠠᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> a person possessed by the devil
<uig rom="jobalang-a daruqdaqsan kümün">ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠠ ᠳᠠᠷᠤᠬᠳᠠᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> a man overwhelmed by sufferings
<uig rom="taciyangγui-a abtaqsan amitan">ᠲᠠᠴᠢᠶᠠᠩᠭᠤᠢ ᠠ ᠠᠪᠲᠠᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠠᠮᠢᠲᠠᠨ</uig> the living beings possessed by vanity

Verbal nouns serving as attributes are rarely used in the passive in the classical and modern language. Even to express passive actions (to be taken, to be eaten, etc.) active verbal nouns are used more frequently. The logical agent is in such cases a genitive (genitivus actoris).
<uig rom="noqai-yin idegsen miqan">ᠨᠣᠬᠠᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠢᠳᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠮᠢᠬᠠᠨ</uig> the meat eaten by the dog
<uig rom="minu bicigsen bicig">ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠪᠢᠴᠢᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠪᠢᠴᠢᠭ</uig> a letter written by me
<uig rom="burqan-u nomlaqsan nom">ᠪᠤᠷᠬᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠨᠣᠮᠯᠠᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠨᠣᠮ</uig> the law preached by Buddha

The literal translation of such a group of words is "the dog's eaten meat." This does not mean "dog's meat which has been eaten (by someone)" but "meat which was eaten by the dog." As for "meat of a dog which has been eaten," this would be idegsen <uig rom="noqai-yin miqan">ᠨᠣᠬᠠᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠢᠬᠠᠨ</uig> where, as we see, the order of words is different, so that there cannot be any misunderstanding.
Any declinable part of speech can be qualified by a word particularizing the idea expressed by the former. Such a word qualifying another serves as an attribute.
A noun with an attribute :
<uig rom="sayin nökör">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠨᠥᠺᠥᠷ</uig> the good friend
A pronoun with an attribute
<uig rom="ücügüken bi">ᠦᠴᠦᠭᠦᠺᠡᠨ ᠪᠢ</uig> little I
A substantivated numeral as an attribute :
<uig rom="baraγun dörben">ᠪᠠᠷᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ</uig> the right hand (i. e., the Western) Four (a Mongol group)
A verbal noun with an attribute :
<uig rom="sayin suruqci">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠰᠤᠷᠤᠬᠴᠢ</uig> the good pupil (lit., "learning")
The attribute can be a noun, a pronoun, a numeral, or a verbal noun.
Noun as an attribute :
<uig rom="modun bayising">ᠮᠣᠳᠤᠨ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠰᠢᠩ</uig> a wooden building
<uig rom="sayin nökör">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠨᠥᠺᠥᠷ</uig> a good friend
Pronoun as an attribute :
<uig rom="ene kümün">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> this person
<uig rom="yambar nom">ᠶᠠᠮᠪᠠᠷ ᠨᠣᠮ</uig> what book
Numeral as an attribute
<uig rom="γurban erdeni">ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠡᠷᠳᠡᠨᠢ</uig> the Three Jewels (i. e., Buddha, his teachings, and the Buddhist clergy)
<uig rom="γutuγar bölög">ᠭᠤᠲᠤᠭᠠᠷ ᠪᠥᠯᠥᠭ</uig> third chapter
Verbal noun as an attribute:
<uig rom="irekü jil">ᠢᠷᠡᠺᠦ ᠵᠢᠯ</uig> next year (lit., "the year to come")
<uig rom="ükügsen kümün">ᠦᠺᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> the dead person
Verbal nouns may be linked with converbs. Thus a converb can be a component element of an attribute :
<uig rom="niscü iregsen sibaγun">ᠨᠢᠰᠴᠦ ᠢᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠰᠢᠪᠠᠭᠤᠨ</uig> a bird which came flying
<uig rom="nom ungsiju saγuγsan kümün">ᠨᠣᠮ ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠵᠤ ᠰᠠᠭᠤᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> a person who was sitting and reading

The attribute is always placed before the word to which it refers. An exception is the genitive of the personal pronoun serving as an attribute, which is placed after the word to which it refers. The genitive of the pronouns of the third person <uig rom="inu">ᠢᠨᠤ</uig> "his" and <uig rom="anu">ᠠᠨᠤ</uig> "their" is always placed after the word concerned and never before the latter, although in the most ancient texts (in the language of the Secret History which is not Written Mongolian) it may be placed either before or after.
<uig rom="minu aq-a">ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠠᠬ ᠠ</uig> or <uig rom="aq-a minu">ᠠᠬ ᠠ ᠮᠢᠨᠤ</uig> my elder brother
<uig rom="manu baqsi">ᠮᠠᠨᠤ ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ</uig> or <uig rom="baqsi manu">ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠮᠠᠨᠤ</uig> our teacher nom inu his book

As these cases are the only exceptions, it may be better not to regard them as cases of an attribute. In such cases, the personal pronoun has almost become a possessive suffix. Such suffixes exist in Colloquial Mongolian (e. g., Khalkha dümin "my younger brother", dütsin "your younger brother", Buriat axam "my elder brother", axasni "your elder brother", and so on). It is also important to point out that such pronouns in postnominal position become enclitics, lose their stress, and change in form to <uig rom="mini">ᠮᠢᠨᠢ</uig> , <uig rom="cini">ᠴᠢᠨᠢ</uig> , <uig rom="mani">ᠮᠠᠨᠢ</uig> , <uig rom="tani">ᠲᠠᠨᠢ</uig> :
<uig rom="aq-a mini">ᠠᠬ ᠠ ᠮᠢᠨᠢ</uig> any elder brother
<uig rom="aq-a cini">ᠠᠬ ᠠ ᠴᠢᠨᠢ</uig> your elder brother

The attribute does not agree in case with the qualified word. In the classical and modern language it does not agree in number either, but in the pre-classical language there was agreement in number. In the classical language only the demonstrative pronouns agree.
<uig rom="ene kümün">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> this person
<uig rom="ede nököd">ᠡᠳᠡ ᠨᠥᠺᠥᠳ</uig> these friends
<uig rom="qoyin-a irekün jobalang-ud">ᠬᠣᠶᠢᠨ ᠠ ᠢᠷᠡᠺᠦᠨ ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠤᠳ</uig> the sufferings which will come afterward
<uig rom="eldeb yirtincü-dür bükün qoor-nuγud">ᠡᠯᠳᠡᠪ ᠶᠢᠷᠲᠢᠨᠴᠦ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠪᠦᠺᠦᠨ ᠬᠣᠣᠷ ᠎ᠨᠤᠭᠤᠳ</uig> various sufferings existing in the world
<uig rom="enelkün amitan">ᠡᠨᠡᠯᠺᠦᠨ ᠠᠮᠢᠲᠠᠨ</uig> suffering living beings
<uig rom="jobalang-a tencirdegsed amitan">ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠠ ᠲᠡᠨᠴᠢᠷᠳᠡᠭᠰᠡᠳ ᠠᠮᠢᠲᠠᠨ</uig> living beings overwhelmed by sufferings
<uig rom="yeke bilig-ten burqad">ᠶᠡᠺᠡ ᠪᠢᠯᠢᠭ ᠎ᠲᠡᠨ ᠪᠤᠷᠬᠠᠳ</uig> the Buddhas possessing great wisdom
<uig rom="sansar-un gindan-dur enelkün amitan">ᠰᠠᠨᠰᠠᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠭᠢᠨᠳᠠᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠡᠨᠡᠯᠺᠦᠨ ᠠᠮᠢᠲᠠᠨ</uig>n living beings suffering in the prison of the material existence
<uig rom="maγus aran">ᠮᠠᠭᠤᠰ ᠠᠷᠠᠨ</uig> bad people
<uig rom="busud buyan-nuγud">ᠪᠤᠰᠤᠳ ᠪᠤᠶᠠᠨ ᠎ᠨᠤᠭᠤᠳ</uig> other virtues
<uig rom="bilig ügegün qulaγas">ᠪᠢᠯᠢᠭ ᠦᠭᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠬᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠᠰ</uig> thieves not having any intellect
As remarked above, the attribute does not agree in case with the word qualified. Regardless of the case of the word qualified, the attribute is a nominative, just as in English.
Nominative <uig rom="sayin morin">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ</uig> the good horse
Genitive <<uig rom="sayin morin-u">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠤ</uig> of the good horse
Dative-Locative <uig rom="sayin morin-dur">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ</uig> to the good horse
Accusative <uig rom="sayin morin-i">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠢ</uig> the good horse
Ablative <uig rom="sayin morin-aca">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ</uig> from the good horse
Instrumental <uig rom="sayin mori-bar">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢ ᠎ᠪᠠᠷ</uig> with the good horse
Comitative <uig rom="sayin morin-luγ-a">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠯᠤᠭ ᠠ</uig> together with the good horse

Thus the attribute is always a nominative. Another kind of attribute is the genitive attribute, showing to whom the object concerned belongs, e. g.,<uig rom="aq-a-yin nom">ᠠᠬ ᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠨᠣᠮ</uig> "the book of the elder brother."

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Nominative as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: Nouns expressing qualities and serving as adjectives in European languages are always nominative, regardless of the case of the word they modify.
<uig rom="ulaγan cilaγun">ᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠴᠢᠯᠠᠭᠤᠨ</uig> the red stone
<uig rom="sayin nom">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠨᠣᠮ</uig> the good book
<uig rom="jegerde morin">ᠵᠡᠭᠡᠷᠳᠡ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ</uig> a chestnut horse
<uig rom="türgen γool">ᠲᠦᠷᠭᠡᠨ ᠭᠣᠣᠯ</uig> a fast river (i. e., a torrent)
<uig rom="öndür aγula">ᠥᠨᠳᠦᠷ ᠠᠭᠤᠯᠠ</uig> a high mountain
<uig rom="möngke tngri">ᠮᠥᠩᠺᠡ ᠲᠩᠷᠢ</uig> the eternal heaven
<uig rom="γuu-a ökin">ᠭᠤᠤ ᠠ ᠥᠺᠢᠨ</uig> a beautiful girl
<uig rom="kögsin em-e">ᠺᠥᠭᠰᠢᠨ ᠡᠮ ᠡ</uig> an old woman
<uig rom="baγ-a keüken">ᠪᠠᠭ ᠠ ᠺᠡᠦᠺᠡᠨ</uig> a little child

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Nominative as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: Although there is no grammatical gender, words expressing the age and the coat of animals have double forms : a masculine and a feminine one.
<uig rom="γunan buqa">ᠭᠤᠨᠠᠨ ᠪᠤᠬᠠ</uig> a three-year-old bull
<uig rom="γunajin üniy-e">ᠭᠤᠨᠠᠵᠢᠨ ᠦᠨᠢᠶ ᠡ</uig> a three-year-old cow
<uig rom="dönen buqa">ᠳᠥᠨᠡᠨ ᠪᠤᠬᠠ</uig> a four-year-old bull
<uig rom="dönejin üniy-e">ᠳᠥᠨᠡᠵᠢᠨ ᠦᠨᠢᠶ ᠡ</uig> a four-year-old cow
<uig rom="ulaγan buqa">ᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠪᠤᠬᠠ</uig> a red bull
<uig rom="ulaγaqcin üniy-e">ᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠᠬᠴᠢᠨ ᠦᠨᠢᠶ ᠡ</uig> a red cow
<uig rom="sir-a γaqai">ᠰᠢᠷ ᠠ ᠭᠠᠬᠠᠢ</uig> a yellow boar
<uig rom="siraqcin γaqai">ᠰᠢᠷᠠᠬᠴᠢᠨ ᠭᠠᠬᠠᠢ</uig> a yellow sow

The last two examples show that names of animals referring both to the male and the female may be qualified by an attribute in a masculine form, when the animal concerned is a male, and in a feminine form, when the animal concerned is a female. Here are some additional examples :
<uig rom="caγan takiy-a">ᠴᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠲᠠᠺᠢᠶ ᠠ</uig> a white cock
<uig rom="caγaqcin takiy-a">ᠴᠠᠭᠠᠬᠴᠢᠨ ᠲᠠᠺᠢᠶ ᠠ</uig> a white hen
<uig rom="boro qarcaγai">ᠪᠣᠷᠣ ᠬᠠᠷᠴᠠᠭᠠᠢ</uig> a grey hawk
<uig rom="boroqcin qarcaγai">ᠪᠣᠷᠣᠬᠴᠢᠨ ᠬᠠᠷᠴᠠᠭᠠᠢ</uig> a grey female hawk

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Nominative as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: Nouns designating material and corresponding to European substantives are also in the nominative case.
<uig rom="modun bayising">ᠮᠣᠳᠤᠨ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠰᠢᠩ</uig> a wooden building (lit., "wood building")
<uig rom="altan bilecüg">ᠠᠯᠲᠠᠨ ᠪᠢᠯᠡᠴᠦᠭ</uig> a golden ring (lit., "gold ring")
<uig rom="mönggün kituγ-a">ᠮᠥᠩᠭᠦᠨ ᠺᠢᠲᠤᠭ ᠠ</uig> a silver knife
<uig rom="temür jida">ᠲᠡᠮᠦᠷ ᠵᠢᠳᠠ</uig> an iron spear
<uig rom="cilaγun süm-e">ᠴᠢᠯᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠰᠦᠮ ᠡ</uig> a stone temple

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Nominative as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: Nouns designating living beings may also serve as attributes in the nominative.
<uig rom="eme takiy-a">ᠡᠮᠡ ᠲᠠᠺᠢᠶ ᠠ</uig> hen (lit., "a female cock" or even "a woman cock")
<uig rom="ebügen kümün">ᠡᠪᠦᠭᠡᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> an old man (lit., "oldster person")
<uig rom="kümün görügesün">ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠭᠥᠷᠦᠭᠡᠰᠦᠨ</uig> ape (lit., "a man animal")
<uig rom="lama sibaγun">ᠯᠠᠮᠠ ᠰᠢᠪᠠᠭᠤᠨ</uig> a yellow duck (lit., "a lama bird", so called because of its reddish-yellow color resembling a coat of a lama. Its Latin name is anas nigra L.)
<uig rom="tarbaγan kümün">ᠲᠠᠷᠪᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> dwarf (lit., "a marmot man")
<uig rom="morin qaracaγai">ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠬᠠᠷᠠᠴᠠᠭᠠᠢ</uig> wagtail (lit., "a horse-swallow")
<uig rom="morin jil">ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠵᠢᠯ</uig> the horse year (the seventh year of the duodenary cycle)
<uig rom="üker quluγan-a">ᠦᠺᠡᠷ ᠬᠤᠯᠤᠭᠠᠨ ᠠ</uig> rat (lit., "an ox mouse")
<uig rom="üker buu">ᠦᠺᠡᠷ ᠪᠤᠤ</uig> cannon (lit., "an ox gun")
<uig rom="qan siregen">ᠬᠠᠨ ᠰᠢᠷᠡᠭᠡᠨ</uig> throne (lit., "a khan seat")
<uig rom="qaγan köbegün">ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠺᠥᠪᠡᠭᠦᠨ</uig> prince (lit., "a khaghan's son")

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Nominative as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: All pronouns, except the personal and reflexive pronouns, can serve as attributes in the nominative.
<uig rom="ene kümün">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> this person
<uig rom="aliba kümün">ᠠᠯᠢᠪᠠ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> whatever person
<uig rom="ken kümün">ᠺᠡᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> what man (lit., "who man")
<uig rom="yambar cu kümün">ᠶᠠᠮᠪᠠᠷ ᠴᠤ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> whatever person, any person
<uig rom="ele kereg">ᠡᠯᠡ ᠺᠡᠷᠡᠭ</uig> this business

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Nominative as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: The demonstrative pronouns agree in number with the word qualified. This is usual in the classical language and at times also occurs in modern books.
<uig rom="ene kümün">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> this person
<uig rom="ede kümün-nügüd">ᠡᠳᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠎ᠨᠦᠭᠦᠳ</uig> or <uig rom="edeger kümün-nügüd">ᠡᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠎ᠨᠦᠭᠦᠳ</uig> these people
<uig rom="tere kümün">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> that person
<uig rom="tede kümüs">ᠲᠡᠳᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠰ</uig> or <uig rom="tedeger kümüs">ᠲᠡᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠰ</uig> those people

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Nominative as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: All numerals, except the collective and multiplicative numerals, serve as attributes.
<uig rom="qoyar qani">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠬᠠᠨᠢ</uig> two friends
<uig rom="tabuduγar boti">ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠳᠤᠭᠠᠷ ᠪᠣᠲᠢ</uig> the fifth volume
<uig rom="arbaγad kümün">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠭᠠᠳ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> about ten people

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Nominative as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: All verbal nouns serve as attribute in the nominative case. In the pre-classical language they agreed in number with the word to which they referred.
<uig rom="irekü jil">ᠢᠷᠡᠺᠦ ᠵᠢᠯ</uig> next year (lit., "the year which will come")
<uig rom="ungsiqci sabi">ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠬᠴᠢ ᠰᠠᠪᠢ</uig> the reading pupil
<uig rom="ükügsen kümün">ᠦᠺᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> a dead person
<uig rom="aburaqci yurban erdeni">ᠠᠪᠤᠷᠠᠬᠴᠢ ᠶᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠡᠷᠳᠡᠨᠢ</uig> the saving Three jewels (i. e., Buddha, his teachings, and the Buddhist clergy)
<uig rom="enelkün amitan">ᠡᠨᠡᠯᠺᠦᠨ ᠠᠮᠢᠲᠠᠨ</uig> the suffering creatures (pre-classical)
<uig rom="jobaqsad amitan">ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠬᠰᠠᠳ ᠠᠮᠢᠲᠠᠨ</uig> the suffering creatures (pre-classical)

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Nominative as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: Compound nouns serve as attributes. A compound nominal attribute may consist of two words, jointly expressing one idea. A very usual compound nominal attribute is a group of words denoting a color. In this manner the idea of various shades of colors can be expressed.
<uig rom="küren ulaγan debel">ᠺᠦᠷᠡᠨ ᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠳᠡᠪᠡᠯ</uig> a dark red coat
<uig rom="sir-a ulaγan cirai">ᠰᠢᠷ ᠠ ᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠴᠢᠷᠠᠢ</uig> a yellow-red face
<uig rom="qurca ulaγan öngge">ᠬᠤᠷᠴᠠ ᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠥᠩᠭᠡ</uig> glaring red color
<uig rom="qar-a eriyen bars">ᠬᠠᠷ ᠠ ᠡᠷᠢᠶᠡᠨ ᠪᠠᠷᠰ</uig> a black-dappled tiger

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Nominative as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: A compound attribute often consists of a noun expressing a color preceded by another word designating something of which the main characteristic is the color in question, e. g., "snow-white."
<uig rom="cisun ulaγan tuq">ᠴᠢᠰᠤᠨ ᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠲᠤᠬ</uig> a blood-red flag
<uig rom="γal ulaγan öngge">ᠭᠠᠯ ᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠥᠩᠭᠡ</uig> fire-red color
<uig rom="altan gir-a naran">ᠠᠯᠲᠠᠨ ᠭᠢᠷ ᠠ ᠨᠠᠷᠠᠨ</uig> gold-yellow sun
<uig rom="casun caγan caγasun">ᠴᠠᠰᠤᠨ ᠴᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠴᠠᠭᠠᠰᠤᠨ</uig> snow-white paper
<uig rom="dung caγan sidün">ᠳᠤᠩ ᠴᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠰᠢᠳᠦᠨ</uig> shell-white teeth
<uig rom="ünegen ulaγan üsün">ᠦᠨᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠦᠰᠦᠨ</uig> fox-red hair

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Nominative as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: Another kind of compound attribute is a group of words of which one designates an object and the other a quality. Such groups correspond to the English "barefooted," "pink-faced," etc., with the difference that in Mongolian the order of the words is reversed: not "barefooted" but "foot-bare."
<uig rom="köl nicügen kümün">ᠺᠥᠯ ᠨᠢᠴᠦᠭᠡᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> a barefooted person (lit., "a foot-naked person")
<uig rom="am-a caγan quluγan-a">ᠠᠮ ᠠ ᠴᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠬᠤᠯᠤᠭᠠᠨ ᠠ</uig> a mouse with a white mouth (lit., "a mouthwhite mouse")

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Nominative as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: The diminutive suffix <uig rom=" -qan/-ken">ᠬᠠᠨ/ᠺᠡᠨ</uig> (cf. § 124) of a noun serving as an attribute often transforms the word qualified into a diminutive without affecting the meaning of the stem to which it refers. In other words, the diminutive Suffix, although belonging to one word, changes the meaning of the following word.
<uig rom="ulaγaqan (diminutive) ceceg">ᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠᠬᠠᠨ ᠴᠡᠴᠡᠭ</uig> a nice little red flower or a red floweret
<uig rom="baγaqan (diminutive) morin">ᠪᠠᠭᠠᠬᠠᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ</uig> a nice little horse

In the above examples the words <uig rom="ceceg">ᠴᠡᠴᠡᠭ</uig> "flower" and <uig rom="morin">ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ</uig> "horse" are not diminutives, but their attributes are diminutives. Nevertheless, we translate them as "floweret" and "nice horse," because the diminutive suffixes on their attributes refer to them and not to the attributes.

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Nominative as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: In the same manner, the feminine forms of words expressing the ages or colors of animals not having different names for males and females indicate that the animal in question is a female (see § 457).
<uig rom="qar-a sibaγun">ᠬᠠᠷ ᠠ ᠰᠢᠪᠠᠭᠤᠨ</uig> a black male bird
<uig rom="qaraqcin sibaγun">ᠬᠠᠷᠠᠬᠴᠢᠨ ᠰᠢᠪᠠᠭᠤᠨ</uig> a black female bird
<uig rom="dönen jaγan">ᠳᠥᠨᠡᠨ ᠵᠠᠭᠠᠨ</uig> a four-year-old male elephant
<uig rom="dönejin jaγan">ᠳᠥᠨᠡᠵᠢᠨ ᠵᠠᠭᠠᠨ</uig> a four-year-old female elephant
There is but one type of apposition in Mongolian: that of a noun serving as the proper name given to a person or an object.

Proper names, names of persons, cities, rivers, mountains, countries, and so on, are usually followed by an appellative. This means that the proper name is placed first and only the appellative takes the grammatical termination. As for the proper name, it is always a nominative regardless of the case of the appellative.
<uig rom="cinggis qan">ᠴᠢᠩᠭᠢᠰ ᠬᠠᠨ</uig> Chingis Khan
<uig rom="cinggis qan-dur">ᠴᠢᠩᠭᠢᠰ ᠬᠠᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ</uig> to Chingis Khan
<uig rom="kentei aγula">ᠺᠡᠨᠲᠡᠢ ᠠᠭᠤᠯᠠ</uig> the Kentei mountain range
<uig rom="ulaγan baγatur qota">ᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠪᠠᠭᠠᠲᠤᠷ ᠬᠣᠲᠠ</uig> the city of Ulan Bator
<uig rom="ulaγan baγatur qotan-a">ᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠪᠠᠭᠠᠲᠤᠷ ᠬᠣᠲᠠᠨ ᠠ</uig> in the city of Ulan Bator
In cases of less common proper names, the proper name is linked to the appellative noun by the converb kemen and the word <uig rom="nere-tü">ᠨᠡᠷᠡ ᠎ᠲᠦ</uig> "bearing the name."
<uig rom="ranjaqraγ kemen nere-tü balγasun">ᠷᠠᠨᠵᠠᠬᠷᠠᠭ ᠺᠡᠮᠡᠨ ᠨᠡᠷᠡ ᠎ᠲᠦ ᠪᠠᠯᠭᠠᠰᠤᠨ</uig> the city by the name of Rājagṛha
<uig rom="iravadi kemen nere-tü mören">ᠢᠷᠠᠸᠠᠳᠢ ᠺᠡᠮᠡᠨ ᠨᠡᠷᠡ ᠎ᠲᠦ ᠮᠥᠷᠡᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="iravadi nere-tü mören">ᠢᠷᠠᠸᠠᠳᠢ ᠨᠡᠷᠡ ᠎ᠲᠦ ᠮᠥᠷᠡᠨ</uig> the river Irrawaddy
In modern language the appellative noun sometimes precedes the proper name, a fact which must be attributed to foreign influence.
<uig rom="sayid amur">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠳ ᠠᠮᠤᠷ</uig> Minister Amur
<uig rom="nökör gendüng">ᠨᠥᠺᠥᠷ ᠭᠡᠨᠳᠦᠩ</uig> Comrade Gendung
In many cases the attribute expresses, together with the word to which it refers, a single idea. Such constructions can be regarded, from the point of view of their meanings, as one word.
<uig rom="sir-a sibaγun">ᠰᠢᠷ ᠠ ᠰᠢᠪᠠᠭᠤᠨ</uig> horned owl (lit., "the yellow bird")
<uig rom="caγan budaγ-a">ᠴᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠪᠤᠳᠠᠭ ᠠ</uig> rice (lit., "white millet")
<uig rom="qar-a modun">ᠬᠠᠷ ᠠ ᠮᠣᠳᠤᠨ</uig> larch tree (lit., "black tree")
<uig rom="qar-a görügesün">ᠬᠠᠷ ᠠ ᠭᠥᠷᠦᠭᠡᠰᠦᠨ</uig> bear (lit., "black animal")
<uig rom="caγan sibaγun">ᠴᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠰᠢᠪᠠᠭᠤᠨ</uig> swan (lit., "white bird")
To this category also special idiomatic expressions belong.
<uig rom="caγan toluγai">ᠴᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠲᠣᠯᠤᠭᠠᠢ</uig> primer (lit., "the white head")
<uig rom="qar-a kümün">ᠬᠠᠷ ᠠ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> ordinary man, layman (lit., "black person")
<uig rom="sir-a šajin">ᠰᠢᠷ ᠠ ᠱᠠᠵᠢᠨ</uig> Buddhism of the Tsonkapa sect, lamaism (lit., "the Yellow Religion")
<uig rom="sir-a tosun">ᠰᠢᠷ ᠠ ᠲᠣᠰᠤᠨ</uig> butter (lit., "yellow fat")
<uig rom="ömükei tosun">ᠥᠮᠦᠺᠡᠢ ᠲᠣᠰᠤᠨ</uig> naphtha, rock oil (lit., "the stinking oil")
<uig rom="qalaγun ger">ᠬᠠᠯᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠭᠡᠷ</uig> bath (lit., "hot house")
<uig rom="boro ger">ᠪᠣᠷᠣ ᠭᠡᠷ</uig> kitchen (lit., "grey house")
<uig rom="qar-a ger">ᠬᠠᠷ ᠠ ᠭᠡᠷ</uig> jail (lit., "black house")
<uig rom="muqur tergen">ᠮᠤᠬᠤᠷ ᠲᠡᠷᠭᠡᠨ</uig> motor car (lit., "a carriage without horns")
<uig rom="altan γadasun">ᠠᠯᠲᠠᠨ ᠭᠠᠳᠠᠰᠤᠨ</uig> day star (lit., "the Golden Peg")

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Interrogative as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: The Mongolian language has almost no relative subordinate clauses. Their function is performed by special constructions with interrogative pronouns serving as attributes referring to the word following the interrogative pronoun. Such constructions can be called relative attributive constructions.
These constructions with an interrogative pronoun can serve as subject, attribute, or object of any long sentence.
<uig rom="ken deyilügsen inu abumui">ᠺᠡᠨ ᠳᠡᠶᠢᠯᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠠᠪᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He who has vanquished will take.
<uig rom="ali üjegsen kümün-ece asaγubai">ᠠᠯᠢ ᠦᠵᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠠᠰᠠᠭᠤᠪᠠᠢ</uig> He asked people who had seen. (Lit., "He asked what having Seen people.")
<uig rom="ali dur-a-tai kümün bügesü tegün-i abcu bolumui">ᠠᠯᠢ ᠳᠤᠷ ᠠ ᠎ᠲᠠᠢ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠰᠦ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠠᠪᠴᠤ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> Anyone willing may take it. (Lit., "If there is what willing person may take it.")

<uig rom="ene yeke kölgen sudur-i ken ungsiqu kümün inu bodi qutuγ-i olqu boltuγai">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠶᠡᠺᠡ ᠺᠥᠯᠭᠡᠨ ᠰᠤᠳᠤᠷ ᠢ ᠺᠡᠨ ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠬᠤ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠪᠣᠳᠢ ᠬᠤᠲᠤᠭ ᠢ ᠣᠯᠬᠤ ᠪᠣᠯᠲᠤᠭᠠᠢ</uig> May the people who read this Mahāyāna sūtra obtain holiness! (Lit., "This Mahāyāna sūtra who reading people may obtain holiness!")

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Genitive as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: The genitive of any declinable part of speech may serve as attribute. Usually such a genitive indicates the possessor of the object concerned and answers the question "whose?," though a genitive attribute may also have other meanings.
All particulars concerning the genitive will be found in the sections dealing with the genitive (see § 500ff.); only a few remarks will be made here.

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Attribute - Genitive as attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: A word modified by a genitive attribute indicating the possessor can be followed by the genitive of the personal pronouns <uig rom="inu">ᠢᠨᠤ</uig> "his" and <uig rom="anu">ᠠᠨᠤ</uig> "their," which connect the attribute and the modified word more closely.
<uig rom="qaγan-u cerig inu">ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠴᠡᠷᠢᠭ ᠢᠨᠤ</uig> khaghan's army (lit., "khaghan's army his")
<uig rom="baγatud-un morid anu">ᠪᠠᠭᠠᠲᠤᠳ ᠤᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠳ ᠠᠨᠤ</uig> the heroes' horses (lit., "the heroes' horses theirs")
<uig rom="tegün-ü nom inu">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠤ ᠨᠣᠮ ᠢᠨᠤ</uig> his book (lit., "his book his")
<uig rom="teden-ü nom-nuγud anu">ᠲᠡᠳᠡᠨ ᠤ ᠨᠣᠮ ᠎ᠨᠤᠭᠤᠳ ᠠᠨᠤ</uig> their books (lit., "their books theirs")

A word can have several attributes. In such case, all attributes precede the word modified. An attribute indicating the most important quality or characteristic of an object is always placed as near as possible to the word modified. One attriute qualifying another must immediately precede it. Othereise both would be attributes of the same word. This is the case with the genitive attributes, the attributes of which always precede and can not be placed between the genitive and the word modified.

Words indicating coats of animals or other living beings as invariable, permanent characteristics are placed as near as possible to the word to be modified. They usually are placed immediately before the latter.
<uig rom="qurdun qar-a morin">ᠬᠤᠷᠳᠤᠨ ᠬᠠᠷ ᠠ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ</uig> a quick black horse
<uig rom="sayin jegerde morin">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠵᠡᠭᠡᠷᠳᠡ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ</uig> a good chestnut-colored horse
<uig rom="kögsin jegerde morin">ᠺᠥᠭᠰᠢᠨ ᠵᠡᠭᠡᠷᠳᠡ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ</uig> an old chestnut-colored horse
Words denoting the material of which an object consists are placed as closely to it as possible.
<uig rom="öndür modun bayising">ᠥᠨᠳᠦᠷ ᠮᠣᠳᠤᠨ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠰᠢᠩ</uig> a high wooden building
<uig rom="ulaγan cilaγun kerem">ᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠴᠢᠯᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠺᠡᠷᠡᠮ</uig> a red stone castle
<uig rom="urtu temür jida">ᠤᠷᠲᠤ ᠲᠡᠮᠦᠷ ᠵᠢᠳᠠ</uig> a long iron spear
Demonstrative and interrogative pronouns immediately precede other attributes in the nominative case.
<uig rom="tere caγan aγula">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠴᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠠᠭᠤᠯᠠ</uig> that white mountain
<uig rom="yambar kögsin kümün">ᠶᠠᠮᠪᠠᠷ ᠺᠥᠭᠰᠢᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> what old man?
A genitive attribute is placed before the nominative attribute. Otherwise the latter would be its attribute.
<uig rom="baqsi-yin sin-e nom">ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠰᠢᠨ ᠡ ᠨᠣᠮ</uig> the teacher's new book
<uig rom="qaγan-u yeke baγatur">ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠶᠡᠺᠡ ᠪᠠᠭᠠᠲᠤᠷ</uig> the khaghan's great knight
Numerals precede nominative attributes and follow genitive attributes.
<uig rom="dörben qar-a morin">ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ ᠬᠠᠷ ᠠ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ</uig> four black horses
<uig rom="tabun sin-e nom">ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠰᠢᠨ ᠡ ᠨᠣᠮ</uig> five new books
In cases when it is necessary to stress the number of the objects concerned the numeral may be placed immediately before the word to be modified.

<uig rom="qar-a dörben morin jegerde tabun morin">ᠬᠠᠷ ᠠ ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠵᠡᠭᠡᠷᠳᠡ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ</uig><uig rom="">ᠬᠠᠷ᠎ᠠ ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ</uig> qar-a dörben morin jegerde tabun morin black horses four, chestnut colored horses five
Verbal nouns with or without converbs are placed before a nominative attribute, but after numerals.
<uig rom="iregsen kögsin kümün">ᠢᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠺᠥᠭᠰᠢᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> an old man who has come
<uig rom="qoyar ükügsen kümün">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠦᠺᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> two dead persons
Of two attributes, that ending in <uig rom="-tai/-tei">ᠲᠠᠢ</uig> (see § 138) or <uig rom=" -tu/-tü">᠎ᠲᠤ</uig> (See § 140) occupies the first place.
<uig rom="moritai qar-a kümün">ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠲᠠᠢ ᠬᠠᠷ ᠠ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> a mounted layman (if <uig rom="qar-a">ᠬᠠᠷ᠎ᠠ </uig> were placed first, such a construction would mean "a person with a black horse")
As remarked above, an attribute which qualifies another attribute immediately precedes it.
<uig rom="sin-e baqsi-yin nom">ᠰᠢᠨ ᠡ ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠨᠣᠮ</uig> the book of the new teacher
<uig rom="olan maltai kümün">ᠣᠯᠠᠨ ᠮᠠᠯᠲᠠᠢ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> a person possessing many cattle

A special case is that of nouns ending in <uig rom="-tai/-tei">᠎ᠲᠠᠢ</uig> (see § 138) and serving as attributes. When there is an attribute of such a word ending in <uig rom="-tai/-tei">ᠲᠠᠢ</uig> , e. g. <uig rom="sayin moritai kümün">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠲᠠᠢ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> "a person possessing good horses," the order of the attributes can be reversed. In this event, the word <uig rom="sayin">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ</uig> "good" (which is an attribute of "horse") takes the suffix <uig rom="-tai"> ᠎ᠲᠠᠢ</uig> and the word <uig rom="moritai">ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠲᠠᠢ</uig> "possessing horses" loses its suffix. The result is <uig rom="morin sayitai kümün">ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠲᠠᠢ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> "a person possessing good horses" (lit., "possessing something good in the way of horses").
<uig rom="sayin keletei kümün">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠺᠡᠯᠡᠲᠡᠢ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> or <uig rom="sayin amatai kümün">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠠᠮᠠᠲᠠᠢ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> a man having a good tongue (or mouth), i. e., a man talking pleasantly
<uig rom="kele sayitai">ᠺᠡᠯᠡ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠲᠠᠢ</uig> or <uig rom="am-a sayitai">ᠠᠮ ᠠ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠲᠠᠢ</uig> id.
<uig rom="yeke usutai γajar">ᠶᠡᠺᠡ ᠤᠰᠤᠲᠠᠢ ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ</uig> or <uig rom="usu yeketei γajar">ᠤᠰᠤ ᠶᠡᠺᠡᠲᠡᠢ ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ</uig> "a country abundant in water
Both nominal and verbal forms may be qualified by adverbs. The latter immediately precede the word they modify.
Many nouns and even numerals may serve as adverbs without changing their form.
Nouns expressing qualities may be qualified by adverbs (adverbia modi).
<uig rom="masi sayin">ᠮᠠᠰᠢ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ</uig> very good
<uig rom="yeke maγu">ᠶᠡᠺᠡ ᠮᠠᠭᠤ</uig> very bad
<uig rom="ülemji sayin">ᠦᠯᠡᠮᠵᠢ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ</uig> exceedingly good
<uig rom="ilangγui-a ciqula">ᠢᠯᠠᠩᠭᠤᠢ ᠠ ᠴᠢᠬᠤᠯᠠ</uig> extremely important
<uig rom="tong buruγu">ᠲᠣᠩ ᠪᠤᠷᠤᠭᠤ</uig> completely wrong
<uig rom="qab qar-a">ᠬᠠᠪ ᠬᠠᠷ ᠠ</uig> completely black
Adverbs may be qualified by other adverbs (adverbia modi).
<uig rom="masi sayin ungsidaγ šabi">ᠮᠠᠰᠢ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠳᠠᠭ ᠱᠠᠪᠢ</uig> a pupil who reads very well tong
<uig rom="buruγu kelebei">ᠪᠤᠷᠤᠭᠤ ᠺᠡᠯᠡᠪᠡᠢ</uig> He spoke completely in error.
<uig rom="masi qol-a odba">ᠮᠠᠰᠢ ᠬᠣᠯ ᠠ ᠣᠳᠪᠠ</uig> He went very far.
Adverbs (adverbia loci, temporis, modi) may refer to verbs.
<uig rom="ci qamiγ-a odumui">ᠴᠢ ᠬᠠᠮᠢᠭ ᠠ ᠣᠳᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> Where are you going?
<uig rom="cinaqsi yabuba">ᠴᠢᠨᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠪᠠ</uig> He went further.
<uig rom="bi marγasi iremüi">ᠪᠢ ᠮᠠᠷᠭᠠᠰᠢ ᠢᠷᠡᠮᠦᠢ</uig> I shall come tomorrow.
<uig rom="sayin ungsimui">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He reads well.
<uig rom="γurbanta daγudabai">ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨᠲᠠ ᠳᠠᠭᠤᠳᠠᠪᠠᠢ</uig> He called three times.
<uig rom="qoyar asaγuba">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠠᠰᠠᠭᠤᠪᠠ</uig> He asked twice.
<uig rom="genedte irebei">ᠭᠡᠨᠡᠳᠲᠡ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡᠢ</uig> He came suddenly.
Many nouns in various oblique cases, primarily in the instrumental, may serve as adverbs.
<uig rom="türgen-iyer mordobai">ᠲᠦᠷᠭᠡᠨ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠮᠣᠷᠳᠣᠪᠠᠢ</uig> He galloped quickly.
<uig rom="maγui-a jobaγamui">ᠮᠠᠭᠤᠢ ᠠ ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠭᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He torments fearfully.
Converbs may serve as adverbs.
<uig rom="dakin irebei">ᠳᠠᠺᠢᠨ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡᠢ</uig> He came again. (Lit., "repeating," conv. modale of <uig rom="daki-">ᠳᠠᠺᠢ ᠎</uig> "to repeat.")
<uig rom="ci yaγakin irebei">ᠴᠢ ᠶᠠᠭᠠᠺᠢᠨ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡᠢ</uig> Why did you come? (Lit., "What doing did you come ? ")

A sentence can be introduced by or include words not governed by any member of the sentence and not serving as subject, predicate, or attribute. Such words do not refer to any member of the sentence and can easily be omitted without any effect upon the sentence as a whole. Such words are comparable, in thisa respect, to certain conjunctions ("notwithstanding," "yet"), direct address ("Father, give me a book!") and so on in English.

entry.title: Syntax - Sentence - Isolated words
entry.title2: Syntax - Sentence - Isolated words - Direct address

paragraphs.paragraph: Nouns and pronouns are used in the nominative case in direct address. Nouns are accompanied, in such cases, by the interjection a (pronounced ā) which is placed after the noun. In old grammars the interjection a is erroneously called the vocative suffix, which, in reality, does not exist in Mongolian.
<uig rom="qaγan minu-a minu üge sonosun soyurq-a">ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠠ ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠦᠭᠡ ᠰᠣᠨᠣᠰᠤᠨ ᠰᠣᠶᠤᠷᠬ ᠠ</uig> Ah, my Khaghan, deign to listen to my words !
<uig rom="burqan-a">ᠪᠤᠷᠬᠠᠨ ᠠ</uig> Ah, Buddha!
<uig rom="ci egün-i buu ab">ᠴᠢ ᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠪᠤᠤ ᠠᠪ</uig> You must not take this! (Lit,, "You, do not take this !")
The interjections are what may be called isolated words.
<uig rom="qalaγ qoqoi juru ci yaγakiγsan bui">ᠬᠠᠯᠠᠭ ᠬᠣᠬᠣᠢ ᠵᠤᠷᠤ ᠴᠢ ᠶᠠᠭᠠᠺᠢᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> Alas, Juru, what have you done?
<uig rom="j-a ci ken bui">ᠵ ᠠ ᠴᠢ ᠺᠡᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> Well, who are you?

The nominative is the case of the subject, attribute, and predicate. The subject is either a simple nominative of a declinable part of speech or a nominative with a aubject designator. The latter is the pronoun inu or anu, the particle <uig rom="ber">ᠪᠡᠷ</uig> (which should not be confused with the instrumental suffix <uig rom="-bar/-ber">᠎ᠪᠠᠷ</uig>), or the converbs <uig rom="bolbasu">ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤ</uig> or <uig rom="bügesü">ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠰᠦ</uig> .
The simple nominative as subject has been discussed in § 441.
See also §280

The subject may be emphasized by the above-mentioned designators. It is always emphasized by one of them, if the word serving as a subject is a part of speech which usually serves as an attribute, e. g., a demonstrative pronoun, a noun expressing a quality (e. g., <uig rom="sayin">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ</uig> "good"), or a verbal noun. Such words can be easily misunderstood, if they are not followed by a designator, e. g., <uig rom="ene kümün">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> without a designator after <uig rom="ene">ᠡᠨᠡ</uig> is "this man," but with <uig rom="bolbasu">ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤ</uig> (<uig rom="ene bolbasu kümün">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig>) we have a sentence lacking the copula: "This is a man." (Lit., "If it be this-a man.")

entry.title: Syntax - Cases - Nominiative
entry.title2: Cases - Nominiative - Pronouns inu and anu

paragraphs.paragraph: The pronouns <uig rom="inu">ᠢᠨᠤ</uig> "his" and <uig rom="anu">ᠠᠨᠤ</uig> "their" are the genitive forms of the extinct personal pronouns *i "he" and *a "they." They indicate that the person or object in question belongs to the third person.
<uig rom="aq-a inu irebei">ᠠᠬ ᠠ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡᠢ</uig> His elder brother came.
<uig rom="blam-a-nar anu quralduba">ᠪᠯᠠᠮ ᠠ ᠎ᠨᠠᠷ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠬᠤᠷᠠᠯᠳᠤᠪᠠ</uig> Their lamas assembled.

These pronouns are frequently used, when the persons or objects in question do not belong, in the direct sense, to anybody. In reality, there is nothing in the world which does not belong to something. There is nothing which stands outside all groups (sui generis) : sun and moon are parts of the universe, birds and insects belong to the animal kingdom, and so on. The primitive Mongol of ancient times was unable to imagine anything not being part of a group. Therefore, even in cases where ownership was out of the question, he tried to place objects into groups, considering them as belonging to their respective groups, hence the expressions "Their birds go in autumn and return in spring," "Its sun has risen," and so on. Besides, the person or thing indicated by the designator inu or anu is distinguished from all other similar persons or things, as one or something acting in the manner expressed by its predicate, as distinguished from other persons or things not acting in this manner.

The following examples are classified into two groups: the first group contains examples of sentences with the pronouns <uig rom="inu">ᠢᠨᠤ</uig> or <uig rom="anu">ᠠᠨᠤ</uig> in their literal senses with reference to a possessor, and the second group contains examples of sentences with the same pronouns used with no reference to a possessor.
First group
<uig rom="tegün-ü aci inu tegün-ece ülemji nemeyü">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠤ ᠠᠴᠢ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠦᠯᠡᠮᠵᠢ ᠨᠡᠮᠡᠶᠦ</uig> Its benefit inereases (becoming) more than it.
<uig rom="nadur jobalang-un qoor-a inu daki yaγun j-e bolqu">ᠨᠠᠳᠤᠷ ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠤᠨ ᠬᠣᠣᠷ ᠠ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠳᠠᠺᠢ ᠶᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠵ ᠡ ᠪᠣᠯᠬᠤ</uig> What will be the evil of suffering to me?

<uig rom="olan qoor-nuγud-i nemegülkü-yin γaqca siltaγan inu minu jirüken-dür maγad büged">ᠣᠯᠠᠨ ᠬᠣᠣᠷ ᠎ᠨᠤᠭᠤᠳ ᠢ ᠨᠡᠮᠡᠭᠦᠯᠺᠦ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠭᠠᠬᠴᠠ ᠰᠢᠯᠲᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠵᠢᠷᠦᠺᠡᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠮᠠᠭᠠᠳ ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠳ</uig> The only cause of the increase of many evils is certainly in my heart.
<uig rom="bui inu adali-yin tulada nigen bolqu">ᠪᠤᠢ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠠᠳᠠᠯᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠲᠤᠯᠠᠳᠠ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠬᠤ</uig> As their existence is similar (they) will be one and the same.

<uig rom="urida bolju bütüjü nögcigsen-ece üleküi inu edüge nadur yaγun bui">ᠤᠷᠢᠳᠠ ᠪᠣᠯᠵᠤ ᠪᠦᠲᠦᠵᠦ ᠨᠥᠭᠴᠢᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠦᠯᠡᠺᠦᠢ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠡᠳᠦᠭᠡ ᠨᠠᠳᠤᠷ ᠶᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> What is to me now the remainder of what had appeared in the past and has ceased to be?
<uig rom="jirγalang-un siltaγan anu nigen nigen-te boluyu">ᠵᠢᠷᠭᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠤᠨ ᠰᠢᠯᠲᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠎ᠲᠡ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠶᠤ</uig> Each cause of happiness comes into existence (only) once.
<uig rom="bodisadu-a-nar-un yabudal anu teyimü bui">ᠪᠣᠳᠢᠰᠠᠳᠤ ᠠ ᠎ᠨᠠᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠳᠠᠯ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠲᠡᠶᠢᠮᠦ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> Such are the deeds of the Bodhisattvas.

<uig rom="mongγol-un γajar oron anu γadaγadu dalai-aca neliyed qola bayimui">ᠮᠣᠩᠭᠣᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ ᠣᠷᠣᠨ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠭᠠᠳᠠᠭᠠᠳᠤ ᠳᠠᠯᠠᠢ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠨᠡᠯᠢᠶᠡᠳ ᠬᠣᠯᠠ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠮᠤᠢ</uig> Mongolia (lit., "the country of the Mongols") is quite far away from the ocean (lit., "the outer sea").
<uig rom="mongγol-un caq ularil anu qaγurai bayimui">ᠮᠣᠩᠭᠣᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠴᠠᠬ ᠤᠯᠠᠷᠢᠯ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠬᠠᠭᠤᠷᠠᠢ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠮᠤᠢ</uig> The climate of Mongolia is dry.

<uig rom="mongγol γajar-a aγar-un kei inu masi qaγurai bayimui">ᠮᠣᠩᠭᠣᠯ ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ ᠠ ᠠᠭᠠᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠺᠡᠢ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠮᠠᠰᠢ ᠬᠠᠭᠤᠷᠠᠢ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠮᠤᠢ</uig> The air is very dry in Mongolia. (Lit., "The air of the atmosphere is very dry in the Mongolian country.")
Second group
<uig rom="nasu caq-tur tere metü kereg inu uqaju üiledtügei">ᠨᠠᠰᠤ ᠴᠠᠬ ᠲᠤᠷ ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠮᠡᠲᠦ ᠺᠡᠷᠡᠭ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠤᠬᠠᠵᠤ ᠦᠢᠯᠡᠳᠲᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> Through all the span of life such things should be done understandingly.
<uig rom="erkin inu busud-un tusa-yi sedkigdeküi">ᠡᠷᠺᠢᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠪᠤᠰᠤᠳ ᠤᠨ ᠲᠤᠰᠠ ᠶᠢ ᠰᠡᠳᠺᠢᠭᠳᠡᠺᠦᠢ</uig> The sublime must think of the profit of the others.
<uig rom="ünen inu ese oldabasu">ᠦᠨᠡᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠡᠰᠡ ᠣᠯᠳᠠᠪᠠᠰᠤ</uig> if truth is not to be found
<uig rom="ebül inu masi küiten jun anu masi qalaγun amui">ᠡᠪᠦᠯ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠮᠠᠰᠢ ᠺᠦᠢᠲᠡᠨ ᠵᠤᠨ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠮᠠᠰᠢ ᠬᠠᠯᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> Winter is very cold (and) summer is very hot.

Although there is a slight difference between the examples of the two groups, the use of the pronouns <uig rom="inu">ᠢᠨᠤ</uig> and <uig rom="anu">ᠠᠨᠤ</uig> is justified even from the point of view of their original meaning:

<uig rom="tegün-ü aci inu">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠤ ᠠᠴᠢ ᠢᠨᠤ</uig> "its benefit" (lit., "its benefit its") and <uig rom="erkin inu">ᠡᠷᠺᠢᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ</uig> "the sublime" (lit., "his sublime"), because the others, not mentioned here, are not sublime and he is the only sublime among them; hence "his or their sublime."

The sentence <uig rom="ebül inu masi küiten jun anu masi qalaγun amui">ᠡᠪᠦᠯ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠮᠠᠰᠢ ᠺᠦᠢᠲᠡᠨ ᠵᠤᠨ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠮᠠᠰᠢ ᠬᠠᠯᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> "Winter is very cold (and) summer is very hot" contains also the pronouns <uig rom="inu">ᠢᠨᠤ</uig> and <uig rom="anu">ᠠᠨᠤ</uig> . In this sentence winter and summer are opposed to each other and, therefore, even here the use of the pronouns <uig rom="inu">ᠢᠨᠤ</uig> and <uig rom="anu">ᠠᠨᠤ</uig> is justified: "Of them winter is very cold and of them summer is very hot."
However, the original meanings of <uig rom="inu">ᠢᠨᠤ</uig> and <uig rom="anu">ᠠᠨᠤ</uig> are no longer apparent in all cases and, therefore, they are often omitted, e. g., in this sentence:
<uig rom="jobalang-un siltaγan masi olan bolumui">ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠤᠨ ᠰᠢᠯᠲᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠮᠠᠰᠢ ᠣᠯᠠᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> "The causes of suffering are very numerous."
This sentence immediately follows, in the same book, the sentence:
<uig rom="jirγalang-un siltaγan anu nigen nigen-te boluyu">ᠵᠢᠷᠭᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠤᠨ ᠰᠢᠯᠲᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠎ᠲᠡ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠶᠤ</uig> "The causes of happines each come into existence once."
In two similar constructions the designator anu is present one time and it is omitted the other time.
The first meaning of the particle <uig rom="ber">ᠪᠡᠷ</uig> is "too" or "even." This often serves as a designator of the subject.
<uig rom="qamiγ-a bolqu tere metü buyan ber">ᠬᠠᠮᠢᠭ ᠠ ᠪᠣᠯᠬᠤ ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠮᠡᠲᠦ ᠪᠤᠶᠠᠨ ᠪᠡᠷ</uig> Where will there be a virtue like that?
<uig rom="basa basa nigül-nügüd ber masida törömüi">ᠪᠠᠰᠠ ᠪᠠᠰᠠ ᠨᠢᠭᠦᠯ ᠎ᠨᠦᠭᠦᠳ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠮᠠᠰᠢᠳᠠ ᠲᠥᠷᠥᠮᠦᠢ</uig> Again and again sins are born in great numbers.
<uig rom="egün-ece yeke mungqaq ber ügei bui">ᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠶᠡᠺᠡ ᠮᠤᠩᠬᠠᠬ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> There is no greater foolishness than this.
<uig rom="nadur ken ber ögkü">ᠨᠠᠳᠤᠷ ᠺᠡᠨ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠥᠭᠺᠦ</uig> Who will give me?

<uig rom="qamuq tengri-ner asuri-nar ker ber minu dayisun bolbasu ber tede ber ayus tamu-yin γal-un dotor-a uduridcu oroγul-un ülü cidaqun">ᠬᠠᠮᠤᠬ ᠲᠡᠩᠷᠢ ᠎ᠨᠡᠷ ᠠᠰᠤᠷᠢ ᠎ᠨᠠᠷ ᠺᠡᠷ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠳᠠᠶᠢᠰᠤᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠲᠡᠳᠡ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠠᠶᠤᠰ ᠲᠠᠮᠤ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠭᠠᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠳᠣᠲᠣᠷ ᠠ ᠤᠳᠤᠷᠢᠳᠴᠤ ᠣᠷᠣᠭᠤᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠦᠯᠦ ᠴᠢᠳᠠᠬᠤᠨ</uig> Even if all deities and Asura became my enemies, they could not lead and put me into the fire of the terrible hell.

<uig rom="urin taciyangγui terigüten dayisud-un γar köl terigüten ber ügei buyu">ᠤᠷᠢᠨ ᠲᠠᠴᠢᠶᠠᠩᠭᠤᠢ ᠲᠡᠷᠢᠭᠦᠲᠡᠨ ᠳᠠᠶᠢᠰᠤᠳ ᠤᠨ ᠭᠠᠷ ᠺᠥᠯ ᠲᠡᠷᠢᠭᠦᠲᠡᠨ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ ᠪᠤᠶᠤ</uig> There are no hands and feet (nor) anything else of foes such as anger and passion.
<uig rom="nigül ber ülü bolun buyan-nuγud nemeyü">ᠨᠢᠭᠦᠯ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠦᠯᠦ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠨ ᠪᠤᠶᠠᠨ ᠎ᠨᠤᠭᠤᠳ ᠨᠡᠮᠡᠶᠦ</uig> There is no sin and the virtues increase.

<uig rom="tedüi kü jobalang-i üjejü bür-ün tegün-ü tonilqui ber inu ügei bui">ᠲᠡᠳᠦᠢ ᠺᠦ ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠢ ᠦᠵᠡᠵᠦ ᠪᠦᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠤ ᠲᠣᠨᠢᠯᠬᠤᠢ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> In consequence of witnessing so many sufferings there is even no salvation for him. (Lit., "there is even no salvation of his.")
<uig rom="tede bügüde ber nigültü sedkil-ece boluqsan buyu">ᠲᠡᠳᠡ ᠪᠦᠭᠦᠳᠡ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠨᠢᠭᠦᠯᠲᠦ ᠰᠡᠳᠺᠢᠯ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠪᠤᠶᠤ</uig> All that happened from the sinful thought.
See also §682

entry.title: Syntax - Cases - Nominiative
entry.title2: Cases - Nominiative - Converbs bolbasu and bügesü

paragraphs.paragraph: The converb <uig rom="bolbasu">ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤ</uig> "if he becomes" of the verb <uig rom="bol-">ᠪᠣᠯ ᠎</uig> "to become" and the converb <uig rom="bügesü">ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠰᠦ</uig> "if he is" of the verb <uig rom="bü-">ᠪᠦ ᠎</uig> "to be" serve as designators of the subject. Sentences such as <uig rom="mongγol ulus bolbasu aγuu yeke amui">ᠮᠣᠩᠭᠣᠯ ᠤᠯᠤᠰ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤ ᠠᠭᠤᠤ ᠶᠡᠺᠡ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> can be translated literally as "If it is Mongolia, it is wide and large." In English idiom the sentence should read: "Mongolia is wide and large."
