As remarked above, certain parts of speech usually serve as attributes. Such parts of speech, attributive par excellence, are demonstrative pronouns, verbal nouns, and nouns expressing qualitiea and acting as adjectives in the European languages.

Such expressions as <uig rom="ene nom">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠨᠣᠮ</uig> , <uig rom="iregsen kümün">ᠢᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> , and so on, consist of nouns with attributes: "this book," "the person who has come." The only way of converting these attributes into subjects is to separate the pronoun <uig rom="ene">ᠡᠨᠡ</uig> "this" or the verbal noun <uig rom="iregsen">ᠢᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ</uig> "who has come" from the words <uig rom="nom">ᠨᠣᠮ</uig> "book" or <uig rom="kümün">ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> "person" by an element which emphasizes the subject. This is the only possible means of indicating that the words in question serve as subjects. Therefore, in all such cases in the modern language the converbs <uig rom="bolbasu">ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤ</uig> and <uig rom="bügesü">ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠰᠦ</uig> are used. The presence of a converb after the word which, without a converb, would serve as an attribute, and before another word, indicates that the group concerned does not constitute an attributive construction, since no member of a sentence may be placed between an attribute and a word to be modified. In other words, an attribute is always placed immediately before the word to whieh it refers.
All other designators (<uig rom="inu">ᠢᠨᠤ</uig> , <uig rom="anu">ᠠᠨᠤ</uig> , and <uig rom="ber">ᠪᠡᠷ</uig> ) are subject to the same rules.

<uig rom="negüdelcin arad bolbasu üker aduγu qoni imaγa jerge-yin mal öskejü usu belciger-i daγaju negüdel-iyer amiduramui">ᠨᠡᠭᠦᠳᠡᠯᠴᠢᠨ ᠠᠷᠠᠳ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤ ᠦᠺᠡᠷ ᠠᠳᠤᠭᠤ ᠬᠣᠨᠢ ᠢᠮᠠᠭᠠ ᠵᠡᠷᠭᠡ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠠᠯ ᠥᠰᠺᠡᠵᠦ ᠤᠰᠤ ᠪᠡᠯᠴᠢᠭᠡᠷ ᠢ ᠳᠠᠭᠠᠵᠤ ᠨᠡᠭᠦᠳᠡᠯ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠠᠮᠢᠳᠤᠷᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> The nomads (lit., "nomad people") raise cattle, horses, sheep, goats, and other stock, follow water and pasturage, and lead a nomadic life.

<uig rom="erkim bayan bolbasu erdem bilig, dumdadu bayan bolbasu eregül sayin, adaq bayan bolbasu aduγu mal bui">ᠡᠷᠺᠢᠮ ᠪᠠᠶᠠᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤ ᠡᠷᠳᠡᠮ ᠪᠢᠯᠢᠭ᠃ ᠳᠤᠮᠳᠠᠳᠤ ᠪᠠᠶᠠᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤ ᠡᠷᠡᠭᠦᠯ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ᠃ ᠠᠳᠠᠬ ᠪᠠᠶᠠᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤ ᠠᠳᠤᠭᠤ ᠮᠠᠯ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> The highest wealth is science and intellect, the intermediate wealth is health, the lowest wealth is horses and cattle. (A proverb.)
<uig rom="qaγan qatun bügesü bügüdeger masi bayasbai">ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠬᠠᠲᠤᠨ ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠰᠦ ᠪᠦᠭᠦᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ ᠮᠠᠰᠢ ᠪᠠᠶᠠᠰᠪᠠᠢ</uig> The khaghan and the queen were both very glad.
The genitive is governed by a noun. A genitive with a postposition serves as an object governed by a verb.
There are three principal kinds of genitive

a) The attributive genitive
b) The predicative genitive (very rare in Written Mongolian)
c) The genitive with a postposition
See also §281
The attributive genitive (genitivus attributivus) acts as an attribute. There are several special cases.
A. Genitivua appositivus
The appositive genitive occurs in proper names similar to the English "the city of New York."
<uig rom="ong-un γool">ᠣᠩ ᠤᠨ ᠭᠣᠣᠯ</uig> the Ongin River (lit., "the river of Ong," i. e. the river of Wang, Chin. "king")
<uig rom="tariyatu-yin keyid">ᠲᠠᠷᠢᠶᠠᠲᠤ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠺᠡᠶᠢᠳ</uig> the Tariyatu Monastery (lit., "the monastery of Tariyatu")
<uig rom="terki-yin caγan naγur">ᠲᠡᠷᠺᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠴᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠨᠠᠭᠤᠷ</uig> Lake Terkin Chaghan (lit., "the White Lake of Terki")
B. Genitiws possessivus
The possessive genitive indicates the possessor - in the widest sense of the word - of something. There are several kinds of possessive genitive.
a) Genitivus possessoris : this genitive indicates the possessor or owner in the narrow sense of the word.
<uig rom="šabi-yin nom">ᠱᠠᠪᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠨᠣᠮ</uig> the pupil's book
<uig rom="aq-a-yin morin">ᠠᠬ ᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ</uig> the horse of the elder brother
<uig rom="baqsi-yin ger">ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠭᠡᠷ</uig> the teacher's house
<uig rom="ecige-yin mal">ᠡᠴᠢᠭᠡ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠠᠯ</uig> father's cattle

b) Genitivus subjectivus or genitivus activus: this genitive designates the acting person. From the grammatical point of view, such a genitive is an attribute, but logically it is a subject. The genitivus activus designates the performer of an action and answers the question "whose action ? "
The genitive qualifies both nouns and verbal nouns. The latter are always active verbs, but in such constructions they may serve as passive verbs.
The genitive occurs only in attributive constructions, such as "the meat eaten by the dog," but never in such cases as "The meat was eaten by the dog."
<uig rom="burqan-u nomlal">ᠪᠤᠷᠬᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠨᠣᠮᠯᠠᠯ</uig> Buddha's sermon
<uig rom="bodisadu-a-nar-un yabudal-nuγud">ᠪᠣᠳᠢᠰᠠᠳᠤ ᠠ ᠎ᠨᠠᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠳᠠᠯ ᠎ᠨᠤᠭᠤᠳ</uig> the deeds of the Bodhisattvas
<uig rom="cinu abuqsan nom">ᠴᠢᠨᠤ ᠠᠪᠤᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠨᠣᠮ</uig> the book taken by you (lit., "your taken book")
<uig rom="baqsi-yin kelegsen üge">ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠺᠡᠯᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠦᠭᠡ</uig> the word spoken by the teacher (lit., "the teacher's spoken word")

It is not difficult to discover that all the above constructions can be converted into sentences of which the subject is the present active genitive: "Buddha is teaching," "The teacher spoke a word," and so on.

c) Genitivus objectivus: this genitive (genitivus objecti or genitivus passivus) designates the object of someone's action, e. g., "worship of the sun" : the latter construction can be converted into a sentence with "the sun" as an object (complement): "They are worahipping the sun."
<uig rom="miqan-u qudalduγ-a">ᠮᠢᠬᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠬᠤᠳᠠᠯᠳᠤᠭ ᠠ</uig> butcher's shop (lit., "shop of meat")
<uig rom="modun-u darqan">ᠮᠣᠳᠤᠨ ᠤ ᠳᠠᠷᠬᠠᠨ</uig> carpenter (lit., "smith of wood")
<uig rom="nidün-ü emci">ᠨᠢᠳᠦᠨ ᠤ ᠡᠮᠴᠢ</uig> oculist (lit., "a physician of eyes")
<uig rom="kelen-ü surγaγuli">ᠺᠡᠯᠡᠨ ᠤ ᠰᠤᠷᠭᠠᠭᠤᠯᠢ</uig> school of languages
C. Genitivus qualitatis

Genitivus qualitatis or the qualitative genitive expresses qualities and functions as the adjective in European languages. A special case is the genitivus quantitatis, i. e., the genitive of quantity.
<uig rom="eldeb öngge-yin ceceg-nügüd">ᠡᠯᠳᠡᠪ ᠥᠩᠭᠡ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠴᠡᠴᠡᠭ ᠎ᠨᠦᠭᠦᠳ</uig> flowers of various colors
<uig rom="olan jüil-ün amitan-nuγud">ᠣᠯᠠᠨ ᠵᠦᠢᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠠᠮᠢᠲᠠᠨ ᠎ᠨᠤᠭᠤᠳ</uig> living creatures of many kinds j
<uig rom="jaγun jil-ün üy-e">ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠵᠢᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠦᠶ ᠡ</uig> a period of a hundred years
<uig rom="qoyar daγun-u γajar">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠳᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠤ ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ</uig> a distance of two voices (a distance of one voice is the distance the human voice is heard)
<uig rom="γurban jil-ün γajar">ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠵᠢᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ</uig> a distance of three years' travel
D. Genitivus partitivus
The partitive genitive expresses the whole of which a part is talked about.
<uig rom="teden-ü nigen">ᠲᠡᠳᠡᠨ ᠤ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ</uig> one of them
This genitive occurs in two other particular cases : in the expression of fractions and in constructions corresponding semantically to the superlative of European languages.
a) Fractions : the denominator is either a numeral with the following word <uig rom="qubi-yin">ᠬᠤᠪᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ</uig> (genitive of qubi "part") or a genitive of a numeral without qubi-yin.
<uig rom="tabun qubi-yin nigen">ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠬᠤᠪᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ</uig> one fifth (lit., "one of five parts")
<uig rom="arban-u nigen qubi">ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠬᠤᠪᠢ</uig> one tenth (lit., "one part of ten")
In modern books the idea of percentage is expressed in the same manner.
<uig rom="jaγun-u qoyar qubi">ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠤ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠬᠤᠪᠢ</uig> two per cent (lit., "two parts of hundred")

b) Genitivus superlativi: the Mongolian languages have no superlative as a grammatical form. The idea of the highest degree of a quality is expressed by a genitive of a noun (e. g., "man") followed by tho basic form of a noun expressing a quality (e. g., "good"). Thus such a construction may literally be translated as "the good of men." Instead of a neun (e. g., "man"), the word qamuy "all" may be used: the literal translation of such a construction is "the good of all."
<uig rom="er-e-yin sayin">ᠡᠷ ᠡ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ</uig> the best of men
<uig rom="qamuq-un γayiqamsiq-tu">ᠬᠠᠮᠤᠬ ᠤᠨ ᠭᠠᠶᠢᠬᠠᠮᠰᠢᠬ ᠎ᠲᠤ</uig> the most admirable (lit., "the admirable of all")
The predicative genitive is a predicate. In Written Mongolian it occurs with a copula.
<uig rom="ene nom minu bui">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠨᠣᠮ ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> This book is mine.
<uig rom="tere morin geser-ün buyu">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠭᠡᠰᠡᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠪᠤᠶᠤ</uig> Is that horse Geser's?
Many postpositions govern the genitive. Such a genitive together with its postposition is, in turn, governed by a verb and serves as an object.
The following postpositions govern the genitive
<uig rom="tula">ᠲᠤᠯᠠ</uig> for, for the sake of, because of
<uig rom="tölüge">ᠲᠥᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> for, for the sake of, in order to
<uig rom="tuqai">ᠲᠤᠬᠠᠢ</uig> concerning, about, of (e. g., to speak about or of something)
<uig rom="door-a">ᠳᠣᠣᠷ᠎ᠠ</uig> under
<uig rom="dotor-a">ᠳᠣᠲᠣᠷ᠎ᠠ</uig> in, within
<uig rom="deger-e">ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ᠎ᠡ</uig> on
<uig rom="dergede">ᠳᠡᠷᠭᠡᠳᠡ</uig> at, by (e. g., at the table, by the table)
<uig rom="inadu">ᠢᠨᠠᠳᠤ</uig> on this side of
<uig rom="cinadu">ᠴᠢᠨᠠᠳᠤ</uig> on that side of
<uig rom="qoyin-a">ᠬᠣᠶᠢᠨ᠎ᠠ</uig> behind
<uig rom="γadan-a">ᠭᠠᠳᠠᠨ᠎ᠠ</uig> out of, outside
<uig rom="qoγorundu">ᠬᠣᠭᠣᠷᠤᠨᠳᠤ</uig> between
<uig rom="emün-e">ᠡᠮᠦᠨ᠎ᠡ</uig> in front of, before, etc.
Examples
<uig rom="tegün-ü tula">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠤ ᠲᠤᠯᠠ</uig> for its sake
<uig rom="ger-ün dergede">ᠭᠡᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠳᠡᠷᠭᠡᠳᠡ</uig> by the house
<uig rom="aγula-yin qoyin-a">ᠠᠭᠤᠯᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠬᠣᠶᠢᠨ ᠠ</uig> behind the mountain
<uig rom="tegün-ü tuqai">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠤ ᠲᠤᠬᠠᠢ</uig> concerning that
The dative-locative, in general, answers the questiona "to whom?," "at whom?," "where?," and "whither?" There are also many other meanings in particular cases.
The dative-locative is governed by verbs and nouns.
See also §285

entry.title: Syntax - Cases - Dative-locative
entry.title2: Cases - Dative-locative - Dativus commodi atque incommodi

paragraphs.paragraph: The dativus commodi answers the question "to whom?". It is used to indicate the immediate recipient of something, e. g., "He gave the book to the pupil."
The dativus incommodi answers the question "for whom?." It is used to indicate the ultimate recipient of something, e. g., "I gave you a book for your son."
<uig rom="eke-degen ögbe">ᠡᠺᠡ ᠳ᠋ᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠥᠭᠪᠡ</uig> He gave to his mother.
<uig rom="qaγan-dur eyin kemen ögülerün">ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠡᠶᠢᠨ ᠺᠡᠮᠡᠨ ᠥᠭᠦᠯᠡᠷᠦᠨ</uig> He said this to the khaghan.
<uig rom="bi köbegün-degen qatun erimüi">ᠪᠢ ᠺᠥᠪᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠬᠠᠲᠤᠨ ᠡᠷᠢᠮᠦᠢ</uig> I am seeking a wife for my son.
<uig rom="burqan-dur süsüg-tei">ᠪᠤᠷᠬᠠᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠰᠦᠰᠦᠭ ᠎ᠲᠡᠢ</uig> believing in Buddha (lit., "possessing belief in Buddha")
The dativus f inalis is the dative of the purpose. This expresses the ultimate aim of an action.
a) Dativus terminalis: this indicates the aim of an action.
<uig rom="usun-dur yabumui">ᠤᠰᠤᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He goes after water (i. e., to fetch water).
<uig rom="yaγun-dur irebei">ᠶᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡᠢ</uig> Why did he come? (lit., "What did he come for?")

A particular case is the dative of the nomen futuri in <uig rom="-qui/-küi">ᠬᠤᠢ/ᠺᠦᠢ</uig> . The dative suffix is here <uig rom="-a/-e">ᠡ</uig> . Thus the endings of such a form are <uig rom="-qui-a/ -küi-e">ᠬᠤᠢ᠎ᠠ/ᠺᠦᠢ᠎ᠡ</uig> . The meaning of such a form is that of the converbum finale or the Latin supinum, i. e., the aim of an action, e. g., "in order to take."
<uig rom="abqui-a irebei">ᠠᠪᠬᠤᠢ ᠠ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡᠢ</uig> He came to take.
<uig rom="bi tegün-i üjeküi-e irebei">ᠪᠢ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠦᠵᠡᠺᠦᠢ ᠡ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡᠢ</uig> I have come to see him.
b) Dativus translativus: this dative indicates something into which something is being transformed, e. g., "He was appointed teacher" (Lit., "He was appointed to teacher.")
<uig rom="tedeger tegün-i sayid-tur songγuba">ᠲᠡᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠳ ᠲᠤᠷ ᠰᠣᠩᠭᠤᠪᠠ</uig> They elected him minister (Lit., "They elected him to minister.")
This dative, also called the active dative, indicates the acting person, when the action is expressed by the passive voice of a verb.
<uig rom="cinu-a-dur bariγdaγsan qonin">ᠴᠢᠨᠤ ᠠ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠪᠠᠷᠢᠭᠳᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠬᠣᠨᠢᠨ</uig> a sheep caught by a wolf
<uig rom="dayisun-dur alaγdabai">ᠳᠠᠶᠢᠰᠤᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠠᠯᠠᠭᠳᠠᠪᠠᠢ</uig> He was killed by the enemy.
The temporal dative (dativus temporalis or dativus temporis) indicates the time during or at which an action takes place. This answers the question "when?"
<uig rom="ene sara-yin nigen edür-e">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠰᠠᠷᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠡᠳᠦᠷ ᠡ</uig> on the first of this month (lit., "on the first day of this month")
<uig rom="minu baγa-dur">ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠪᠠᠭᠠ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ</uig> when I was a child (lit., "in my little")

A particular case of the temporal dative is the dative-locative of the nomen futuri or nomen perfecti. The former of these verbal nouns indicates an uncompleted action during which an action is or will be performed (e. g., "when he is" or "when he will be here"); the latter indicates the completed past during which the action has been performed (e. g., "when he did something"). Such constructions act as the Latin ablativus absolutus or as subordinate temporal clauses in modern European languages.
<uig rom="tende irekü-dür">ᠲᠡᠨᠳᠡ ᠢᠷᠡᠺᠦ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ</uig> when he comes there (lit., "in the future coming there")
<uig rom="tegün-ü ükügsen-dür">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠤ ᠦᠺᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ</uig> when he died (lit., "in his past dying")
The person acting is indicated in such constructions by the genitivus subjectivus (gen. activus).
The locative answers the questions "where?," "whither?"
a) Locativus allativus-illativus: this locative indicates the place to which someone or something is moving. It answers the question "whither?"
<uig rom="qota-dur yabumui">ᠬᠣᠲᠠ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He goes to town.
<uig rom="usun-dur orobai">ᠤᠰᠤᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠣᠷᠣᠪᠠᠢ</uig> He entered the water. (Lit., "He entered into the water.")
b) Locativus inessivus: this locative answers the question "in what?" or "within what?"
<uig rom="ger-tür saγumui">ᠭᠡᠷ ᠲᠤᠷ ᠰᠠᠭᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He lives in a house.
<uig rom="surγaγuli ene bayising-dur bayimui">ᠰᠤᠷᠭᠠᠭᠤᠯᠢ ᠡᠨᠡ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠰᠢᠩ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠮᠤᠢ</uig> School is in this building.
c) Locativus adessivus: the adessive locative answers the question "on what ?" or "by what ? "
<uig rom="sibaγun modun-u üjügür-tür saγumui">ᠰᠢᠪᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠮᠣᠳᠤᠨ ᠤ ᠦᠵᠦᠭᠦᠷ ᠲᠤᠷ ᠰᠠᠭᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> The bird sits on the top of the tree.
<uig rom="nadur nom ügei">ᠨᠠᠳᠤᠷ ᠨᠣᠮ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> I do not have any books. (Lit., "There are no books at or by me.")
In Mongolian there is no verb "to have." The idea of "to have" is expressed by the locative with the verb "to be."
<uig rom="nadur morin bui">ᠨᠠᠳᠤᠷ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> I have a horse. (Lit., "There is a horse to me.")

The only postposition occurring with a dative is <uig rom="kürtele">ᠺᠦᠷᠲᠡᠯᠡ</uig> "till." By origin this is a converbal form (converbum terminale of <uig rom="kür- ">ᠺᠦᠷ ᠎</uig> "to reach, to arrive").
<uig rom="qota-dur kürtele">ᠬᠣᠲᠠ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠺᠦᠷᠲᠡᠯᠡ</uig> till the town
The double genitive-dative case acts as locative.
a) As allativus answering the question "whither?"
<uig rom="blam-a-yin-dur odba">ᠪᠯᠠᠮ ᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠣᠳᠪᠠ</uig> He went to the lama.
b) As adessivus answering the question "at whose?"
<uig rom="blam-a-yin-dur saγuju amui">ᠪᠯᠠᠮ ᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠰᠠᠭᠤᠵᠤ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He is living at the lama's.

The accusative is governed only by transitive verbs. The accusative is the case of the direct complement and is only used to indicate a definite object or person already known to the reader, especially when the person or thing in question is modified by an attribute. On the other hand, certain parts of speech, when serving as a direct complement, are always accusative forms. The accusative is used, in general, in cases in which the definite article in English is used.

Besides, there is a special construction bearing a certain resemblance to the Latin accusativus cum in f initivo, another construction resembling the English double accusative, and an accusativus relativus explained below.
See also §288
The so-called accusativus objecti is the direct complement.
a) Pronouns serving as a direct complement are always accusative forms. They do not occur suffixless.
<uig rom="tegün-i üjebe">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠦᠵᠡᠪᠡ</uig> He saw him.
<uig rom="ci namayi yaγun-dur daγudabai">ᠴᠢ ᠨᠠᠮᠠᠶᠢ ᠶᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠳᠠᠭᠤᠳᠠᠪᠠᠢ</uig> Why did you call me?
b) Nouns serving as a direct complement and modified by a pronominal attribute are always accusative forms.
<uig rom="ene selm-e-yi ab">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠰᠡᠯᠮ ᠡ ᠶᠢ ᠠᠪ</uig> Take this sabre!
<uig rom="tere mori-yi unuba">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠮᠣᠷᠢ ᠶᠢ ᠤᠨᠤᠪᠠ</uig> He rode that horse.
c) The accusative is used, when there is an indication of the possessor of the object concerned.
<uig rom="nom-i inu ungsiba">ᠨᠣᠮ ᠢ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠪᠠ</uig> He read his (ejus) book.
<uig rom="aq-a-yin mori-yi unuba">ᠠᠬ ᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢ ᠶᠢ ᠤᠨᠤᠪᠠ</uig> He rode the horse of the elder brother.
d) The words <uig rom="bügüde">ᠪᠦᠭᠦᠳᠡ</uig> "all," <uig rom="bükü">ᠪᠦᠺᠦ</uig> "all," and all numerals summarizing the total amount of the persons or things in question are used in the accusative.
<uig rom="bi cinu kereg bükün-i bütügesügei">ᠪᠢ ᠴᠢᠨᠤ ᠺᠡᠷᠡᠭ ᠪᠦᠺᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠪᠦᠲᠦᠭᠡᠰᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> I shall fulfil all your needs.
<uig rom="tere inu yaγum-a bügüde-yi cidamui">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠶᠠᠭᠤᠮ ᠠ ᠪᠦᠭᠦᠳᠡ ᠶᠢ ᠴᠢᠳᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He can [do] everything.
<uig rom="ci nom debter qoyar-i ab">ᠴᠢ ᠨᠣᠮ ᠳᠡᠪᠲᠡᠷ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠢ ᠠᠪ</uig> Take the book and the notebook!
e) Proper names serving as a direct complement are put in the accusative.
<uig rom="cinggis qan-i üjebe">ᠴᠢᠩᠭᠢᠰ ᠬᠠᠨ ᠢ ᠦᠵᠡᠪᠡ</uig> He saw Chinghis Khan.

f) Nouns serving as direct complements are in the accusative, when the person or thing in question was mentioned in a previous context and is supposed to be known to the reader, or when there are any attributes making it distinguishable from other, similar persons er things, or in cases where in English the definite article would be used.
<uig rom="tende nigen süme bui. süme-yi üjemüi-uu">ᠲᠡᠨᠳᠡ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠰᠦᠮᠡ ᠪᠤᠢ᠅ ᠰᠦᠮᠡ ᠶᠢ ᠦᠵᠡᠮᠦᠢ ᠤᠤ</uig> There is a temple. Will you see the temple ?

entry.title: Syntax - Cases - Accusative
entry.title2: Cases - Accusative - Accusativus cum nomine verbali

paragraphs.paragraph: The accusative with a verbal noun acts like the English accusative with the infinitive without "to" (e. g., "I saw him come,") or the Latin accusative with the infinitive (e. g., puto eos vincere). The only difference is that in Mongolian both the noun a-nd the verbal noun are in the accusative like in Latin constructions such as Juravit uterque se sine dolo irulutias conservaturum.
<uig rom="geser-i yabuqu-yi üjebe">ᠭᠡᠰᠡᠷ ᠢ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠬᠤ ᠶᠢ ᠦᠵᠡᠪᠡ</uig> He saw Geser go.
<uig rom="tegün-i ükügsen-i medebe">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠦᠺᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠢ ᠮᠡᠳᠡᠪᠡ</uig> He learned that he had died. (Lit., "He learned him to have died.")
Accusativus relativus or relationis can be translated into English as "concerning someone" or "in reference to someone."

<uig rom="cimayi yaγu abqu bui kemen qaγan asaγumui">ᠴᠢᠮᠠᠶᠢ ᠶᠠᠭᠤ ᠠᠪᠬᠤ ᠪᠤᠢ ᠺᠡᠮᠡᠨ ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠠᠰᠠᠭᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> The khaghan will ask what you would like to take. (Lit., "The khaghan will ask, referring to you, what will he take.")

The accusative of the predicate is the same as the double accusative in English (e. g., "They proclaimed him emperor") or in Latin (e. g., Homines caecos reddit cupiditas). This accusative occurs mainly with the verb <uig rom="bolγa-">ᠪᠣᠯᠭᠠ ᠎</uig> "to make" and expresses that into which something is being transformed.
<uig rom="qaγan inu tere ekener-i qatun-iyan bolγabai">ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠡᠺᠡᠨᠡᠷ ᠢ ᠬᠠᠲᠤᠨ ᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠭᠠᠪᠠᠢ</uig> The khaghan made that woman his wife.
<uig rom="tere ulus tegün-i qaγan-iyan ergübei">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠤᠯᠤᠰ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠡᠷᠭᠦᠪᠡᠢ</uig> That people proclaimed him their khaghan.

This accusative is the accusative of the person acting and indicates the person acting in verbal-nominal and converbal constructions. The verbal noun or converb is an intransitive verb. The accusative replaces the genitive of the acting person.
<uig rom="tegün-i yabuqu-dur">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠬᠤ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ</uig> when he goes
<uig rom="tegün-i iretele">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠢᠷᠡᠲᠡᠯᠡ</uig> until he comes

Instead of the accusative with the usual suffixes <uig rom="-yi"> ᠎ᠶᠢ</uig> and <uig rom="-i">ᠢ</uig> a suffixless form coinciding with the nominative is used in certain cases, but this, of course, is not a nominative. This form is used in cases where in English the indefinite article is used or where there is no article at all. This form serves as a direct complement, temporal, etc.

entry.title: Syntax - Cases - Suffixless oblique case
entry.title2: Cases - Suffixless oblique case - As a direct complement

paragraphs.paragraph: The suffixless form functions as an accusative in the following cases:

a) If the word in question expresses something not mentioned in the previous context and, therefore, is unknown to the reader; if the word in question has no attribute distinguishing it from other, similar, objects, the direct complement has no suffix.
<uig rom="usu uyuqu">ᠤᠰᠤ ᠤᠶᠤᠬᠤ</uig> to drink water
<uig rom="nadur miqa ög">ᠨᠠᠳᠤᠷ ᠮᠢᠬᠠ ᠥᠭ</uig> Give me (some) meat!
<uig rom="bi mori unuju irebe">ᠪᠢ ᠮᠣᠷᠢ ᠤᠨᠤᠵᠤ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡ</uig> I came riding a horse.
ᠪᠢ ᠺᠥᠪᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠬᠠᠲᠤᠨ ᠡᠷᠢᠵᠦ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠮᠤᠢ I go seeking a wife for my son.
b) The direct complement always lacks a suffix in the following expressions, among others :
<uig rom="nom ungsi-">ᠨᠣᠮ ᠤᠩᠰᠢ ᠎</uig> to read a book
<uig rom="bicig bici-">ᠪᠢᠴᠢᠭ ᠪᠢᠴᠢ ᠎</uig> to write letters
<uig rom="kele sur-">ᠺᠡᠯᠡ ᠰᠤᠷ ᠎</uig> to learn language
<uig rom="mori unu-">ᠮᠣᠷᠢ ᠤᠨᠤ ᠎</uig> to ride a horse
<uig rom="üniy-e saγa-">ᠦᠨᠢᠶ ᠡ ᠰᠠᠭᠠ ᠎</uig> to milk a cow

entry.title: Syntax - Cases - Suffixless oblique case
entry.title2: Cases - Suffixless oblique case - As temporal

paragraphs.paragraph: This form expresses time.
<uig rom="γurban sar-a yabuqu">ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠰᠠᠷ ᠠ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠬᠤ</uig> to travel three months
<uig rom="bi önggeregsen jil irebei">ᠪᠢ ᠥᠩᠭᠡᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠵᠢᠯ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡᠢ</uig> I came last year.
<uig rom="edür süni ügei yabuqu">ᠡᠳᠦᠷ ᠰᠦᠨᠢ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠬᠤ</uig> to travel day and night
<uig rom="baqsi irekü jil iremüi">ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠢᠷᠡᠺᠦ ᠵᠢᠯ ᠢᠷᠡᠮᠦᠢ</uig> The teacher will come next year.

entry.title: Syntax - Cases - Suffixless oblique case
entry.title2: Cases - Suffixless oblique case - With a verbal noun

paragraphs.paragraph: The suffixless form is sometimes used instead of the accusative with verbal nouns and indicates the person acting (v. § 514).
<uig rom="bi kümün yabuqu-yi ese üjebe">ᠪᠢ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠬᠤ ᠶᠢ ᠡᠰᠡ ᠦᠵᠡᠪᠡ</uig> I did not see anybody walk.

entry.title: Syntax - Cases - Suffixless oblique case
entry.title2: Cases - Suffixless oblique case - The suffixless form of the predicate

paragraphs.paragraph: This form functions as accusativus praedicati (v. § 516). If the noun of a predicate contains an indication of the possessor, it is an accusative, but, if there is no indication of the possessor, the noun of the predicate is suffixless.
<uig rom="tedener tegün-i qaγan ergübe">ᠲᠡᠳᠡᠨᠡᠷ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠡᠷᠭᠦᠪᠡ</uig> They proclaimed him khaghan.

<uig rom="baγ-a qural-un terigülegcid nökör amur-i terigün sayid songγuba">ᠪᠠᠭ ᠠ ᠬᠤᠷᠠᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠲᠡᠷᠢᠭᠦᠯᠡᠭᠴᠢᠳ ᠨᠥᠺᠥᠷ ᠠᠮᠤᠷ ᠢ ᠲᠡᠷᠢᠭᠦᠨ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠳ ᠰᠣᠩᠭᠤᠪᠠ</uig> The Standing Committee of the Small National Assembly elected Comrade Amur prime minister.

entry.title: Syntax - Cases - Suffixless oblique case
entry.title2: Cases - Suffixless oblique case - As indication of place

paragraphs.paragraph: The suffixless form indicates the place or the direction of someone's motion.
<uig rom="tere γajar saγuju amui">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ ᠰᠠᠭᠤᠵᠤ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He is living in that country.
<uig rom="bida qota yabumui">ᠪᠢᠳᠠ ᠬᠣᠲᠠ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> We shall go to town.

The ablative, in general, indicates the starting point of an action. There are several categories of ablative: ablativus separativus, abl. temporis, abl. actoris, abl. compensationis, abl. verbi, and ablativus cum postpositione.
See also §290

The separative ablative answers the questions "from whom?" or "from where?" and "from within what?" There are the following particular kinds of this ablative: ablativus separativus externus, abl. elativus, abl. originis, abl. causae, abl. partitivus, abl. exclusivus, and ablativus comparationis.
a) Ablativus separativus externus : this ablative answers the questions "from whom?" and "from where?" This indicates the person or thing from whom or from what something is moving.
<uig rom="qaγan-aca abuba">ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠠᠪᠤᠪᠠ</uig> He took from the khaghan.
b) Ablativus elativus: this ablative answers the question "from within what?" It indicates the thing or the place from within which something is coming out.
<uig rom="ger-ece γaruba">ᠭᠡᠷ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠭᠠᠷᠤᠪᠠ</uig> He came out of the house.
c) Ablativus originis: the ablative of origin indicates the origin of someone or something.
<uig rom="qaγan-u qatun-aca nigen köbegün töröbei">ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠬᠠᠲᠤᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠺᠥᠪᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠲᠥᠷᠥᠪᠡᠢ</uig> A son was born of the khaghan's wife.
<uig rom="mongγol-aca γaruqsan nigen yasun">ᠮᠣᠩᠭᠣᠯ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠭᠠᠷᠤᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠶᠠᠰᠤᠨ</uig> a tribe of Mongolian origin (lit., "a tribe which came out of the Mongols")
d) Ablativus causae : the ablative of the cause indicates the cause of something.
<uig rom="jobalang anu nisvanis-aca bolumui">ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠨᠢᠰᠸᠠᠨᠢᠰ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> Suffering comes from attachment to the world.
<uig rom="jirγalang buyan-aca bolumui">ᠵᠢᠷᠭᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠪᠤᠶᠠᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> Happiness comes from virtue.
e) Ablativus partitivus: the partitive ablative indicates objects which are only partially affected by the action.
<uig rom="cai-aca uγuba">ᠴᠠᠢ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠤᠭᠤᠪᠠ</uig> He drank some tea. (Lit., "He drank from the tea.")
<uig rom="yaγum-a-aca oyulcaba">ᠶᠠᠭᠤᠮ ᠠ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠣᠶᠤᠯᠴᠠᠪᠠ</uig> He took part in sewing things. (Lit., "He took part in sewing from something.")

f) Ablativus exclusivus: the exclusive ablative occurs in constructions corresponding to the English "besides something" and "except something." This ablative is followed by the word <uig rom="busu">ᠪᠤᠰᠤ</uig> "another" or <uig rom="öger-e">ᠥᠭᠡᠷ᠎ᠡ</uig> "another" or <uig rom="γadan-a">ᠭᠠᠳᠠᠨ᠎ᠠ</uig> "outside."
<uig rom="tegün-ece γadan-a">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠭᠠᠳᠠᠨ ᠠ</uig> besides that
<uig rom="yabuqu-aca busu arγ-a ügei">ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠬᠤ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠪᠤᠰᠤ ᠠᠷᠭ ᠠ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> There remains nothing but to go. (Lit., "There is no other way out of going.")
<uig rom="nigen üker-ece öger-e ed ügei">ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠦᠺᠡᠷ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠥᠭᠡᠷ ᠡ ᠡᠳ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> no other property than one ox

g) Ablativus comparationis : an ablative immediately followed by a noun expressing a quality functions as the comparative in European languages. To be precise we should add that the ablative indicates the person or thing which possesses the inferior quality.
<uig rom="nama-aca yeke">ᠨᠠᠮᠠ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠶᠡᠺᠡ</uig> bigger than I
<uig rom="cima-aca aq-a">ᠴᠢᠮᠠ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠠᠬ ᠠ</uig> older than you (lit., "from you an elder brother")
The temporal ablative indicates the time since which an action takes place. This ablative indicates the starting time.
<uig rom="önggeregsen tabun jil-ece">ᠥᠩᠭᠡᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠵᠢᠯ ᠡᠴᠡ</uig> since the last five year period
<uig rom="marγasi-yin edür-ece ekilen">ᠮᠠᠷᠭᠠᠰᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠡᠳᠦᠷ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠡᠺᠢᠯᠡᠨ</uig> beginning from to-morrow (lit., "beginning from the day of morrow")
The ablative of the person acting indicates the originator of an aetion.
<uig rom="qural-aca toγtaγaba">ᠬᠤᠷᠠᠯ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠲᠣᠭᠲᠠᠭᠠᠪᠠ</uig> A resolution was passed by (lit., "from") the assembly.
This ablative indicates things serving as compensation for something else, or things in exchange for which other things are to be given. It is to be translated into English by "for . . ."
<uig rom="tegün-i mönggün-ece ögbe">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠮᠥᠩᠭᠦᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠥᠭᠪᠡ</uig> He gave it for money.
Certain verbs govern the ablative
<uig rom="ayi-">ᠠᠶᠢ ᠎</uig> or <uig rom="ayu-">ᠠᠶᠤ ᠎</uig> to be afraid of (someone)
<uig rom="asayu-">ᠠᠰᠠᠶᠤ ᠎</uig> to ask (someone)
<uig rom="ice-">ᠢᠴᠡ ᠎</uig> to be ashamed of
<uig rom="bari-">ᠪᠠᠷᠢ ᠎</uig> to take by (e. g., to take by the hand ; otherwise <uig rom="bari-">ᠪᠠᠷᠢ ᠎</uig> governa the accusative)
<uig rom="daba-">ᠳᠠᠪᠠ ᠎</uig> to violate (a law, regulations)
<uig rom="sur-">ᠰᠤᠷ ᠎</uig> to ask (someone)
<uig rom="uya-">ᠤᠶᠠ ᠎</uig> to bind to, to tie to something
<uig rom="elgü-">ᠡᠯᠭᠦ ᠎</uig> to hang on
<uig rom="tata-">ᠲᠠᠲᠠ ᠎</uig> to pull at

entry.title: Syntax - Cases - Ablative
entry.title2: Cases - Ablative - Postposition governing the ablative

paragraphs.paragraph: The following postpositions govern the ablative
<uig rom="γadan-a">ᠭᠠᠳᠠᠨ ᠠ</uig> besides
<uig rom="qoyisi">ᠬᠣᠶᠢᠰᠢ</uig> after
<uig rom="urida">ᠤᠷᠢᠳᠠ</uig> before
<uig rom="cinaγsi">ᠴᠢᠨᠠᠭᠰᠢ</uig> farther from
<uig rom="inaγsi">ᠢᠨᠠᠭᠰᠢ</uig> nearer in this direction
The instrumental, in general, indicates the means of performing an action. It answers the question "by means of what?"

There are some particular cases of application of the instrumental. The following kinds of instrumental are recognizable: the "pure" instrumental indicating the tool of an action (instrumentalis instructivus), the sociative instrumental (instrumentalis sociativus) answering the question "together with whom?," the instrumental of manner (instrumentalis modi) indicating the manner in which an action is performed, and the compensative instrumental (instrumentalis compensationis) indicating things as price for other things.
See also §293, §682

The instructive instrumental indicates the tool of an action. This ineludes the instrumentalis instrumenti, instr. actoris, instr. materiae, instr. f ormae, instr. causae & propositi, instr. itineris, and instrumentalis cum nominibus opiae atque inopiae.
a) Instrumentalis instrumenti: this instrumental indicates the means of performing actions (tools, transportation means, etc.).
<uig rom="modu-bar coki-">ᠮᠣᠳᠤ ᠎ᠪᠠᠷ ᠴᠣᠺᠢ ᠎</uig> to beat with a stick
<uig rom="süke-ber cabci-">ᠰᠦᠺᠡ ᠎ᠪᠡᠷ ᠴᠠᠪᠴᠢ ᠎</uig> to cleave with an ax
<uig rom="köl-iyer giski-">ᠺᠥᠯ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠭᠢᠰᠺᠢ ᠎</uig> to tread on with the foot
<uig rom="ongγoca-bar yabu-">ᠣᠩᠭᠣᠴᠠ ᠎ᠪᠠᠷ ᠶᠠᠪᠤ ᠎</uig> to go by boat
<uig rom="temege-ber jüge-">ᠲᠡᠮᠡᠭᠡ ᠎ᠪᠡᠷ ᠵᠦᠭᠡ ᠎</uig> to carry by camel (or camel caravan)
b) Instrumentalis actoris: this instrumental indicates the person acting. This is used with both active and passive verbs.
<uig rom="qaγan inu jarliq-iyan elci-ber medegülbei">ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠵᠠᠷᠯᠢᠬ ᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠡᠯᠴᠢ ᠎ᠪᠡᠷ ᠮᠡᠳᠡᠭᠦᠯᠪᠡᠢ</uig> The khaghan made his order known through a messenger.
<uig rom="qural-iyar songγuqsan daruγ-a">ᠬᠤᠷᠠᠯ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠰᠣᠩᠭᠤᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠳᠠᠷᠤᠭ ᠠ</uig> or <uig rom="qural-iyar songγuqdaqsan daruγ-a">ᠬᠤᠷᠠᠯ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠰᠣᠩᠭᠤᠬᠳᠠᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠳᠠᠷᠤᠭ ᠠ</uig> the chairman elected by the assembly
c) Instrumentalis materiae : this instrumental indicates the material or stuff of which something ia made.
<uig rom="modu-bar bariqsan bayising">ᠮᠣᠳᠤ ᠎ᠪᠠᠷ ᠪᠠᠷᠢᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠰᠢᠩ</uig> bayising a building made of wood
<uig rom="altan-iyar kigsen qayircaγ">ᠠᠯᠲᠠᠨ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠺᠢᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠬᠠᠶᠢᠷᠴᠠᠭ</uig> a box made of gold
d) Instrumentalis formae : this instrumental indicates the shape in which something is made (in English: "in the shape of").
<uig rom="eldeb jüil-ün erdenis-iyer beleg kürgebe">ᠡᠯᠳᠡᠪ ᠵᠦᠢᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠡᠷᠳᠡᠨᠢᠰ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠪᠡᠯᠡᠭ ᠺᠦᠷᠭᠡᠪᠡ</uig> He brought gifts in the shape of jewels of various kinds.
<uig rom="-bar bügeljijü bayidaγ quluγan-a">᠎ᠪᠠᠷ ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠯᠵᠢᠵᠦ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠳᠠᠭ ᠬᠤᠯᠤᠭᠠᠨ ᠠ</uig> a mouse which vomits gold (lit., "vomiting with gold" )
e) Instrumentalis causae atque propositi: thia instrumental indicates the cause or the aim.
<uig rom="kereg-iyer yabu-">ᠺᠡᠷᠡᠭ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠶᠠᠪᠤ ᠎</uig> to go on business
<uig rom="tegün-i medegsen ügei-ber aldaγ-a γarγaba">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠮᠡᠳᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ ᠎ᠪᠡᠷ ᠠᠯᠳᠠᠭ ᠠ ᠭᠠᠷᠭᠠᠪᠠ</uig> He made a mistake because he did not know (Lit., "because of not knowing").
The instrumental of a future noun (nomen futuri) expresses the aim or the purpose of an action.
<uig rom="tegün-i üjekü-ber irebe">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠦᠵᠡᠺᠦ ᠎ᠪᠡᠷ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡ</uig> He came in order to see him.
<uig rom="cai uγuqu-bar irebe">ᠴᠠᠢ ᠤᠭᠤᠬᠤ ᠎ᠪᠠᠷ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡ</uig> He came to drink tea.
f) Instrumentalis itineris: this instrumental can be also called instr. itineris atque loci and indicates the way of someone's motion or the place over which something is scattered.
<uig rom="jam-iyar yabu-">ᠵᠠᠮ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠶᠠᠪᠤ ᠎</uig> to go by road
<uig rom="egüde-ber oro-">ᠡᠭᠦᠳᠡ ᠎ᠪᠡᠷ ᠣᠷᠣ ᠎</uig> to enter by the door
<uig rom="aγularqaγ γajar-iyar nutuqlamui">ᠠᠭᠤᠯᠠᠷᠬᠠᠭ ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠨᠤᠲᠤᠬᠯᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> They live scattered in a mountainous country.

g) Instrumentalis cum nomine : this instrumental occurs only with the so-called nomina opiae & inopiae, i. e. such as <uig rom="bayan">ᠪᠠᠶᠠᠨ</uig> "rich," <uig rom="elbeg">ᠡᠯᠪᠡᠭ</uig> "abundant," and so on, and indicates goods in which someone is rich (or which he lacks).
<uig rom="mal-iyar bayan">ᠮᠠᠯ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠪᠠᠶᠠᠨ</uig> rich in cattle
<uig rom="eldeb jüil-iyer ügei">ᠡᠯᠳᠡᠪ ᠵᠦᠢᠯ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> poor in everything
The sociative instrumental expresses the idea of companionship with someone or connection with something, answering the question "together with whom?".
<uig rom="manu morin tegün-ü mori-iyar belcimüi">ᠮᠠᠨᠤ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠤ ᠮᠣᠷᠢ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠪᠡᠯᠴᠢᠮᠦᠢ</uig> Our horse grazes together with his horse
<uig rom="utaγan-iyar degdebe">ᠤᠲᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠳᠡᠭᠳᠡᠪᠡ</uig> He went up together with the smoke
This instrumental is a special case of the sociative instrumental. It indicates the time with which an action coincides.
<uig rom="qoyar jil-iyer cerig-ün alban-dur oroba">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠵᠢᠯ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠴᠡᠷᠢᠭ ᠤᠨ ᠠᠯᠪᠠᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠣᠷᠣᠪᠠ</uig> He was conscripted for two years. (Lit., "He entered the military service for two years.")
The modal instrumental indicates the manner in which an action is performed. It corresponds sometimes to an adverb in European languages.
<uig rom="tedeger cuγ-iyar-iyan qariba">ᠲᠡᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ ᠴᠤᠭ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠬᠠᠷᠢᠪᠠ</uig> All of them went back. (Lit., "They went back with their totality.")
<uig rom="türgen-iyer yabumui">ᠲᠦᠷᠭᠡᠨ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He goes fast.

This is a special case of the instrumental of manner, indicating something in accordance with which an action is performed (in English "according to . . .," "in accordance with . . ." or "after the pattern of. . ..")
<uig rom="bi cinu jarliγ-iyar yabumui">ᠪᠢ ᠴᠢᠨᠤ ᠵᠠᠷᠯᠢᠬ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> I shall act according to your order.
<uig rom="ci yaγu kelekü bolbasu bi tegüber bolqu">ᠴᠢ ᠶᠠᠭᠤ ᠺᠡᠯᠡᠺᠦ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤ ᠪᠢ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠪᠡᠷ ᠪᠣᠯᠬᠤ</uig> If you say anything, I shall behave according to it.
This instrumental indicates things regarded as the price of something (English "for. . .").
<uig rom="mal-iyar soli-">ᠮᠠᠯ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠰᠣᠯᠢ ᠎</uig> to exchange for cattle
<uig rom="bi egün-i alta-bar öggümüi">ᠪᠢ ᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠠᠯᠲᠠ ᠎ᠪᠠᠷ ᠥᠭᠭᠦᠮᠦᠢ</uig> I shall give this for gold.
The comitative answers the question "together with whom?"
<uig rom="köbegün-lüge jolγalduba">ᠺᠥᠪᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠯᠦᠭᠡ ᠵᠣᠯᠭᠠᠯᠳᠤᠪᠠ</uig> He met the boy. (Lit., "He met with the boy.")
<uig rom="tegün-lüge neyileldübe">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠯᠦᠭᠡ ᠨᠡᠶᠢᠯᠡᠯᠳᠦᠪᠡ</uig> He joined him.
See also §295
The comitative occurs with the following postpositions
<uig rom="qamtu">ᠬᠠᠮᠲᠤ</uig> together with
<uig rom="nigen-e">ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ᠎ᠡ</uig> together with
<uig rom="saca">ᠰᠠᠴᠠ</uig> simultaneously with
<uig rom="cuγ">ᠴᠤᠭ</uig> with
<uig rom="selte">ᠰᠡᠯᠲᠡ</uig> or <uig rom="selte-ber">ᠰᠡᠯᠲᠡ ᠎ᠪᠡᠷ</uig> with
The double comitative-instrumental case form acts as a simple comitative, i. e., answers the question "with whom?"
<uig rom="qaγan-luγ-a-bar">ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠯᠤᠭ ᠠ ᠎ᠪᠠᠷ</uig> together with the khaghan
<uig rom="eke-lüge-ber">ᠡᠺᠡ ᠯᠦᠭᠡ ᠎ᠪᠡᠷ</uig> with the mother
This double case occurs also with the same postpositions as the simple comitative.
<uig rom="nökör-lüge-ber qamtu">ᠨᠥᠺᠥᠷ ᠯᠦᠭᠡ ᠎ᠪᠡᠷ ᠬᠠᠮᠲᠤ</uig> together with the friend

entry.title: Syntax - Agreement - Agreement of the attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: As remarked above (§ 455-§456), there is no agreement in case. Thia means that in Mongolian an attribute does not agree as to case with the word to be modified and is the same as English in this respect.
<uig rom="sayin morin-dur">ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ</uig> to the good horse
<uig rom="öndür aγula-aca">ᠥᠨᠳᠦᠷ ᠠᠭᠤᠯᠠ ᠡᠴᠡ</uig> from the high mountain

entry.title: Syntax - Agreement - Agreement of the attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: In modern Mongolian the attribute usually does not agree in number, either, with the word to be modified.
<uig rom="öndür aγulas">ᠥᠨᠳᠦᠷ ᠠᠭᠤᠯᠠᠰ</uig> high mountains
<uig rom="jegerde morid">ᠵᠡᠭᠡᠷᠳᠡ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠳ</uig> chestnut-colored horses

entry.title: Syntax - Agreement - Agreement of the attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: However, in a few cases the attribute does agree in number even in the modern language.
In the modern language only the demonstrative pronouns ene "this" and tere "that" agree in number with the word to be modified, but this is not obligatory.
<uig rom="ene kümün">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> this person
<uig rom="ede kümüs">ᠡᠳᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠰ</uig> these persons
<uig rom="tere kümün">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> that person
<uig rom="tede kümüs">ᠲᠡᠳᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠰ</uig> those persons

entry.title: Syntax - Agreement - Agreement of the attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: In the pre-classical language agreement in number was a more frequent phenomenon and all parts of apeech acting as attributes agreed in number with the word to be modified. This refers, however, only to the attributes in the nominative.
<uig rom="ede cidküd">ᠡᠳᠡ ᠴᠢᠳᠺᠦᠳ</uig> these devils
<uig rom="jobaqu kümün">ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠬᠤ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> a suffering person, but <uig rom="jobaqun kümün-nügüd">ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠬᠤᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠎ᠨᠦᠭᠦᠳ</uig> suffering people
<uig rom="jobalangtu eme">ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠯᠠᠩᠲᠤ ᠡᠮᠡ</uig> a suffering woman, but <uig rom="jobalangtan amitan-nuγud">ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠯᠠᠩᠲᠠᠨ ᠠᠮᠢᠲᠠᠨ ᠎ᠨᠤᠭᠤᠳ</uig> suffering creatures

entry.title: Syntax - Agreement - Agreement of the attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: There was also what is called constructio ad sensum. Thia means that an attribute is in the plural, although the word to be modified is a grammatical singular form but expresses a multitude. (Cf. the English "The Parliament have passed a resolution.")
<uig rom="maγun irgen">ᠮᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠢᠷᠭᠡᠨ</uig> evil people (<uig rom="maγun">ᠮᠠᠭᠤᠨ</uig> is a plural of <uig rom="maγui">ᠮᠠᠭᠤᠢ</uig>)

entry.title: Syntax - Agreement - Agreement of the attribute

paragraphs.paragraph: There is no grammatical gender, there cannot be any agreement in gender. However, in the pre-classical language there was something resembling agreement in gender, although it was different from the Latin congruentia in genere. In reference to female beings, special words were used.
In the first place the numeral jirin "two" is to be mentioned.
<uig rom="qoyar er-e">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠡᠷ ᠡ</uig> two men
<uig rom="jirin qatud">ᠵᠢᠷᠢᠨ ᠬᠠᠲᠤᠳ</uig> two ladies
In modern Written Mongolian only words indicating the age or the color of female animals take special suffixes making them different from the same words used in reference to male animals.
<uig rom="γunan buqa">ᠭᠤᠨᠠᠨ ᠪᠤᠬᠠ</uig> a three-year-old bull
<uig rom="γunajin üniy-e">ᠭᠤᠨᠠᠵᠢᠨ ᠦᠨᠢᠶ ᠡ</uig> a three-year-old cow
<uig rom="qar-a buqa">ᠬᠠᠷ ᠠ ᠪᠤᠬᠠ</uig> a black bull
<uig rom="qaraqcin üniy-e">ᠬᠠᠷᠠᠬᠴᠢᠨ ᠦᠨᠢᠶ ᠡ</uig> a black cow
There is no agreement at all.
<uig rom="cinggis qan-dur">ᠴᠢᠩᠭᠢᠰ ᠬᠠᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ</uig> to Chingis Khan
However, if two or more proper names belong to an appellative noun, the latter is put in the plural.
<uig rom="nököd amur gendün qoyar-tur">ᠨᠥᠺᠥᠳ ᠠᠮᠤᠷ ᠭᠡᠨᠳᠦᠨ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠲᠤᠷ</uig> to the comrades Amur and Gendun
In the classical and pre-classical language, the appellative is repeated after each proper name and is always a singular form.
<uig rom="cinggis qan ögedei qan qoyar">ᠴᠢᠩᠭᠢᠰ ᠬᠠᠨ ᠥᠭᠡᠳᠡᠢ ᠬᠠᠨ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ</uig> both Chingis Khan and Ugedei Khan

There is only one form for all persons in the indicative and, therefore, there cannot be agreement in person. As to the imperative and optative forms, some of them are used only in reference to definite persons.
<uig rom="bi yabusuγai">ᠪᠢ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠰᠤᠭᠠᠢ</uig> I shall go.
<uig rom="yabuγ-a">ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠭ ᠠ</uig> Let us go!
In the pre-classical language there is agreement in number with the subject of verbal nouns serving as predicates.
<uig rom="tede jobaqun">ᠲᠡᠳᠡ ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠬᠤᠨ</uig> Those will suffer.
<uig rom="tedeger ükügsed bülüge">ᠲᠡᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ ᠦᠺᠦᠭᠰᠡᠳ ᠪᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> Those were dead.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Generalities

paragraphs.paragraph: The copula is a part of a nominal, verbal-nominal, or converbal predicate. Sometimes it can be omitted. The copula is either a simple or a compound one.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Simple copula
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Simple copula

paragraphs.paragraph: The verbs <uig rom="bui">ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> "is," <uig rom="bolai">ᠪᠣᠯᠠᠢ</uig> "is," <uig rom="bülüge">ᠪᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> "was," and all finite forms of the verbs <uig rom="a-">ᠠ ᠎</uig> "to be," <uig rom="bayi-">ᠪᠠᠶᠢ ᠎</uig> "to be," and <uig rom="bol-">ᠪᠣᠯ ᠎</uig> "to become" usually serve as copula.
<uig rom="ene ken bui">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠺᠡᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> Who is this?
<uig rom="manu baγsi sayin bui">ᠮᠠᠨᠤ ᠪᠠᠭᠰᠢ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> Our teacher is good.
<uig rom="ene morin qurdun bui">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠬᠤᠷᠳᠤᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> This horse is quick.
<uig rom="jobalang-un siltaγan anu nisvanis bui">ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠤᠨ ᠰᠢᠯᠲᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠨᠢᠰᠸᠠᠨᠢᠰ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> The cause of sufferings is attachment to the world.
<uig rom="ene sayin bolai">ᠡᠨᠡ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠠᠢ</uig> This is good.
<uig rom="cinu kereg yaγun bülüge">ᠴᠢᠨᠤ ᠺᠡᠷᠡᠭ ᠶᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠪᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> What is your need?
<uig rom="mongγol γajar inu aγudam yeke amui">ᠮᠣᠩᠭᠣᠯ ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠠᠭᠤᠳᠠᠮ ᠶᠡᠺᠡ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> Mongolia is vast and big.
<uig rom="manu köbegün sayin bayimui">ᠮᠠᠨᠤ ᠺᠥᠪᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠮᠤᠢ</uig> Our son is good.
<uig rom="tere inu sayin bolba">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠ</uig> He became good.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Compound copula
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Compound copula

paragraphs.paragraph: A compound copula consists of more than one form of auxiliary verb. Usually it is made up of a converb or a verbal noun and a finite form.
<uig rom="aγsan ajuγu">ᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠠᠵᠤᠭᠤ</uig> was, had been
<uig rom="aγsan bülüge">ᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠪᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> was, had been
<uig rom="bayiju bayimui">ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠵᠤ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠮᠤᠢ</uig> is being
<uig rom="bolqu bui">ᠪᠣᠯᠬᠤ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> will become

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Descriptives verbs
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Descriptives verbs

paragraphs.paragraph: A descriptive verb is something different from an auxiliary verb. The latter expresses the mere idea of existence or being, and as a copula, it only connects the predicative word with the subject and indicates the time of the predicative relation. A descriptive verb expresses a definite action, e. g., "to go." When united with a converb of another verb and serving together with the latter as a single predicate, it preserves its primary meaning (e. g., "to go") and the adjoining converb precisely defines the character of the action of the finite form. Suppose the converb is a form of the verb "to fly." In this event the meaning of the word group is "to go flying." This means "to fly off" or "to fly in a direction away from the speaker." On the other hand, if the finite form means "to come," the word group expresses the idea of "to come flying," i. e., the idea of flying toward the person speaking. In English this can be expressed by prepositions, e. g., "to fly on," "to fly out," and so on. Other languages have such verbs as, e. g., adhaereo "to stick to," defero "to carry down, to remove" (in Latin), etc. Mongolian <uig rom="abcu oci- ">ᠠᠪᠴᠤ ᠣᠴᠢ ᠎</uig> "to take away, to carry away" is more or less the same as Latin defero.
There are many descriptive verbs. Some of them will be discussed in connection with the converbs (§576).
<uig rom=" ire-">ᠢᠷᠡ ᠎</uig> "to come" indicates that the action is performed in the direction toward the person speaking: <uig rom="abcu ire-">ᠠᠪᠴᠤ ᠢᠷᠡ ᠎</uig> "to bring" (lit., "to come taking").
<uig rom="oro-">ᠣᠷᠣ ᠎</uig> "to enter" indicates that a motion is made into the thing concerned: <uig rom="güijü oro-">ᠭᠦᠢᠵᠦ ᠣᠷᠣ ᠎</uig> "to run into" (lit., "to enter running").

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Nominal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Nominal predicate

paragraphs.paragraph: The nominal predicate is a noun, pronoun, or a numeral. It usually has a copula which can be omitted.
A. The Nominal Predicate with Copula
<uig rom="manu baqsi sayin bui">ᠮᠠᠨᠤ ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> Our teacher is good.
<uig rom="narasun inu modun bui">ᠨᠠᠷᠠᠰᠤᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠮᠣᠳᠤᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> The pine is a tree.
<uig rom="buriyad anu mongγol yasun-u nigen ulus amui">ᠪᠤᠷᠢᠶᠠᠳ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠮᠣᠩᠭᠣᠯ ᠶᠠᠰᠤᠨ ᠤ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠤᠯᠤᠰ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> The Buriats are a people of Mongolian descent.
B. The Nominal Predicate with Copula Omitted

<uig rom="qoyar anu daqutai qoyar anu daqu ügei">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠳᠠᠬᠤᠲᠠᠢ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠳᠠᠬᠤ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> Two of them have fur coats; two of them have no fur coats. (Lit., "Two of them with fur coats; two of them without fur coats.") This is a riddle of which the solution is : The horns and ears of a cow.
<uig rom="kümün aq-a-tai debel jaqatai">ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠠᠬ ᠠ ᠎ᠲᠠᠢ ᠳᠡᠪᠡᠯ ᠵᠠᠬᠠᠲᠠᠢ</uig> A person has a superior; a coat has a collar. (Lit., "A person with a superior, a coat with a collar.") This is a proverb.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate

paragraphs.paragraph: Verbal nouns act as predicates with a copula. The latter ia usually a finite form of the verbs <uig rom="a-">ᠠ ᠎</uig> "to be," <uig rom="bayi-">ᠪᠠᠶᠢ ᠎</uig> "to be," or the forms <uig rom="bolai">ᠪᠣᠯᠠᠢ</uig> "is," <uig rom="">ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> bui "is," and <uig rom="bülüge">ᠪᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> "was."

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate - Nomen futuri

paragraphs.paragraph: Nomen futuri with the suffix <uig rom="-qu/-kü">ᠬᠤ/ᠺᠦ</uig> occurs with the copula <uig rom="amui">ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> "is" or <uig rom="bayimui">ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠮᠤᠢ</uig> "is" and expresses an intention to perform an action.
<uig rom="marγasi yabuqu amui">ᠮᠠᠷᠭᠠᠰᠢ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠬᠤ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He intends to go to-morrow.
See also §359

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate - Nomen futuri

paragraphs.paragraph: With the copula <uig rom="bui j-a">ᠪᠤᠢ ᠵ ᠠ</uig> this verbal noun expresses actions which probably will take place.
<uig rom="ükükü bui j-a">ᠦᠺᠦᠺᠦ ᠪᠤᠢ ᠵ ᠠ</uig> He will probably die.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate - Nomen futuri

paragraphs.paragraph: With finite forms of the verb <uig rom="bol-">ᠪᠣᠯ ᠎</uig> "to become" this verbal noun expresses the beginning of an action.
<uig rom="ungsiqu bolba">ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠬᠤ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠ</uig> He started reading.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate - Nomen futuri

paragraphs.paragraph: With the copula <uig rom="bülüge">ᠪᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> the future noun serves as the conditional in the English "He would have done something, (if he had been told to)".
<uig rom="mönggün bui abasu bi qudalduju abqu bülüge">ᠮᠥᠩᠭᠦᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ ᠠᠪᠠᠰᠤ ᠪᠢ ᠬᠤᠳᠠᠯᠳᠤᠵᠤ ᠠᠪᠬᠤ ᠪᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> If there were (any) money, I would buy.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate - Nomen futuri

paragraphs.paragraph: With the copula <uig rom="bui">ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> the future noun expresses the necessity of acting.
<uig rom="edüge yabuqu bui">ᠡᠳᠦᠭᠡ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠬᠤ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> Now it is necessary to go.
On the other hand, the future noun occurs with the copula <uig rom="bui">ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> in sentences containing interrogative words.
<uig rom="manu baqsi kejiy-e irekü bui">ᠮᠠᠨᠤ ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠺᠡᠵᠢᠶ ᠡ ᠢᠷᠡᠺᠦ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> When will our teacher come?
<uig rom="ta qamiγ-a yabuqu bui">ᠲᠠ ᠬᠠᠮᠢᠭ ᠠ ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠬᠤ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> Where will you go?

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate - Nomen futuri

paragraphs.paragraph: With the negative noun <uig rom="ügei">ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> the future noun is usually employed without any verbal copula.
<uig rom="manu baqsi irekü ügei">ᠮᠠᠨᠤ ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠢᠷᠡᠺᠦ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> Our teacher will not come.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate - Nomen imperfecti

paragraphs.paragraph: In Written Mongolian this form occurs only with the negatives <uig rom="ügei">ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> "not" and <uig rom="edüi">ᠡᠳᠦᠢ</uig> "not yet."
<uig rom="irege ügei">ᠢᠷᠡᠭᠡ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> He has not come yet.
<uig rom="irege edüi">ᠢᠷᠡᠭᠡ ᠡᠳᠦᠢ</uig> He has not come yet.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate - Nomen perfecti

paragraphs.paragraph: The nomen perfecti occurs with the finite forms of the verbs <uig rom="a-">ᠠ ᠎</uig> "to be" and <uig rom="ayi-">ᠪᠠᠶᠢ ᠎</uig> b "to be" and the defective verbs <uig rom="bui">ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> "is," <uig rom="bolai">ᠪᠣᠯᠠᠢ</uig> "is," and <uig rom="bülüge">ᠪᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> "was."
<uig rom="iregsen amui">ᠢᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He has come.
<uig rom="ükügsen bui">ᠦᠺᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> He has died.
<uig rom="törögsen bülüge">ᠲᠥᠷᠥᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠪᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> He was born.
See also §364

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate - Nomen perfecti

paragraphs.paragraph: The nomen perfecti with the negative <uig rom="ügei">ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> often lacks a verbal copula.
<uig rom="iregsen ügei">ᠢᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> He did not come.
<uig rom="ükügsen ügei">ᠦᠺᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> He was not dead.

entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate - Nomen perfecti

paragraphs.paragraph: The nomen per f ecti occurs often with the copula <uig rom="">ᠠᠵᠤᠭᠤ</uig> ajuγu "was" and such a construction corresponds to the English pluperfect tense.
<uig rom="">ᠦᠺᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠠᠵᠤᠭᠤ</uig> ükügsen ajuγu He had died.
<uig rom="">ᠢᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠠᠵᠤᠭᠤ</uig> iregsen ajuγu He had come.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate - Nomen usus

paragraphs.paragraph: The nomen usus expresses, as predicate, a repeated or habitual action. This form occurs with the copula <uig rom="bui">ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> "is," <uig rom="bülüge">ᠪᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> "was," and the finite forms of the verbs <uig rom="a-">ᠠ ᠎</uig> "to be" and <uig rom="bayi-">ᠪᠠᠶᠢ ᠎</uig> "to be."
<uig rom="iredeg bui">ᠢᠷᠡᠳᠡᠭ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> (or <uig rom="amui">ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> or <uig rom="bayimui">ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠮᠤᠢ</uig>) He usually comes.
<uig rom="iredeg bülüge">ᠢᠷᠡᠳᠡᠭ ᠪᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> He used to come.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate - Nomen usus

paragraphs.paragraph: The nomen usus with the negative <uig rom="ügei">ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> sometimes lacks the verbal copula. The copula is not omitted when the habitual action refers to the past.
<uig rom="iredeg ügei">ᠢᠷᠡᠳᠡᠭ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> He usually does not come.
<uig rom="iredeg ügei bülüge">ᠢᠷᠡᠳᠡᠭ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ ᠪᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> He used not to come.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Verbal-nominal predicate - Nomen actoris

paragraphs.paragraph: The nomen actoris seldom occurs as a predicate. With finite forms of the verb <uig rom="bol-">ᠪᠣᠯ ᠎</uig> "to become" this expresses the simulation of an action.
<uig rom="umtaqci bolba">ᠤᠮᠲᠠᠬᠴᠢ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠ</uig> He pretended to be asleep.
<uig rom="ese üjegci bolba">ᠡᠰᠡ ᠦᠵᠡᠭᠴᠢ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠ</uig> He pretended not to see.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Converbal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Converbal predicate

paragraphs.paragraph: The converbs serve as predicates of complete sentences only with a copula. Without a copula they cannot act as predicates of complete sentences. All converbs do not act as predicates: only the converbum imperfecti, perfecti, and modale serve as predieates.

The following forms serve as copula : all finite forms of the auxiliary verbs (<uig rom="a-">ᠠ ᠎</uig> "to be," <uig rom="bayi-">ᠪᠠᠶᠢ ᠎</uig> "to be," <uig rom="bol-">ᠪᠣᠯ ᠎</uig> "to become," <uig rom="bui">ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> "is," <uig rom="bülüge">ᠪᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> "was") and all finite forms of descriptive verbs.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Converbal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Converbal predicate - Converbum imperfecti

paragraphs.paragraph: The converbum imperfecti of any verb with a finite form of the auxiliary verbs <uig rom="">ᠠ ᠎</uig> a- "to be," <uig rom="">ᠪᠠᠶᠢ ᠎</uig> bayi- "to be" or the defective verbs <uig rom="bui">ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> "is" and <uig rom="bülüge">ᠪᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> "was" functions in the same manner as the English progressive.
<uig rom="yabuju bui">ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠵᠤ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> He is going.
<uig rom="ungsiju bülüge">ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠵᠤ ᠪᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> He was reading.
<uig rom="yabuju amui">ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠵᠤ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He is walking.
<uig rom="umtaju abai">ᠤᠮᠲᠠᠵᠤ ᠠᠪᠠᠢ</uig> He was sleeping.
<uig rom="ungsiju bayimui">ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠵᠤ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He is reading.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Converbal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Converbal predicate - Converbum imperfecti

paragraphs.paragraph: The imperfect converb with finite forms of the verb <uig rom="bol-">ᠪᠣᠯ ᠎</uig> "to become" expresses actions which can be or are permitted to be performed.
<uig rom="idejü bolumui">ᠢᠳᠡᠵᠦ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> It is possible to eat.
<uig rom="tamaki tataju bolumui">ᠲᠠᠮᠠᠺᠢ ᠲᠠᠲᠠᠵᠤ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠮᠤᠢ</uig> Smoking is allowed.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Converbal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Converbal predicate - Converbum perfecti

paragraphs.paragraph: The perfect converb seldom occurs as a predicate of a complete sentence. With finite forms of the verbs <uig rom="a-">ᠠ ᠎</uig> and <uig rom="bayi-">ᠪᠠᠶᠢ ᠎</uig> "to be" it expresses actions which were begun before the absolute time of the copula and continue to the time of the latter.
<uig rom="yabuγad amui">ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠭᠠᠳ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He is gone. (Lit., "He after having gone he is.")

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Converbal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Converbal predicate - Converbum modale

paragraphs.paragraph: The modal converb with <uig rom="bui">ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> "is" or with finite forms of the verbs <uig rom="bayi-">ᠪᠠᠶᠢ ᠎</uig> and <uig rom="a-">ᠠ ᠎</uig> "to be" expresses continuous actions.
<uig rom="yabun bayimui">ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He is continually walking.
<uig rom="yabun amui">ᠶᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> He is continually walking.
<uig rom="ungsin bui">ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ</uig> He is continually reading.

entry.title: Syntax - Nominal and converbal predicate - Converbal predicate
entry.title2: Nominal and converbal predicate - Converbal predicate - Converbs with descriptive verbs

paragraphs.paragraph: The imperfect or modal converb is used with descriptive verbs (§ 555) to form predicates expressing combined actions. The finite form expresses the general idea of the action, e. g., "He went," and the converb defines this idea and indicates the manner of its realization, e. g., "flying," "jumping," "riding," etc.: this means that the action of going ("He went") was performed not on foot but by flying (not by pacing but by jumping, not by walking but by riding a horse, respectively). On the other hand, the finite form indicates the time and the direction of the flying (or jumping or riding): as the meaning of the finite form ia "He went" the whole group means "He went flying," i. e. "He flew away" or "He flew off" (or "He jumped away" or "He jumped off," "He rode away," respectively). In the same manner the combination "He came flying" expresses the concept that he flew in or he flew in the direction of the person speaking.
As examples of such descriptive verbs the following ones will be given.
a) The verbs <uig rom="ire-">ᠢᠷᠡ ᠎</uig> "to come" and <uig rom="od-">ᠣᠳ ᠎</uig> "to go"
<uig rom="niscü irebe">ᠨᠢᠰᠴᠦ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡ</uig> He flew in. (He came flying.)
<uig rom="niscü odba">ᠨᠢᠰᠴᠦ ᠣᠳᠪᠠ</uig> He flew off. (He went flying.)
b) The verb <uig rom="yabu-">ᠶᠠᠪᠤ ᠎</uig> "to walk":
<uig rom="egürcü yabu-">ᠡᠭᠦᠷᠴᠦ ᠶᠠᠪᠤ ᠎</uig> to carry away (to walk carrying)
c) The verbs <uig rom="oro-">ᠣᠷᠣ ᠎</uig> "to enter" and <uig rom="γar-">ᠭᠠᠷ ᠎</uig> "to walk out, to leave" :
<uig rom="güijü oroba">ᠭᠦᠢᠵᠦ ᠣᠷᠣᠪᠠ</uig> He ran in. (He entered running.)
<uig rom="güijü γaruba">ᠭᠦᠢᠵᠦ ᠭᠠᠷᠤᠪᠠ</uig> He ran out. (He came out running.)
d) The verbs <uig rom="ab-">ᠠᠪ ᠎</uig> "to take" and <uig rom="ög-">ᠥᠭ ᠎</uig> "to give" express an action performed for oneself and for others :
<uig rom="qudalduju abuba">ᠬᠤᠳᠠᠯᠳᠤᠵᠤ ᠠᠪᠤᠪᠠ</uig> He bought. (He took trading.)
<uig rom="bicijü abuba">ᠪᠢᠴᠢᠵᠦ ᠠᠪᠤᠪᠠ</uig> He wrote down for himself. (He took writing.)
<uig rom="qudalduju ögbe">ᠬᠤᠳᠠᠯᠳᠤᠵᠤ ᠥᠭᠪᠡ</uig> He sold. (He gave trading.)
<uig rom="bicijü ögbe">ᠪᠢᠴᠢᠵᠦ ᠥᠭᠪᠡ</uig> He wrote for other people. (He gave writing.)
e) The verb <uig rom="orki-">ᠣᠷᠺᠢ ᠎</uig> "to throw, to cast" as a descriptive copula indicates that the action completely affected the object:
<uig rom="tegün-i alaju orkiba">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠠᠯᠠᠵᠤ ᠣᠷᠺᠢᠪᠠ</uig> He killed him. (He threw killing him.)
<uig rom="jalgiju orkiba">ᠵᠠᠯᠭᠢᠵᠤ ᠣᠷᠺᠢᠪᠠ</uig> He devoured him. (He threw devouring him.)
f) The verbs <uig rom="ekile-">ᠡᠺᠢᠯᠡ ᠎</uig> "to start" and <uig rom="dügür-">ᠳᠦᠭᠦᠷ ᠎</uig> "to finish" indicate the beginning or the end of an action:
<uig rom="angnaju ekilebe">ᠠᠩᠨᠠᠵᠤ ᠡᠺᠢᠯᠡᠪᠡ</uig> He started hunting.
<uig rom="angnaju dügürbe">ᠠᠩᠨᠠᠵᠤ ᠳᠦᠭᠦᠷᠪᠡ</uig> He finished hunting.
g) The verb <uig rom="alda-">ᠠᠯᠳᠠ ᠎</uig> "to be unable to keep" or "to fail" indicates that an action was almost performed, but the subject failed to accomplish it:
<uig rom="unan aldaba">ᠤᠨᠠᠨ ᠠᠯᠳᠠᠪᠠ</uig> He almost fell down.
<uig rom="güicen aldaba">ᠭᠦᠢᠴᠡᠨ ᠠᠯᠳᠠᠪᠠ</uig> He almost overtook him. (He failed overtaking.)

entry.title: Syntax - Predicate of incomplete sentences - General remarks
entry.title2: Predicate of incomplete sentences - General remarks

paragraphs.paragraph: The predicate of juxtaposed incomplete sentences or clauses is a converb: either an imperfect converb (less usual is converbum modale) or a perfect converb without a copula.

entry.title: Syntax - Predicate of incomplete sentences - Converbum imperfecti
entry.title2: Predicate of incomplete sentences - Converbum imperfecti

paragraphs.paragraph: The imperfect converb expresses actions simultaneous with the action of the finite verb.
<uig rom="negüdelcin arad bolbasu mal öskejü negüdel-iyer amiduramui">ᠨᠡᠭᠦᠳᠡᠯᠴᠢᠨ ᠠᠷᠠᠳ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤ ᠮᠠᠯ ᠥᠰᠺᠡᠵᠦ ᠨᠡᠭᠦᠳᠡᠯ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠠᠮᠢᠳᠤᠷᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> The nomads raise cattle and live by transhuming.

<uig rom="ebügen mal-iyan taγuju arban oγotuna egürcü nigen γar-taγan yisün salaγ-a-tu temür uraγa circü irebe">ᠡᠪᠦᠭᠡᠨ ᠮᠠᠯ ᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠲᠠᠭᠤᠵᠤ ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠣᠭᠣᠲᠤᠨᠠ ᠡᠭᠦᠷᠴᠦ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠭᠠᠷ ᠎ᠲᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠶᠢᠰᠦᠨ ᠰᠠᠯᠠᠭ ᠠ ᠎ᠲᠤ ᠲᠡᠮᠦᠷ ᠤᠷᠠᠭᠠ ᠴᠢᠷᠴᠦ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡ</uig> The old man came, driving his cattle and carrying ten oγotuna (Lagomys) and dragging with one hand an iron hook with nine prongs.
See also §372

entry.title: Syntax - Predicate of incomplete sentences - Converbum modale
entry.title2: Predicate of incomplete sentences - Converbum modale

paragraphs.paragraph: The converbum modale expresses an action which is simultaneous with the action of the finite verb and usually merges with the latter to express a single action, although sometimes it expresses an independent action.

<uig rom="tere kümün ber köbegün-i mören-ü jaq-a-dur abcu γajar erüjü oroγulun alabai">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠺᠥᠪᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠮᠥᠷᠡᠨ ᠤ ᠵᠠᠬ ᠠ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠠᠪᠴᠤ ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ ᠡᠷᠦᠵᠦ ᠣᠷᠣᠭᠤᠯᠤᠨ ᠠᠯᠠᠪᠠᠢ</uig> That person took the boy to the river bank, dug the earth, and killed him by interring. (Lit., "and killed him interring.")

<uig rom="bey-e inu ebedcin-iyer enelün künesün-ecegen qaγacaju tabun erketen inu baγuramui">ᠪᠡᠶ ᠡ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠡᠪᠡᠳᠴᠢᠨ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠡᠨᠡᠯᠦᠨ ᠺᠦᠨᠡᠰᠦᠨ ᠡᠴᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠴᠠᠵᠤ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠡᠷᠺᠡᠲᠡᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠪᠠᠭᠤᠷᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> His body being tortured by disease, he refuses food, and his five senses (i. e., eyesight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch) become weak.
See also §373

entry.title: Syntax - Predicate of incomplete sentences - Converbum perfecti
entry.title2: Predicate of incomplete sentences - Converbum perfecti

paragraphs.paragraph: The perfect converb expresses an action which takes place before that of the finite verb and, therefore, may be translated as "after doing . . ."
<uig rom="tegün-i üjeged ecige inu kilinglejü numu sumun-i abubai">ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠦᠵᠡᠭᠡᠳ ᠡᠴᠢᠭᠡ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠺᠢᠯᠢᠩᠯᠡᠵᠦ ᠨᠤᠮᠤ ᠰᠤᠮᠤᠨ ᠢ ᠠᠪᠤᠪᠠᠢ</uig> After seeing him, his father, getting angry, took the bow and arrow.
<uig rom="öndüyiged boscu ülü cidanam">ᠥᠨᠳᠦᠶᠢᠭᠡᠳ ᠪᠣᠰᠴᠤ ᠦᠯᠦ ᠴᠢᠳᠠᠨᠠᠮ</uig> He cannot get up after raising himself.
<uig rom="mal-iyan dergede saγuγad kelebe">ᠮᠠᠯ ᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠳᠡᠷᠭᠡᠳᠡ ᠰᠠᠭᠤᠭᠠᠳ ᠺᠡᠯᠡᠪᠡ</uig> He sat down near his cattle and talked.

<uig rom="teden-i nom-dur oroγuluγad γurban jaγun aqta-yi abuγad qariju irebe">ᠲᠡᠳᠡᠨ ᠢ ᠨᠣᠮ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠣᠷᠣᠭᠤᠯᠤᠭᠠᠳ ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠠᠬᠲᠠ ᠶᠢ ᠠᠪᠤᠭᠠᠳ ᠬᠠᠷᠢᠵᠤ ᠢᠷᠡᠪᠡ</uig> Having converted them to the religion, he took three hundred geldings and returned.
See also §374

entry.title: Syntax - Predicate of incomplete sentences - Converbum perfecti
entry.title2: redicate of incomplete sentences - Converbum perfecti

paragraphs.paragraph: The perfect converb is often followed by the word <uig rom="saca">ᠰᠠᠴᠠ</uig> "as soon as" and in this event it expresses an action which is immediately followed by that of the finite verb.
<uig rom="burqan-dur mörgüged saca tonilba">ᠪᠤᠷᠬᠠᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠮᠥᠷᠭᠦᠭᠡᠳ ᠰᠠᠴᠠ ᠲᠣᠨᠢᠯᠪᠠ</uig> As soon as he bent before Buddha, he was freed (from his sins).
The verbal predicate is a finite verb. In the following sections both the indicative and imperative (optative) forms will be discussed.

The indicative forms express real actions which either were or are or will be performed. There are several indicative forms expressing the present tense. On the other hand, there are several forms expressing the past. But there are no special forms expressing the future. The latter is expressed by the present form.

As for the various present or past forms, there is no difference between the time of one present form and that of another. In the same manner, there is no great difference between the time of one past form and that of another. The difference is not in time (i. e., actions which took place long ago or recently) but in the subjective attitude of the person speaking toward the action: actions which, from his point of view, are doubtless facts or actions about which he cannot say anything definite. Thus there is no temporal difference between various present (or past) forms, but only a difference of the point of view of the person speaking and the latter's subjective attitude.

In English we use in such cases supplementary expressions such as "as a matter of fact," "of course," "possibly," "certainly," and so on. In Mongolian some of these nuances are inherent in the verbal form.
The present form ending in <uig rom="-mui/ -müi">ᠮᠤᠢ</uig> or <uig rom="-nam/-nem">ᠨᠠᠮ</uig> expresses an action which is present or customary or future.
<uig rom="nigen ekener jimis tegümüi">ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠡᠺᠡᠨᠡᠷ ᠵᠢᠮᠢᠰ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠮᠦᠢ</uig> A woman is picking berries (now).
<uig rom="negüdelcin arad negüdel-iyer amiduramui">ᠨᠡᠭᠦᠳᠡᠯᠴᠢᠨ ᠠᠷᠠᠳ ᠨᠡᠭᠦᠳᠡᠯ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠠᠮᠢᠳᠤᠷᠠᠮᠤᠢ</uig> The nomads live by transhumance (usually or always).
<uig rom="γobi-yin amitan quduγ-un usun-dur itegemüi">ᠭᠣᠪᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠠᠮᠢᠲᠠᠨ ᠬᠤᠳᠤᠭ ᠤᠨ ᠤᠰᠤᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠢᠲᠡᠭᠡᠮᠦᠢ</uig> The living beings of the Gobi depend upon the water of wells (usually or always).
<uig rom="manu baqsi marγasi iremüi">ᠮᠠᠨᠤ ᠪᠠᠬᠰᠢ ᠮᠠᠷᠭᠠᠰᠢ ᠢᠷᠡᠮᠦᠢ</uig> Our teacher will come to-morrow (future).
See also §347

The other present form ends in <uig rom="-yu/-yü">ᠶᠤ</uig> . This, too, expresses an action which is present or customary or future. The difference between this form and the form in <uig rom="-mui"> ᠎ᠮᠤᠢ</uig> (<uig rom="-nam">᠎ᠨᠠᠮ</uig> ) is that the latter is a mere statement of fact ("he comes," "he will come," and so on) while the form ending in -yu expresses an action which is a logical conclusion of the previous context.

<uig rom="mergen inu ucir siltaγan bügüde-yi medemüi. teneg inu ülü medejü osolduyu">ᠮᠡᠷᠭᠡᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠤᠴᠢᠷ ᠰᠢᠯᠲᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠪᠦᠭᠦᠳᠡ ᠶᠢ ᠮᠡᠳᠡᠮᠦᠢ᠅ ᠲᠡᠨᠡᠭ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠦᠯᠦ ᠮᠡᠳᠡᠵᠦ ᠣᠰᠣᠯᠳᠤᠶᠤ</uig> The sage knows all circumstances and causes. The fool, not knowing, consequently makes mistakes.

<uig rom="qar-a noqai inu bügeljisün-i idemüi. arsalang inu görüged-ün qayan bolqu tula teyimü busu buyu">ᠬᠠᠷ ᠠ ᠨᠣᠬᠠᠢ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠯᠵᠢᠰᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠢᠳᠡᠮᠦᠢ᠅ ᠠᠷᠰᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠭᠥᠷᠦᠭᠡᠳ ᠤᠨ ᠬᠠᠶᠠᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠬᠤ ᠲᠤᠯᠠ ᠲᠡᠶᠢᠮᠦ ᠪᠤᠰᠤ ᠪᠤᠶᠤ</uig> The ordinary (lit., "black") dog eats vomit. The lion, because he is the king of animals, consequently is not so.
Usually the form in <uig rom="-yu"> ᠎ᠶᠤ</uig> expresses an action which may be considered the opposite of a previous action.

<uig rom="jirγalang-un siltaγan inu buyan bui. kilince-ece jobalang anu töröyü">ᠵᠢᠷᠭᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠤᠨ ᠰᠢᠯᠲᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠪᠤᠶᠠᠨ ᠪᠤᠢ᠅ ᠺᠢᠯᠢᠨᠴᠡ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠵᠣᠪᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠲᠥᠷᠥᠶᠦ</uig> The cause of happiness is virtue, (whereas) suffering issues from sin.
See also §349
There are three past forms. They end in <uig rom="-ba"> ᠎ᠪᠠ</uig> or <uig rom="-bai">᠎ᠪᠠᠢ</uig>, <uig rom="-luγa"> ᠎ᠯᠤᠭᠠ</uig> , and <uig rom="-juqui"> ᠎ᠵᠤᠬᠤᠢ</uig> .

The past form ending in <uig rom="-ba/-bai"> ᠎ᠪᠠ/᠎ᠪᠠᠢ</uig> is used with reference to all persons and expresses an action completed in the past. Such an action is considered a mere statement without any particular nuance.
<uig rom="qoyar kümün bayising dotor-a orobai">ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠰᠢᠩ ᠳᠣᠲᠣᠷ ᠠ ᠣᠷᠣᠪᠠᠢ</uig> Two persons entered the house.

<uig rom="duu-a soqor-un köbegüd anu oyirad-un ögeled baγatud qoyid kergüd dörben oboqtan bolbai">ᠳᠤᠤ ᠠ ᠰᠣᠬᠣᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠺᠥᠪᠡᠭᠦᠳ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠣᠶᠢᠷᠠᠳ ᠤᠨ ᠥᠭᠡᠯᠡᠳ ᠪᠠᠭᠠᠲᠤᠳ ᠬᠣᠶᠢᠳ ᠺᠡᠷᠭᠦᠳ ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ ᠣᠪᠣᠬᠲᠠᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠢ</uig> The sons of Duua Sokhor became ancestors of the four tribes Ogeled, Baghatud, Khoyid, and Kergud of the Oirats.

<uig rom="dörben aq-a-nar-taγan aγurlaju onon mören ögede γaγcaγar yorcibai">ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ ᠠᠬ ᠠ ᠎ᠨᠠᠷ ᠎ᠲᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠠᠭᠤᠷᠯᠠᠵᠤ ᠣᠨᠣᠨ ᠮᠥᠷᠡᠨ ᠥᠭᠡᠳᠡ ᠭᠠᠬᠴᠠᠭᠠᠷ ᠶᠣᠷᠴᠢᠪᠠᠢ</uig> He became angry with his four brothers and went upstream along the Onon River.
<uig rom="jiγasun sungγun dalai-yin iruγar odbai">ᠵᠢᠭᠠᠰᠤᠨ ᠰᠤᠩᠭᠤᠨ ᠳᠠᠯᠠᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠢᠷᠤᠭᠠᠷ ᠣᠳᠪᠠᠢ</uig> The fish dived and went to the bottom of the sea.
The past form ending in <uig rom="-ba"> ᠎ᠪᠠ</uig> (but never in <uig rom=" -bai"> ᠎ᠪᠠᠢ</uig>) is sometimes used as a concessive converb.
<uig rom="ükübe yaba jayaγan minu medetügei">ᠦᠺᠦᠪᠡ ᠶᠠᠪᠠ ᠵᠠᠶᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠮᠡᠳᠡᠲᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> Whether I shall die or what will happen (to me) my destiny must know!

The past form ending in <uig rom=" -luγa"> ᠎ᠯᠤᠭᠠ</uig> expresses an action of a little longer duration than that expressed by the form ending in <uig rom="-ba"> ᠎ᠪᠠ</uig> (or <uig rom="-bai"> ᠎ᠪᠠᠢ</uig> ) and is considered a fact well known to everyone or witnessed by someone and, therefore, beyond doubt. This form is less common in Modern Mongolian. Sometimes it expresses an action which almost took place or which did not take place at all but the completion of which in the near future is considered so probable that it may be considered as completed in the past.
<uig rom="qalaγ qoqoi tere maγu inu namayi alaluγa">ᠬᠠᠯᠠᠭ ᠬᠣᠬᠣᠢ ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠮᠠᠭᠤ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠨᠠᠮᠠᠶᠢ ᠠᠯᠠᠯᠤᠭᠠ</uig> Alas, that evil person killed me !
<uig rom="γucin baγatur anu ükülüge">ᠭᠤᠴᠢᠨ ᠪᠠᠭᠠᠲᠤᠷ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠦᠺᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡ</uig> His thirty heroes died.
<uig rom="ci tegün-i ese üjelüü">ᠴᠢ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠡᠰᠡ ᠦᠵᠡᠯᠦᠦ</uig> Did not you see him?

The past form in <uig rom="-juqui"> ᠎ᠵᠤᠬᠤᠢ</uig> expresses completed, but unexpected actions. Such actions took place long before all the other actions of the context and the person speaking is somewhat surprised when discovering this. This form is not used with reference to the first person of the singular or plural.
<uig rom="ger dotor-a-aca tabiγad cerig γarcuqui">ᠭᠡᠷ ᠳᠣᠲᠣᠷ ᠠ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠲᠠᠪᠢᠭᠠᠳ ᠴᠡᠷᠢᠭ ᠭᠠᠷᠴᠤᠬᠤᠢ</uig> About fifty soldiers had come out of the house.

<uig rom="tere bide-yin ulus qotalaγar jöbsiyeldün ene ber ijaγurtan-u köbegün ajuγu kemeldüged">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠪᠢᠳᠡ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠤᠯᠤᠰ ᠬᠣᠲᠠᠯᠠᠭᠠᠷ ᠵᠥᠪᠰᠢᠶᠡᠯᠳᠦᠨ ᠡᠨᠡ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠢᠵᠠᠭᠤᠷᠲᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠺᠥᠪᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠠᠵᠤᠭᠤ ᠺᠡᠮᠡᠯᠳᠦᠭᠡᠳ</uig> That people of the Bide said, while discussing it in its entity, that he turned out to be a scion of noblemen.

<uig rom="erte urida enedkeg-ün emün-e eteged nigen γajar-tur er-e em-e qoyar aqsan ajuγu">ᠡᠷᠲᠡ ᠤᠷᠢᠳᠠ ᠡᠨᠡᠳᠺᠡᠭ ᠤᠨ ᠡᠮᠦᠨ ᠡ ᠡᠲᠡᠭᠡᠳ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ ᠲᠤᠷ ᠡᠷ ᠡ ᠡᠮ ᠡ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ ᠠᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠠᠵᠤᠭᠤ</uig> Formerly there were in a country south of India a man and a woman.

The imperative and all other related forms such as the voluntative, optative, and so on, express actions which, in reality, do not take place. Whereas the indicative forms express actions which either take place in the present or have taken place in the past and are assertions of such actions as real happenings, the imperative forms express actions which are to be performed by persons so ordered. In the same manner, the optative forms express actions which do not take place, but are considered desirable.
The imperative of the second person expresses an order to perform an action. This is the shortest form of the verb and has no ending.
<uig rom="ci ende saγu">ᠴᠢ ᠡᠨᠳᠡ ᠰᠠᠭᠤ</uig> Sit down here !

The Mongolian imperative sentence usually has a subject which here is the person addressed by the speaker. In Latin or in other European languages imperative sentences usually do not have any syntactic subject as the idea of the person acting is inherent in the imperative.

The benedictive also is an imperative form, but this does not express an order but rather a polite request. This form is used with reference to a single person, who cannot be addressed with the pronoun "thou," and also with reference to a group of persons.
<uig rom="manu ger-tür oroqtun">ᠮᠠᠨᠤ ᠭᠡᠷ ᠲᠤᠷ ᠣᠷᠣᠬᠲᠤᠨ</uig> Please enter our house !

The imperative of the third person expresses an order to perform an action, with reference to an absent person: there is a speaker and a listener but the real performer of the action may be absent and is supposed to learn about the order of the person speaking through the listener. This form is used in both singular and plural.
<uig rom="tere kümün iretügei">ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠢᠷᠡᠲᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> Let that person come! (or "That person must come!", or "That person may come!")

The voluntative expresses the wish to perform the action concerned. The voluntative of the first person of the singular expresses the wish of the speaker to act and may be translated as "I want to . . .," "let me. . ." or "I will . . ."
<uig rom="bi odsuγai">ᠪᠢ ᠣᠳᠰᠤᠭᠠᠢ</uig> I will go !
The voluntative of the first person of the plural denotes a wish expressed by several persons, although sometimes this is used instead of the optative of the first person of the singular.
<uig rom="edüge bida ger-tegen qariy-a">ᠡᠳᠦᠭᠡ ᠪᠢᠳᠠ ᠭᠡᠷ ᠎ᠲᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠬᠠᠷᠢᠶ ᠠ</uig> Now let us return home !
The optative of all persons expresses a wish expressed by someone. Usually this form expresses a futile desire which will never be fulfilled and, therefore, has a shade of sadness.
<uig rom="bi tegün-i üjegesei">ᠪᠢ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠦᠵᠡᠭᠡᠰᠡᠢ</uig> Ah, if I could see him !
The dubitative expresses the idea of fear that the action concerned may, contrary to all expectations, take place. This form is used with reference to all persons.
<uig rom="yeke süid boluγujai">ᠶᠡᠺᠡ ᠰᠦᠢᠳ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠭᠤᠵᠠᠢ</uig> A great disaster may occur!, Lot a great disaster not occur!
The imperative, voluntative, and optative forms are used with the prohibitive particle <uig rom="buu">ᠪᠤᠤ</uig> , sometimes with the colloquial <uig rom="bitegei">ᠪᠢᠲᠡᠭᠡᠢ</uig> .
<uig rom="buu ire">ᠪᠤᠤ ᠢᠷᠡ</uig> Do not come !
<uig rom="buu odsuγai">ᠪᠤᠤ ᠣᠳᠰᠤᠭᠠᠢ</uig> I will not go !
<uig rom="buu iretügei">ᠪᠤᠤ ᠢᠷᠡᠲᠦᠭᠡᠢ</uig> He must not come !
In Written Mongolian there are the following voices or genera verbi: the active, factitive, passive, reciprocal, and co-operative.

The subject of an active verb is the person acting. This means that the action is performed by the subject while, for example, the subject of a passive verb does not perform any actions, but undergoes the action of another person.

Active verbs can, for example, be a predicate. Such sentences do not always have a grammatical subject. The latter may be missing when the person acting is mentioned in the previous context and, therefore, is known.

In Written Mongolian, active verbs may also replace passive verbs. For instance, the perfect noun (nomen perfecti) of the verb <uig rom="ükü-">ᠦᠺᠦ ᠎</uig> "to die," <uig rom="ükügsen">ᠦᠺᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ</uig> "dead," may never function as a passive verb, but the same verbal noun of the verb <uig rom="ungsi-">ᠤᠩᠰᠢ ᠎</uig> "to read" may so function: e. g., <uig rom="ungsiγsan kümün">ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> is "a person who read" and <uig rom="ungsiγsan nom">ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠨᠣᠮ</uig> is "a book which was read." It is obvious that the active or passive function of such verbs results only from the meaning of the noun which it qualifies : a person cannot be read and, therefore, <uig rom="ungsiγsan kümün">ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> cannot be understood as "a person who was read ;" on the other hand, a book cannot read and, therefore, <uig rom="ungsiγsan nom ">ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠨᠣᠮ</uig> cannot be understood as "a book which read." It is obvious that the active voice acts as passive only in cases in which the grammatical subject by its nature cannot perform but can only undergo a certain action.

Therefore, active verbs never have a passive function, when the sentence contains only one word which, under various circumstances, can function both as an actor and a passive object of someone's action. Thus <uig rom="alaγsan kümün">ᠠᠯᠠᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> can, in this construction, mean only "a person who killed" (i. e., "killer") and cannot be understood as "a killed person." But if the same construction is enlarged by another word expressing something which, under various circumstances, can function both as actor and object of someone's action, the sense of the construction changes and the verb acquires a passive function. The additional word is always, in such constructions, a genitive of any declinable part of speech. Thus the construction <uig rom="dayisun-u alaγsan kümün">ᠳᠠᠶᠢᠰᠤᠨ ᠤ ᠠᠯᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> means "a person killed by the enemy" (lit., "the enemy's killed person"). The same passive function is also found in the construction <uig rom="noqai-yin idegsen miqan">ᠨᠣᠬᠠᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠢᠳᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠮᠢᠬᠠᠨ</uig> "the meat eaten by the dog" (lit., "the dog's eaten meat"). It may be added that in Written Mongolian in such cases, it is always the active voice that is used and never the passive.
The general rule is, that verbal nouns of active verbs, serving as attributes and preceded by a genitive, always have the function of a passive voice.
<uig rom="cinu-a-yin idegsen qonin">ᠴᠢᠨᠤ ᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠢᠳᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠬᠣᠨᠢᠨ</uig> a sheep eaten by the wolf
<uig rom="šabi-yin ungsiγsan nom">ᠱᠠᠪᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠤᠩᠰᠢᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠨᠣᠮ</uig> a book read by the pupil
<uig rom="manu saγuγsan ger">ᠮᠠᠨᠤ ᠰᠠᠭᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠭᠡᠷ</uig> the house inhabited by us
<uig rom="baγsi-yin oluγsan nom">ᠪᠠᠭᠰᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠣᠯᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠨᠣᠮ</uig> the book found by the teacher

On the other hand, the same constructions with verbs expressing actions which cannot be undertaken by anybody never have a passive meaning, e. g., <uig rom="minu ükügsen ekener">ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠦᠺᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠡᠺᠡᠨᠡᠷ</uig> "my wife, who died."

Is should be pointed out that this has nothing to do with the transitiveness or intransitiveness of the verbs concerned, because even intransitive verbs, which have no direct object, can function as passive verbs, e. g., <uig rom="minu kebtegsen γajar">ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠺᠡᠪᠲᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ</uig> "the place in which I was lying": it is not "the place which was lying" but "the place in which I was lying."
This explains why the terms transitive and intransitive have not been used in this section.

The grammatical subject of a passive verb is, from the logical point of view, not the subject but the object of someone's action. The person really acting is not the grammatical subject, from the logical point of view. Thus in passive sentences the logical and syntactical categories do not coincide.
The logical subject of a passive sentence is a dative-locative, the datives actoris.
<uig rom="qonin cinu-a-dur bariγdaba">ᠬᠣᠨᠢᠨ ᠴᠢᠨᠤ ᠠ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠪᠠᠷᠢᠭᠳᠠᠪᠠ</uig> The sheep was caught by the wolf.

The passive voice is used relatively rarely and, as remarked above, in many cases the idea of a passive action is expressed by the active voice. This take., place primarily in attributive constructions. In the latter, the verba. noun is in an active form and the logical subject is in the genitive. The verbal noun may also be in a passive form and, as remarked above, the logical subject in such cases is a dative-locative. Thus the following constructions, being absolutely different from the syntactical point of view are, nevertheless, equivalent from the point of view of their sense and, therefore, interchangeable :
<uig rom="noqai-dur idegdegsen miqan">ᠨᠣᠬᠠᠢ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠢᠳᠡᠭᠳᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠮᠢᠬᠠᠨ</uig> the meat eaten by the dog = <uig rom="noqai-yin idegsen miqan">ᠨᠣᠬᠠᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠢᠳᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠮᠢᠬᠠᠨ</uig>
<uig rom="dayisun-dur alaqdaqsan kümün">ᠳᠠᠶᠢᠰᠤᠨ ᠳ᠋ᠤᠷ ᠠᠯᠠᠬᠳᠠᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> a person killed by the enemy = <uig rom="dayisun-u alaqsan kümün">ᠳᠠᠶᠢᠰᠤᠨ ᠤ ᠠᠯᠠᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig>

It should be pointed out that the construction <uig rom="noqai-yin idegsen miqan">ᠨᠣᠬᠠᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠢᠳᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠮᠢᠬᠠᠨ</uig> cannot be understood as "dog meat which was eaten" (by someone), because this requires a different word order: <uig rom="idegsen noqai-yin miqan">ᠢᠳᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠨᠣᠬᠠᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠢᠬᠠᠨ</uig>. As remarked above, instead of the passive voice, the active voice may be employed in attributive constructions. This is not so, however, in predicative constructions. The predicate is always a passive verb, if the action concerned is a passive one. Thus the construction <uig rom="cinu-a bariγdaba">ᠴᠢᠨᠤ ᠠ ᠪᠠᠷᠢᠭᠳᠠᠪᠠ</uig> "The wolf was caught," cannot be replaced by anything else.

It is commonly known that in English the passive voice is also used in such sentences as "I was told" or "He was given a book" which are impossible in Latin, French, German, and many other languages. In Written Mongolian there occur constructions resembling such English expressions. They are used primarily in attributive constructions, e. g., <uig rom="">ᠭᠠᠷ</uig> γar oqtaluqdaqsan kümün "a person whose hand was cut off" or "a person cut in respect of his hand." In this construction the verbal noun <uig rom="oγtaluγdaγsan">ᠣᠬᠲᠠᠯᠤᠬᠳᠠᠬᠰᠠᠨ</uig> "cut" is an attribute of <uig rom="kümün">ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> "person" and literally this means "a person who was cut." This may be illustrated better by the following English sentences : "I was amputated my legs," "I was made a surgical operation." Although in common English speech such sentences are impossible, they do not differ much from "I was told a very sad story" or "The pupil was given a new book." Thus the Mongolian sentence given above may be literally translated as "a person who was cut his hand off." In such Mongolian expressions the verbal noun is usually a passive verb. Yet, in a few rare cases, the verbal noun may be an active verb, although the latter would mean that the man himself cut off his hand. To avoid misunderstandings, in such cases the Mongols use the reflexive-possessive suffix or the genitive of the personal pronoun of the third person <uig rom="inu">ᠢᠨᠤ</uig> : <uig rom="γar-iyan oγtaluγdaγsan kümün">ᠭᠠᠷ ᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠣᠭᠲᠠᠯᠤᠭᠳᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> "a person who cut off his own hand" and <uig rom="γar inu oγtaluγdaγsan kümün">ᠭᠠᠷ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠣᠭᠲᠠᠯᠤᠭᠳᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> "a person whose hand was cut off" In the latter construction the word inu indieates that the person performing the cutting (although the person acting is not expressed grammatically) did not cut his own hand (suus), but his (ejus) hand, whereas in the first construction the person performing the action had his own hand as object.
<uig rom="ed abtaγsan (passive) kümün">ᠡᠳ ᠠᠪᠲᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> a person whose property was taken away (lit., "a property taken person")
<uig rom="ed inu quriyan abuγsan kümün">ᠡᠳ ᠢᠨᠤ ᠬᠤᠷᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠠᠪᠤᠬᠰᠠᠨ ᠺᠦᠮᠦᠨ</uig> a person whose property was confiscated (lit., "a person confiscated in respect of his property")
